Cazuza era atitude pura. Hoje as pessoas têm medo de dizer o que pensam, com medo de cancelamento. Mas é isso que faz você sair da curva. É isso que falta: coragem.
title: Read the next generation or die — and Gen Z lacks the patience and courage his generation had

text: **When the physical channel dies, digital is oxygen, not a backup plan.** His central crisis-leadership idea, forged in the pandemic: *"Na hora em que todas as lojas são fechadas, o único oxigênio que você tem é um site."* See Mental models for the full worked example. (Mercado&Consumo, ago/2021)
quotes: Na hora em que todas as lojas são fechadas, o único oxigênio que você tem é um site.
title: When the physical channel dies, digital is oxygen, not a backup plan

text: **"Gestor de marca, ponto." (Brand-manager-only positioning.)** Pick the single highest-leverage link in your value chain and shed the rest. Worked example: he sold all ~130 owned stores and pushed manufacturing to China, keeping brand + design + IP only — and the franchised stores then out-earned his owned ones by 30%. The test: which link, if you let go of it, would let others run it *better* than you? *"Eu vendi 100% das minhas lojas. Hoje... elas faturam 30% mais."* (Money Times; Seu Dinheiro)
quotes: Gestor de marca, ponto.
Eu vendi 100% das minhas lojas. Hoje... elas faturam 30% mais.
title: "Gestor de marca, ponto." (Brand-manager-only positioning.)

text: **"Foco de loja" — don't mix channels, license instead.** A named companion rule to "gestor de marca": when entering an adjacent category, keep it out of the core retail footprint so the store doesn't lose its identity. Worked example: launching Chilli Beans-branded sneakers (2025) purely as a **licensing deal with Ramarim** (RS), sold only through the footwear channel, not through Chilli Beans stores — *"Está aí o segredo: se você começar a misturar muito, você perde o foco da loja... [Será segmentado] no canal de calçados."* Same logic applied to the ChilliDrinks beverage line and a pepper-sauce partnership with Knorr (2024): licensed-out categories, not shelf space inside the optical stores. (O Tempo, set/2025)
quotes: Foco de loja
gestor de marca
Está aí o segredo: se você começar a misturar muito, você perde o foco da loja... [Será segmentado] no canal de calçados.
title: "Foco de loja" — don't mix channels, license instead

text: **Story-first product design.** Don't design a product and market it; design the *story* and let the product carry it — *"A gente conta histórias em tudo o que a gente vende. A gente entende que contar a história do produto faz toda a diferença."* Worked example: the Harry Potter line (five years running, every design J.K. Rowling-approved) and an opportunistic tie-in with the telenovela *Vale Tudo* — while promoting an Ivete Sangalo collection, his team "bateu na porta da TV Globo" [knocked on Globo's door] and got product written into a plot with 50 million viewers per episode: *"Tem coisas que Deus coloca tudo na hora certa: Ivete Sangalo, uma novela, Chilli Beans, moda, óculos... Tem tudo a ver!"* (ABF; Money Times; Forbes Brasil 2022; O Tempo, set/2025)
quotes: A gente conta histórias em tudo o que a gente vende. A gente entende que contar a história do produto faz toda a diferença.
bateu na porta da TV Globo
Tem coisas que Deus coloca tudo na hora certa: Ivete Sangalo, uma novela, Chilli Beans, moda, óculos... Tem tudo a ver!
title: Story-first product design

text: **Rejuvenate an old, sleepy category.** The opportunity isn't always a new product — it's a tired one re-dressed. Worked example: *"Há 25 anos eu comecei a vender óculos escuros, só que pus uma roupagem diferente, um mix de produtos diferentes, vendedores diferentes, marca diferente, de um produto que já se vendia há cem anos. Ainda existem oportunidades em setores antigos e velhos que você pode rejuvenescer."* (Agência Sebrae)
quotes: Há 25 anos eu comecei a vender óculos escuros, só que pus uma roupagem diferente, um mix de produtos diferentes, vendedores diferentes, marca diferente, de um produto que já se vendia há cem anos. Ainda existem oportunidades em setores antigos e velhos que você pode rejuvenescer.
title: Rejuvenate an old, sleepy category

text: **Licensing as borrowed equity.** Rent the cultural capital of an existing IP so a drop launches with an audience already attached. Worked example: the steady cadence of Disney/Marvel/NBA/Beatles/Anitta drops — each one borrowing a fan base — is how a sunglasses SKU arrives "pre-sold." Worked example, from his own reasoning about musicians-as-brands: David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust persona became a licensable logo; Caito treats collaborators the same way — as pre-built fan bases to rent. (ABF; LinkedIn Pulse)
title: Licensing as borrowed equity

text: **"Oxigenação da rede." (Network refresh as maintenance, not crisis.)** Treat the franchise base like a living system that needs continuous oxygen: replace disengaged operators, remodel tired stores, close the distance between owner and floor. Worked example: *"Percebo que o dono está muito longe da realidade... Quando você corta essa distância, as coisas começam a acontecer."* A related, distinct operational lever from the same 2025 push: a network-wide switch to a **5×2 work schedule**, credited with concrete HR outcomes — *"Os franqueados receberam muito bem a nova escala, a retenção aumentou e os currículos que chegam têm uma qualidade muito melhor."* (Jornal do Comércio; ABF Pinga Fogo, out/2025) — note: at the same ABF panel, Tom Moreira Leite (China in Box/Grupo Trigo) used the identical verb "oxigenar a rede" for his own company, suggesting the term may be shared franchising-industry jargon rather than something Caito personally coined.
quotes: Oxigenação da rede.
Percebo que o dono está muito longe da realidade... Quando você corta essa distância, as coisas começam a acontecer.
Os franqueados receberam muito bem a nova escala, a retenção aumentou e os currículos que chegam têm uma qualidade muito melhor.
oxigenar a rede
title: "Oxigenação da rede." (Network refresh as maintenance, not crisis.)

text: **"O único oxigênio que você tem é um site." (Crisis reframing: digital isn't Plan B, it's survival.)** When the physical channel is severed, treat the remaining digital channel as the organism's entire oxygen supply and pour resources into it immediately. Worked example — the fullest crisis narrative in the corpus: on March 17, 2020, 917 stores closed "abruptly"; the website — 5% of sales before the pandemic — was pushed to 18% of sales as physical stores stayed dark, and total e-commerce grew 134% while physical-store sales still grew 10% over 2019 once reopened. The mechanism wasn't just ad spend: a 3D virtual try-on tool was built from scratch because *"as pessoas estavam em casa e tinham medo de comprar óculos escuros"* [people were home and afraid to buy sunglasses (without trying them on)] — click a pair and it renders live on your face, in proportion, matched to skin/hair tone. Franchisees' 798 Instagram pages (already running for years) were converted into a hyperlocal e-commerce network with 2-hour delivery — *"Isso era um projeto que a gente já estava exercitando, mas que foi antecipado de dois anos para dois meses e a coisa funcionou."* [That was a project we were already working on, but it got moved up from two years to two months, and it worked.] (Mercado&Consumo, ago/2021)
quotes: O único oxigênio que você tem é um site.
as pessoas estavam em casa e tinham medo de comprar óculos escuros
Isso era um projeto que a gente já estava exercitando, mas que foi antecipado de dois anos para dois meses e a coisa funcionou.
title: "O único oxigênio que você tem é um site." (Crisis reframing: digital isn't Plan B, it's survival.)

text: **"Visão de Empreendedor" — a named 3-step method, distilled into his first paid course.** After 30 years of "building a brand, making mistakes, course-correcting, deciding amid chaos" ("Eu nunca ensinei isso antes"), he names the method explicitly: *"#01 Entender o que realmente está sustentando o caixa... #02 Crescer o time de forma orgânica e otimizar processos antes de escalar... #03 Planejar com identidade. Ninguém quer a cópia da cópia e o consumidor percebe."* [#01 Understand what's actually sustaining cash flow. #02 Grow the team organically and optimize processes before scaling. #03 Plan with identity — nobody wants a copy of a copy, and the customer notices.] The pattern echoes his own repeated advice against premature scaling and against losing brand identity while expanding. (LinkedIn, 2026)

building a brand, making mistakes, course-correcting, deciding amid chaos
Eu nunca ensinei isso antes

#01 Entender o que realmente está sustentando o caixa... #02 Crescer o time de forma orgânica e otimizar processos antes de escalar... #03 Planejar com identidade. Ninguém quer a cópia da cópia e o consumidor percebe.
title: "Visão de Empreendedor" — a named 3-step method, distilled into his first paid course

text: **The franchisee due-diligence test (two questions).** Advice to anyone buying *any* franchise: (1) *"pergunte para o franqueador se ele consegue te colocar em contato com o franqueado dele. Se ele não conseguir oferecer cinco números de telefone, já indica que tem algo de errado."* (2) *"converse com o franqueado e entenda a realidade dele. Pergunte como está o estoque... essa é uma pergunta importantíssima."* A rare buyer's-side checklist. Chilli Beans's own internal counterpart — cited by the same event's coverage but as paraphrase, not his direct words — is an AI tool that "montra o pedido para o franqueado" [assembles the franchisee's restock order] to smooth inventory swings; the Forbes US profile independently corroborates an inventory-AI initiative with a concrete claimed result: "a 20% sales increase and a reduction in inventory levels from three months to just two weeks." (Money Times; Forbes US, set/2024)
quotes: pergunte para o franqueador se ele consegue te colocar em contato com o franqueado dele. Se ele não conseguir oferecer cinco números de telefone, já indica que tem algo de errado.
converse com o franqueado e entenda a realidade dele. Pergunte como está o estoque... essa é uma pergunta importantíssima.
montra o pedido para o franqueado
a 20% sales increase and a reduction in inventory levels from three months to just two weeks.
title: The franchisee due-diligence test (two questions)

text: **Circle of control vs. circle of worry.** Don't spend energy on what you can't touch. Worked example: *"Coisas que eu não posso pôr a mão, governo, tarifaço, eu não ponho energia. Mas as coisas que eu posso pôr a mão, que estão ao meu alcance, eu não abro mão."* (Exame, NEEX 2025)
quotes: Coisas que eu não posso pôr a mão, governo, tarifaço, eu não ponho energia. Mas as coisas que eu posso pôr a mão, que estão ao meu alcance, eu não abro mão.
title: Circle of control vs. circle of worry

text: **Hire for the "brilho no olho."** Worked example, applied to both employees and Shark Tank founders: *"Eu não vejo o que a pessoa tem de diferente, como raça ou religião, eu vejo o brilho no olho. O olho é a parte que me pega, porque ele transmite o propósito de cada pessoa."* His own LinkedIn "Experience" entry for the Shark Tank role restates the same filter, now explicitly counter-posed to spreadsheet valuation: *"Investir, incentivar, acreditar em pessoas e no amor que elas têm por seus negócios é mais rentável do que a avaliação exclusivamente numérica. E o brilho nos olhos às vezes fala mais alto que o balanço financeiro."* (Exame, "brilho no olho"; LinkedIn Experience section)
quotes: brilho no olho.
Eu não vejo o que a pessoa tem de diferente, como raça ou religião, eu vejo o brilho no olho. O olho é a parte que me pega, porque ele transmite o propósito de cada pessoa.

Investir, incentivar, acreditar em pessoas e no amor que elas têm por seus negócios é mais rentável do que a avaliação exclusivamente numérica. E o brilho nos olhos às vezes fala mais alto que o balanço financeiro.
brilho no olho
title: Hire for the "brilho no olho."

text: **Smart money is experience, not cash.** Worked example, from six years investing on Shark Tank, with a concrete season result attached: *"Muita gente fala que está atrás de smart money, mas muitas vezes nem sabe o que é isso. No smart money você não pega dinheiro, você pega a experiência daquela pessoa, que vale mais do que o dinheiro. Nesta temporada dois caras entraram pedindo R$ 1 e saíram com quase R$ 1 milhão."* (ISTOÉ Dinheiro, jul/2024)
quotes: Muita gente fala que está atrás de smart money, mas muitas vezes nem sabe o que é isso. No smart money você não pega dinheiro, você pega a experiência daquela pessoa, que vale mais do que o dinheiro. Nesta temporada dois caras entraram pedindo R$ 1 e saíram com quase R$ 1 milhão.
title: Smart money is experience, not cash

text: **Get into the game instead of theorizing ("empreendedorismo de palco" vs. real execution).** Named critique of a school of founder behavior: performing entrepreneurship on stage while disconnected from the team, versus his prescribed cure of *"ir para o jogo — acertando, errando e fazendo as coisas acontecerem na vida real."* Worked example: he frames his own 1997 suitcase-and-cart launch and the ~30-year run since as proof of learning by doing rather than by theory. A LinkedIn post makes the same case with a fresher, more tactical framing: *"O mercado não está nem aí para o quanto você trabalhou no seu projeto. Ele só responde a uma coisa: valor... Você não descobre se uma ideia é boa dentro da empresa. Você descobre quando coloca ela na frente de clientes reais. Foi assim que construí a Chilli Beans."* (Amazon/Editora Gente synopsis; LinkedIn, 2026)
quotes: empreendedorismo de palco
ir para o jogo — acertando, errando e fazendo as coisas acontecerem na vida real.

O mercado não está nem aí para o quanto você trabalhou no seu projeto. Ele só responde a uma coisa: valor... Você não descobre se uma ideia é boa dentro da empresa. Você descobre quando coloca ela na frente de clientes reais. Foi assim que construí a Chilli Beans.
title: Get into the game instead of theorizing ("empreendedorismo de palco" vs. real execution)

text: **Own the brand, rent everything else.** Default to outsourcing unless it's the brand/IP itself. (Money Times)
title: Own the brand, rent everything else

text: **If it has no story, don't launch it** — because then you'd compete on price, which he refuses. (Consumidor Moderno; Money Times)
title: If it has no story, don't launch it

text: **Earn your irreverence first.** Don't do the *gracinhas* until the *arroz com feijão* is solid. (Consumidor Moderno)
title: Earn your irreverence first

text: **Pick focus and pay the opportunity cost.** He killed the music dream to go all-in: *"O Brasil perdeu Las Ticas Tienen Fuego, mas ganhou coisa muito melhor."* And: *"Quando você acha o seu lugar na cadeia, o que você ama, tem paixão, ninguém te segura."* (Museu da Pessoa; Agência Sebrae)
quotes: O Brasil perdeu Las Ticas Tienen Fuego, mas ganhou coisa muito melhor.
Quando você acha o seu lugar na cadeia, o que você ama, tem paixão, ninguém te segura.
title: Pick focus and pay the opportunity cost

text: **Chase what "fills your life with pleasure," not a savings target.** His earliest documented public advice to founders: don't run the business as a pure money machine, because every miss against a money target demotivates and drains meaning — *"Só não esquece: acha aquilo que vai encher a sua vida de prazer e o dinheiro com certeza vem. Tira essa pressão do primeiro milhão e… curte!"* (LinkedIn Pulse)
quotes: fills your life with pleasure,
Só não esquece: acha aquilo que vai encher a sua vida de prazer e o dinheiro com certeza vem. Tira essa pressão do primeiro milhão e… curte!
title: Chase what "fills your life with pleasure," not a savings target

text: **Cut the disengaged franchisee.** Absentee or distracted operators are churn targets, not relationships to preserve. (Jornal do Comércio)
title: Cut the disengaged franchisee

text: **Expand into adjacency only when demand is already revealed.** He entered prescription eyewear (Ótica Chilli Beans, 2019) only after *grau* was already ~19% of sales. (Exame, óticas)
title: Expand into adjacency only when demand is already revealed

text: **Don't waste energy on the uncontrollable** (government, tariffs); over-invest in what's in reach. (Exame, NEEX 2025)
title: Don't waste energy on the uncontrollable

text: **When founders pitch, check the valuation reality before the love.** His top diagnosis of failed pitches: overvaluation, stated with a specific mechanism (not just "high valuation" but a pattern across his entire tenure): *"Em seis anos que eu fiquei como participante fixo tiveram inúmeras oportunidades que eu queria entrar em negócios, mas não entrei porque o valuation era muito alto. Muitas pessoas poderiam ter saído de lá com um investidor se tivessem sido mais conscientes na hora de avaliar o negócio."* And a bluntly stated anti-signal for founders chasing him as an investor: *"Quem chega lá e mostra quer ficar milionário não me brilha os olhos."* (ISTOÉ Dinheiro, jul/2024; ISTOÉ Dinheiro, set/2025)
quotes: Em seis anos que eu fiquei como participante fixo tiveram inúmeras oportunidades que eu queria entrar em negócios, mas não entrei porque o valuation era muito alto. Muitas pessoas poderiam ter saído de lá com um investidor se tivessem sido mais conscientes na hora de avaliar o negócio.
Quem chega lá e mostra quer ficar milionário não me brilha os olhos.
title: When founders pitch, check the valuation reality before the love

text: **When entering a new geography, size the channel before scaling it.** On international expansion: *"Estamos testando canais de tamanhos diferentes para entender o que funciona melhor."* Don't standardize a format across markets until you've tested which size actually works locally. (Exame, mar/2026)
quotes: Estamos testando canais de tamanhos diferentes para entender o que funciona melhor.
title: When entering a new geography, size the channel before scaling it

text: **Protect the seeds you already planted before chasing new ones.** On mature international markets (Indonésia, Oriente Médio, Peru): *"A gente tem muita semente que cresceu e que a gente tem que cuidar."* Consolidate and tend existing bets rather than only hunting new ones. (Exame, mar/2026)
quotes: A gente tem muita semente que cresceu e que a gente tem que cuidar.
title: Protect the seeds you already planted before chasing new ones

text: **In an FX shock, change the settlement currency, not just the price.** When the US-China trade war opened a window, he paid a Chinese supplier in Chinese currency for the first time and declared it permanent policy, not opportunism: *"De forma alguma é uma estratégia pontual. Queremos continuar mantendo esta prática. A ideia é que o uso do dólar não volte nunca mais."* [This is by no means a one-off strategy. We want to keep doing this. The idea is that the use of the dollar never comes back.] (Exame/Cazuza, mai/2025)
quotes: De forma alguma é uma estratégia pontual. Queremos continuar mantendo esta prática. A ideia é que o uso do dólar não volte nunca mais.
title: In an FX shock, change the settlement currency, not just the price

text: **In an FX/cost shock, absorb it through volume, not price pass-through — and go renegotiate in person.** During the 2015 real/dollar crisis (70% of the operation in dollars), he cut prices 5–8% instead of raising them, betting on turnover — *"Não repassamos os custos [da alta do dólar] para o consumidor e ganhamos no giro"* — spent 15 days personally in China renegotiating with suppliers (cut input costs ~20%), and diversified sourcing to cut China dependency from 90% to 70% within a year. He also cut headcount 10% in the same year and turned the annual franchisee convention into a 4-day cruise (~4,000 attendees) to keep the network engaged through the downturn. (Forbes Brasil, 2016, via web.archive.org)
quotes: Não repassamos os custos [da alta do dólar] para o consumidor e ganhamos no giro
title: In an FX/cost shock, absorb it through volume, not price pass-through — and go renegotiate in person

text: **Reframe "crisis" as "opportunity" — the word choice is a decision, not just rhetoric.** *"É muito fácil colocar a culpa na crise... Prefiro falar em oportunidade."* (Forbes Brasil, 2016)
quotes: É muito fácil colocar a culpa na crise... Prefiro falar em oportunidade.
title: Reframe "crisis" as "opportunity" — the word choice is a decision, not just rhetoric

text: **Be "optimistic but grounded" — never let optimism become denial.** Self-description used consistently across interviews years apart: *"Eu sou otimista por natureza. Tem gente até que se irrita comigo. Mas eu estou entre otimista e conservador. Eu estou confiante, mas com o pé no chão."* And, in the same spirit, after the pandemic: *"Não existe momento melhor do mundo para começar um negócio."* (Mercado&Consumo, ago/2021)
quotes: optimistic but grounded
Eu sou otimista por natureza. Tem gente até que se irrita comigo. Mas eu estou entre otimista e conservador. Eu estou confiante, mas com o pé no chão.
Não existe momento melhor do mundo para começar um negócio.
title: Be "optimistic but grounded" — never let optimism become denial

text: **Lead a crisis with a fixed cadence of honest bad news, not silence.** During the pandemic he called every franchisee on a fixed schedule regardless of what he had to report: *"ter falado com meus franqueados toda semana, toda quinta-feira às 10h, foi importante. 'Desculpe, hoje eu não tenho notícia boa para te trazer.' Ou: 'Hoje eu tenho notícia boa para te trazer.' Olhar no olho e chorar, curtir, comemorar, é isso que faz a diferença."* Backed by concrete relief actions, not just calls: renegotiated franchisee rent, deployed Chilli Beans' legal department to help franchisees access salary-support benefits for their own staff, extended payment deadlines on inventory owed, and arranged a cheap-credit line via Caixa Econômica Federal. (Mercado&Consumo, ago/2021)
quotes: ter falado com meus franqueados toda semana, toda quinta-feira às 10h, foi importante. 'Desculpe, hoje eu não tenho notícia boa para te trazer.' Ou: 'Hoje eu tenho notícia boa para te trazer.' Olhar no olho e chorar, curtir, comemorar, é isso que faz a diferença.
title: Lead a crisis with a fixed cadence of honest bad news, not silence

text: **View your own commitments through cycles — an exit doesn't need a crisis reason.** On leaving Shark Tank as a fixed judge after six seasons, then returning: *"Como a vida é feita de ciclos, decidi encerrar o meu no ano passado."* [Since life happens in cycles, I decided to end mine last year.] A personal decision framework applied to a public role, not just to the business. (ADNews, 2024)
quotes: Como a vida é feita de ciclos, decidi encerrar o meu no ano passado.
title: View your own commitments through cycles — an exit doesn't need a crisis reason

text: **Patience is the actual moat; ten years is a normal timeline, not a failure.** *"Tenha paciência. Demorei 10 anos para dar certo. Tomei muita porrada. Não desista em dois anos. E mais: existem setores arcaicos esperando por inovação. Dá para vender até ovo com história e atitude."* (Exame/Cazuza, mai/2025)
quotes: Tenha paciência. Demorei 10 anos para dar certo. Tomei muita porrada. Não desista em dois anos. E mais: existem setores arcaicos esperando por inovação. Dá para vender até ovo com história e atitude.
title: Patience is the actual moat; ten years is a normal timeline, not a failure

text: **Make vs. buy / vertical integration.** Decisively *un-integrate*: sold all owned stores, manufactures 100% in China. The Brazilian factory that once made ~20% of volume closed under fines and taxes — *"foi um volume enorme, quase 500 mil peças. A gente levou tanta multa, tanta multa trabalhista, tanto imposto, que o dono da fábrica desistiu... o imposto destrói as empresas."* A later, richer interview on the same theme adds detail: he has been offered ~3 free Brazilian factories and turned them down because the unit economics don't clear even at zero acquisition cost — *"Já me ofereceram de presente umas três fábricas, como se eu fosse arrendar. A conta não fecha. O produto se torna mais caro do que o chinês, fabricando no Brasil."* — while explicitly praising the Chinese state's manufacturer-support model (a state-backed factory insurer, so buyers pay the insurer rather than the supplier directly) as what he'd want to see in Brazil: *"Se quisesse, dava. Se desse incentivo, isenção de imposto, a gente ia voar."* His five Chinese factory partners are in Wenzhou (Zhejiang province, ~10M population, 700+ factories — a city he still calls "small" by Chinese standards). *(Tension worth flagging: he objects to Brazilian state intervention as destructive but praises Chinese state intervention as a model to emulate — the objection tracks whether the intervention costs or subsidizes him, not intervention per se; not reconciled in either source.)* (ISTOÉ Dinheiro / Click P&G; Money Times; ISTOÉ Dinheiro, jun/2025)
quotes: foi um volume enorme, quase 500 mil peças. A gente levou tanta multa, tanta multa trabalhista, tanto imposto, que o dono da fábrica desistiu... o imposto destrói as empresas.
Já me ofereceram de presente umas três fábricas, como se eu fosse arrendar. A conta não fecha. O produto se torna mais caro do que o chinês, fabricando no Brasil.
Se quisesse, dava. Se desse incentivo, isenção de imposto, a gente ia voar.
title: Make vs. buy / vertical integration

text: **Pivot vs. persevere.** He pivoted hard *once* — music → eyewear — then persevered ~30 years inside that choice. Inside the business he doesn't "pivot," he *refreshes* (new collections, formats, verticals) and explicitly frames this as choosing the real "jogo" over theorizing about entrepreneurship. (Museu da Pessoa; ABF; Amazon synopsis)
title: Pivot vs. persevere

text: **How to price.** Refuse to compete on price for sunglasses; let story carry it (~2% annual discount). *Exception:* in the optical vertical he priced frames *below* market (R$149–300 vs. a ~R$400 average) — a deliberate penetration move against incumbent opticians, distinct from his sunglasses stance. A second, older exception under FX shock (2015): he cut prices 5–8% to defend turnover rather than pass currency cost to the consumer. (Money Times; Exame, óticas; Forbes Brasil 2016)
title: How to price

text: **Focus vs. diversify.** Focus at the *level of his role* (brand management only) and at the *level of the store* ("foco de loja" — don't mix channels); diversify the *product surface* aggressively via licensing rather than in-store SKUs — sunglasses → watches → prescription eyewear → sustainable lines → marketplace (a Mercado Livre storefront that "dobrou o faturamento online") → sneakers (Ramarim license) → beverages (ChilliDrinks) → pepper sauce (Knorr partnership). Diversify what you license out; never diversify your job, and never let a new category bleed into the core store's identity. (ABF; Exame; O Tempo, set/2025)
quotes: foco de loja
dobrou o faturamento online
title: Focus vs. diversify

text: **Raise vs. bootstrap / take a partner.** Bootstrapped and franchise-funded for ~25 years; opened to a minority (~30%) sale only in the mid-2020s, earmarked for the optical expansion — *"estamos negociando parte da venda da empresa para apostar no segmento de óticas."* (Exame, óticas)
quotes: estamos negociando parte da venda da empresa para apostar no segmento de óticas.
title: Raise vs. bootstrap / take a partner

text: **Margin vs. ecosystem health.** Chooses to leave margin on the table to keep the franchise chain healthy rather than maximize his own take — reinforced in a 2026 LinkedIn post tied to a franchising-excellence award. (Inteligência Financeira; LinkedIn, 2026)
title: Margin vs. ecosystem health

text: **When to fire / replace a partner.** Replace the franchisee who's "out of the game" — absentee, distracted, or reinvesting profits into rival franchises — via continuous *oxigenação* rather than waiting for a store to fail. *"Tenho um problema que não consigo conter: o cara ganhando dinheiro na franquia da Chilli Beans e gastando em outras franquias ruins."* (Jornal do Comércio)
quotes: out of the game
Tenho um problema que não consigo conter: o cara ganhando dinheiro na franquia da Chilli Beans e gastando em outras franquias ruins.
title: When to fire / replace a partner

text: **Entering a new category.** Wait for revealed demand inside the existing base, then attack on price + brand familiarity (prescription eyewear); or license it out entirely to a category specialist rather than build in-house capability (footwear via Ramarim, beverages, sauces). (Exame, óticas; O Tempo, set/2025)
title: Entering a new category

text: **Entering a new geography.** Size-test the channel/format locally first, then concentrate resources on markets that already show returns (Indonésia, Oriente Médio, Peru) rather than spreading thin across all fronts at once. On the US specifically, growth has a dated numeric target, not just a direction: a Miami store opened in 2025 as part of a stated goal of *"chegar a 60 pontos de venda nos Estados Unidos até 2030"* — with an explicit caveat that the goal isn't store count for its own sake: *"o importante não é quantidade de lojas. E sim levar nossa cultura, criatividade e jeito de fazer negócio para novos mercados."* (Exame, mar/2026; LinkedIn, ~2025)
quotes: chegar a 60 pontos de venda nos Estados Unidos até 2030
o importante não é quantidade de lojas. E sim levar nossa cultura, criatividade e jeito de fazer negócio para novos mercados.
title: Entering a new geography

text: **Small/thin markets that don't support a full-size store.** Rather than skip towns under ~50,000 people where a normal store's unit economics don't work, he designed a cheaper, sustainable, solar-powered container format for gas-station placement — an explicit callback to the brand's original 1997 street-cart format: *"Nós temos muita dificuldade de manter uma loja em cidades com até 50 mil habitantes, a conta simplesmente não fecha. Então, pensamos nessa possibilidade para incluir em postos de gasolina os containers que são sustentáveis e contam com custo mais baixo."* *(Unaddressed in the source: potential channel conflict with existing franchisees whose catchment areas a cheaper company-format channel might now also serve.)* (Forbes Brasil, ago/2022)
quotes: Nós temos muita dificuldade de manter uma loja em cidades com até 50 mil habitantes, a conta simplesmente não fecha. Então, pensamos nessa possibilidade para incluir em postos de gasolina os containers que são sustentáveis e contam com custo mais baixo.
title: Small/thin markets that don't support a full-size store

text: **Real-estate/crisis opportunism.** Read pandemic-era mall vacancy as a buying window rather than a threat: opened ~200 new stores during the pandemic while rents were depressed — *"Nós aproveitamos que os shoppings estavam quase dando as lojas durante aquela incerteza... e aumentamos o nosso portfólio."* (Forbes Brasil, ago/2022)
quotes: Nós aproveitamos que os shoppings estavam quase dando as lojas durante aquela incerteza... e aumentamos o nosso portfólio.
title: Real-estate/crisis opportunism

text: **Sustainability as a founder-triggered pivot, not a marketing layer.** Traces the decision to a personal moment, not a market study: *"Há três anos, o meu filho de nove anos me perguntou o que a minha empresa estava fazendo para ajudar o planeta e aquele momento me marcou muito. Foi aí que começamos a investir em sustentabilidade."* Result cited: a 30%-of-production recycled-materials target and 4M recycled-waste protective cases. (Forbes Brasil, ago/2022)
quotes: Há três anos, o meu filho de nove anos me perguntou o que a minha empresa estava fazendo para ajudar o planeta e aquele momento me marcou muito. Foi aí que começamos a investir em sustentabilidade.
title: Sustainability as a founder-triggered pivot, not a marketing layer

text: **AI in production and marketing: use it, but disclose it.** Of ~30 annual ad campaigns, 10 are made entirely with AI — with a self-imposed transparency rule: *"When we do use it [for advertising], it is deliberate and openly [synthetic]."* He pairs heavy AI adoption (inventory-replenishment AI for franchisees; warehouse robotics in Extrema, MG, expected to handle ~150,000 items/month) with an explicit belief that AI doesn't replace human craft in campaigns: *"Just like in music, having a person craft a song, play the guitar in a studio, breathe, sweat, and put emotion into lyrics makes all the difference to the final result, and I believe the same goes for campaigns."* (Forbes US, set/2024 — quotes are English-original; the interview was conducted in English, so no Portuguese verbatim exists to pair alongside them)
quotes: When we do use it [for advertising], it is deliberate and openly [synthetic].

Just like in music, having a person craft a song, play the guitar in a studio, breathe, sweat, and put emotion into lyrics makes all the difference to the final result, and I believe the same goes for campaigns.
title: AI in production and marketing: use it, but disclose it

text: **Omnichannel / "phygital": both channels, but locally adapted content.** *"I believe that in order to grow, a brand needs to be both in-person and online, but that needs to be well-executed and connected to the changes in retail... The content [brands] provide for each environment will be different, but the two worlds will need to be blended effectively."* Concrete formats: a **"Store 2.0"** in-store live-commerce module (from ~BRL 220,000 investment per store, projected +20% sales) and, since the pandemic, direct store-fulfilled online orders turning every physical location into a hybrid node. (Forbes US, set/2024; Forbes Brasil, ago/2022 — English-original for the Forbes US quotes)
quotes: I believe that in order to grow, a brand needs to be both in-person and online, but that needs to be well-executed and connected to the changes in retail... The content [brands] provide for each environment will be different, but the two worlds will need to be blended effectively.
title: Omnichannel / "phygital": both channels, but locally adapted content

text: **Investing (Shark Tank).** Wants both *love and the math*: a founder who has done the accounting and shows real passion (the "brilho no olho"); kills deals on inflated valuation across his entire tenure, not just isolated cases. He frames his own return to the show — after six seasons (2017–2023), a 2024 guest spot, and now a full-time comeback for the 10th season — as re-committing to a personal "mission," not a paycheck: *"O Shark Tank Brasil é mais do que um programa, é uma missão."* He also credits the show, and his own exposure as a judge, with directly building his personal brand and the company's: *"Foi durante o Shark Tank que nós percebemos que Caito era uma marca"* — with Chilli Beans' market share against Ray-Ban in Brazil cited (by the outlet, not as his direct words) as roughly doubling, from 13% to 26%, over the decade he's been on air. A related program he created for alumni, independent of continued investment: **"Efeito Shark"** [Shark Effect], which follows Shark Tank entrepreneurs whether or not he invested — *"Eu aprendo mais do que ensino. Ver uma hamburgueria bombando dentro de Paraisópolis, com aplicativo próprio, é inspirador. Não é só dinheiro que ajuda. É dividir experiência."* (ISTOÉ Dinheiro, jul/2024; Portal Making Of; ISTOÉ Dinheiro, set/2025; Exame/Cazuza, mai/2025)
quotes: brilho no olho
O Shark Tank Brasil é mais do que um programa, é uma missão.
Foi durante o Shark Tank que nós percebemos que Caito era uma marca
Eu aprendo mais do que ensino. Ver uma hamburgueria bombando dentro de Paraisópolis, com aplicativo próprio, é inspirador. Não é só dinheiro que ajuda. É dividir experiência.
title: Investing (Shark Tank)

text: **HR / labor policy.** The first documented people-ops lever in the corpus, distinct from the brand/franchising decisions elsewhere: rolled out a network-wide **5×2 work schedule**, crediting it with improved franchisee reception, higher retention, and better-quality job applicants — *"Os franqueados receberam muito bem a nova escala, a retenção aumentou e os currículos que chegam têm uma qualidade muito melhor."* Also created a post-pandemic **"Diretoria de Felicidade"** [Happiness Directorate] focused on listening rather than formal programs: *"As pessoas precisam de cuidado muito mais do que a gente imagina. Abrimos canais para ouvir, sem grandes fórmulas. Só ouvir, olhar para o lado e perguntar: 'Tá tudo bem com você?'"* And an explicit, named rejection of superficial perk culture: *"Não adianta ter uma mesa de ping-pong se o time está estressado. O que importa é respeitar as pessoas como elas são... A gente não abre mão de almoçar junto, rir junto."* (ABF Pinga Fogo, out/2025; Exame/Cazuza, mai/2025)
quotes: Os franqueados receberam muito bem a nova escala, a retenção aumentou e os currículos que chegam têm uma qualidade muito melhor.
Diretoria de Felicidade
As pessoas precisam de cuidado muito mais do que a gente imagina. Abrimos canais para ouvir, sem grandes fórmulas. Só ouvir, olhar para o lado e perguntar: 'Tá tudo bem com você?'
Não adianta ter uma mesa de ping-pong se o time está estressado. O que importa é respeitar as pessoas como elas são... A gente não abre mão de almoçar junto, rir junto.
title: HR / labor policy

text: **Macro / timing.** Reads Brazil's interest-rate environment as a binding retail constraint, in increasingly specific language across interviews — *"2025 foi um ano muito difícil. O país não sobrevive a juros de quase 20%"*; *"Na minha visão, os juros, do jeito que estão, não é que eles estrangulam, eles sufocam e matam o varejo... Esse juro do jeito que está é insuportável"*; and looking to 2026, *"Eu espero um país de juros mais baixo. Simples como isso"* — but, per his circle-of-control rule, refuses to *spend energy* on the macro he can't change. He also separately reads pandemic-era loan overhangs as compounding the squeeze: *"muitos empréstimos que foram tomados durante a pandemia estão sendo pagos agora."* *(Tension worth noting: he both invokes macro as a constraint and disclaims it as a distraction.)* (Exame, óticas / mar/2026; ISTOÉ Dinheiro, jun/2025; ISTOÉ Dinheiro, jul/2024)
quotes: 2025 foi um ano muito difícil. O país não sobrevive a juros de quase 20%
Na minha visão, os juros, do jeito que estão, não é que eles estrangulam, eles sufocam e matam o varejo... Esse juro do jeito que está é insuportável
Eu espero um país de juros mais baixo. Simples como isso

title: Macro / timing

text: Warm, extroverted, showman cadence — a frontman who learned to sell from a stage and never stopped. Speaks in punchy, repeatable maxims that end on a hard stop (*"...ponto."*, *"...simples como isso."*), the verbal equivalent of a hook. Heavy on first-person founder myth (the suitcase, the dream-named brand, the bands, the 50kg) and on **story** as both product philosophy and rhetorical method — he *demonstrates* the thesis by telling you a story while explaining that stories sell, and reaches for musicians (David Bowie/Ziggy Stardust) as entrepreneurship case studies rather than business-school examples, explicitly naming Steve Jobs and Jeff Bezos as *not* his heroes. His authored prose (the Metrópoles column) reads noticeably more crafted than his interview cadence — sensory, almost musical sentences ("é aquele primeiro acorde que abre o show e faz a plateia vibrar" — it's the first chord that opens the show) — while staying in the same register of short declaratives and hard stops. In his written voice more broadly (LinkedIn, book synopses) he's a direct, buddy-to-buddy motivator — *"Cara, eu vou te falar uma coisa"* — that leans into vulnerability (being called "Napoleão" by his team; admitting the pandemic "desestabilizou psicologicamente" him "até hoje") before landing the lesson. Reaches for vivid Brazilian register: *arroz com feijão* for the unglamorous basics, *gracinhas* for the bold moves they earn, *brilho no olho* for talent, *estar no jogo* / *virar o jogo* / *coragem de ter atitude* / *ir para o jogo* for the posture he prescribes, *marca mutante* for a brand that must keep changing to survive, and *oxigênio* for whatever channel keeps the business breathing in a crisis. Treats the brand as a living cultural actor that must keep reading youth culture — and is willing to say plainly that a whole generation is missing something ("falta paciência, falta identidade... falta coragem"). Blunt and unsentimental about partners who underperform (*"nos ferramos"*) and about Brazil's tax/industrial failure (*"dá dó," "o imposto destrói as empresas," "uma judiação"*), yet disciplined about not wasting breath on what he can't change (*tarifaço*). Self-deprecating about scale relative to harder things (raising kids). Bilingual register (US years) surfaces in English asides, and when interviewed directly in English (Forbes US) his cadence compresses into shorter, more conventionally corporate sentences than his Portuguese register — a useful tell that some of his "voice" is genre-specific to Brazilian business press. Where Naval compresses to aphorism for *abstraction*, Caito compresses for *salesmanship* — the line is built to be retweeted by a franchisee, not contemplated.

text: **vs. Rony Meisler — brand-as-story vs. brand-as-purpose.** Both are Brazilian brand-builders who refuse to compete on price, but the engine differs. Caito's moat is *narrative + novelty + licensed pop culture* — story for its own commercial sake, a fast-collection flywheel. Meisler's is *purpose and community* ("purpose is the greatest driver of value," audience-before-product). Note the seam: Caito *also* says "uma marca deve ser comunidade" and talks about a brand's "alma" caring for "sociedade e do planeta," so the gap is narrower than it looks — but Caito's community forms around the *product's story*, while Meisler's forms around a *cause*. A founder choosing between "give the product a story" and "give the brand a mission" gets genuinely different playbooks.

title: vs. Rony Meisler — brand-as-story vs. brand-as-purpose

text: **vs. Rony Meisler — keep control vs. sell and hand off.** Caito ran ~25 years founder-controlled and sold only a *minority* stake, ring-fenced to one vertical, and is still operating his company. Meisler sold Reserva outright to Arezzo&Co (~R$715M) and exited, framing departure as "exit at the top of the parabola." Caito's instinct is to retain the brand and keep playing.

title: vs. Rony Meisler — keep control vs. sell and hand off

text: **vs. Rony Meisler — convergent, not opposed: reject "the first million" as the goal.** Both explicitly warn founders off a pure money target. Meisler: *"Não somos uma empresa que pretende vender roupas para pessoas e sim uma empresa de pessoas que vendem roupas."* Caito: *"esquece de uma vez por todas essa história do primeiro milhão... você precisa, assim como eu, de algo que toque o coração, envolva as pessoas, conte histórias."* Where they part again is *what* replaces money: Meisler names a social cause (1P=5P); Caito names story and personal fulfillment, not a cause.

text: **vs. Warren Buffett — durable moat vs. perpetual reinvention.** Buffett prizes a wide, *static* moat ("a business that any idiot can run, because someday one will"). Caito's thesis is the inverse: the moat *is* the rate of change — stop launching weekly, stop rejecting seasonality, stop reading Gen Z, and *"a gente vai morrer."* His book's "marca mutante" [mutant brand] concept literalizes this: a brand that survives by never stopping mutation. Buffett would distrust an advantage re-earned every week; Caito would call a static moat in fashion a death sentence.
quotes: a business that any idiot can run, because someday one will
a gente vai morrer.
title: vs. Warren Buffett — durable moat vs. perpetual reinvention

text: **vs. Bernard Arnault — accessible ubiquity vs. scarcity.** Arnault's luxury logic is controlled scarcity, vertical ownership of maisons, and price as a status signal. Caito runs the inverse on his own product: democratized price, mass franchise ubiquity (~1,400 doors, a target of 3,200 in five years), self-service handling, and *more* drops, not fewer. Both monetize desire through brand; one rations it, the other floods the market. *(Caito's accessibility stance is explicit; the Arnault contrast is inferred from each one's documented model.)*
title: vs. Bernard Arnault — accessible ubiquity vs. scarcity

text: **vs. Jeff Bezos — story/relationship-first vs. customer-metric-first — now partly first-party documented, not just inferred.** Bezos starts from the customer and works backward through data and operational obsession. Caito starts from the *story* and trusts narrative to create the customer (*"a última coisa que o cliente me pede é preço"*), and now says so about Bezos personally, not just about method: *"Não tenho nada contra... o [Jeff] Bezos, da Amazon, que é um cara incrível. Mas as minhas inspirações são mais do mundo da música e da arte."* His own LinkedIn Experience text draws the contrast even sharper: *"Investir... é mais rentável do que a avaliação exclusivamente numérica. E o brilho nos olhos às vezes fala mais alto que o balanço financeiro."* On a tie-break, Bezos reaches for the metric; Caito reaches for the myth and the "brilho no olho" — and he's now on record naming Bezos as a non-model for that reason, not just a different-industry operator.

text: Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck is the originator of the fixed-vs-growth mindset — the lens that beliefs about whether ability is innate or developable causally reorganize goals, effort, and the response to failure. She offers a board the contrarian discipline of distinguishing *signal from slogan*: she publicly attacked her own movement ("false growth mindset," "a journey, not a proclamation"), insists growth mindset is "not just about effort" but strategy and help-seeking, and reframes failure as "Not Yet" rather than a verdict. Her sharpest live edge is organizational — fixed-mindset "cultures of genius" measurably produce employees who "kept secrets, cut corners, and cheated" — making her a counterweight to talent-hoarding, star-system operators, though she is candid that even her own instinct — believing that adults with a growth mindset would automatically pass it to children — turned out to be "deeply flawed." She is also the rare advisor whose own field has run large failed-replication and bias critiques against her (Li & Bates, Sisk et al., Macnamara & Burgoyne, plus a statistical-consistency audit from Nick Brown that found data errors she owned publicly), which she answers less by defending the brand than by recasting nulls as heterogeneity — a move some critics (Didau, Kohn) call unfalsifiable or structurally blind to context. Natural foil to James Clear on whether identity/belief or systems drives change, and to Alfie Kohn on whether the right unit of intervention is the individual's mindset or the structure around them.

text: Carol S. Dweck (b. 1946, Brooklyn) is the Lewis and Virginia Eaton Professor of Psychology at Stanford, where she has been since 2004 after faculty positions at Illinois, Harvard, and Columbia. B.A. Barnard (1967), Ph.D. Yale (1972), member of the National Academy of Sciences. (Stanford Profiles; Wikipedia) She entered academia in an inflection year for women in the field: "I'm grateful that the year that I went on the job market, 1972, was the first year that universities were actively looking for women," and she credits the University of Illinois psychology department with actively welcoming and supporting her — while cautioning that "that is not to deny that other people were in different kinds of places, and not to deny that discriminatory practices still go on today." (Social Science Space, 2019) Her own account of the theory's origin is a three-stage intellectual arc she calls, in retrospect, Attribution era → Goal era → Mindset era: 1970s animal-learning and "learned helplessness" research in children, feeding a 1979 collaboration with colleague John Nicholls on achievement-goal theory ("developing your ability and demonstrating your ability were two quite different goals"), which crystallized in 1983 into the fixed/growth distinction during a dissertation conversation with her student Mary Bandura (Al Bandura's daughter): "The ability that you dearly wish to validate over and over sounded more like a fixed attribute, but the ability that you wish to increase sounded more like a dynamic and malleable quality. Thus, the theories of intelligence (or mindsets) were born." (Child Development Perspectives, 2017) The empirical seed came earlier still: as a Yale graduate student around 1971 she ran New Haven fifth-graders through a rigged block-design task — one experimenter always gave solvable puzzles, another secretly gave unsolvable ones, then quietly switched back to solvable — and found that children who scored as internal-attributers on the Intellectual Achievement Responsibility Scale recovered when success became possible again, while external-attributers stayed helplessly stuck, a direct human analogue of Seligman's learned-helplessness dogs. (Chronicle of Higher Education, 2010) She names an explicit intellectual lineage — Bernie Weiner, Jacque Eccles, Ed Deci, Mark Lepper, Al Bandura, John Nicholls — as the peer cohort who kept motivation research alive when "the cognitive revolution had arrived and somehow cognition and motivation were not seen as natural allies." (ibid.) Her research motive is autobiographical, a habit she names with the field's own term for it: "We have a term in psychology called 'me search.' There's research and there's 'me search.'" The origin scene, retold consistently across at least two interviews four years apart: "my sixth grade teacher seated us around the room in IQ order... it could have scarred me for life. It did, for a while, make me afraid of challenges, but it also probably set me on this course." (Chronicle of Higher Education, 2016; Remarkable People, 2023 — the second telling names the teacher, ASR-uncertain, as "Mrs. Wilson") The 2006 trade book *Mindset* was not an instant hit: "It sat there for a year and hardly sold any copies. I was bitterly disappointed. But then through word of mouth momentum was built." (Social Science Space, 2019) Its origin, in her own account, was externally forced rather than self-initiated: "my graduate students took me aside and held a metaphorical gun to my head. They ordered me to write a book... I obeyed." (Child Development Perspectives, 2017) A separate, earlier turning point pushed her from lab researcher toward public-facing "mission": in the late 1990s, "Betty Hamburg, then the president of the William T. Grant Foundation, took me to lunch. The purpose of the lunch was to inform me that I was going into the real world. 'It's time,' she said. I obeyed and I never looked back." (The Choice to Make a Difference, 2019) She won the inaugural Yidan Prize for Education Research (2017, $3.9–4M, shared with Vicky Colbert), which funded follow-up research on the National Study of Learning Mindsets and a Mary Murphy/Stephanie Fryberg teacher-curriculum project, and the SAGE-CASBS Award (2019); she helped found the Mindset Scholars Network with CASBS's Margaret Levi and psychologist Ellen Konar. (Times Higher Education, 2017; Social Science Space, 2019) As of an August 2023 interview she was contemplating a sequel that would close a gap she says *Mindset* deliberately left open — what to strive for, not just how: "I am now contemplating a book in which I do take the reader to the meaning of their lives... I don't know how I'm gonna do it, it feels really hard, but it's the only book that I want to write next." (Remarkable People, 2023 — unconfirmed as published)

text: **Beliefs about ability shape behavior toward ability.** Believe intelligence is fixed and the goal becomes *looking* smart — effort and error feel like exposure. Believe it can grow and the goal becomes *learning* — effort and error become information. The belief is causal, not just descriptive.
title: Beliefs about ability shape behavior toward ability

text: **Mindsets are "meaning systems," not free-floating opinions.** Each mindset "fosters its own meaning system": fixed mindset bundles performance-avoidance goals, effort-as-a-sign-of-low-ability beliefs, and helpless attributions; growth mindset bundles learning goals, positive effort beliefs, and resilient attributions — a single causal package, not three separate correlations. (Yeager & Dweck 2020; Dweck & Yeager 2019)
quotes: fosters its own meaning system
title: Mindsets are "meaning systems," not free-floating opinions

text: **Failure is feedback, not a verdict.** Her formative 1970s observation: given problems slightly too hard, some 10-year-olds said "I love a challenge," "I was hoping this would be informative," or "Mistakes are our friend," while others experienced catastrophe. Same task, opposite meaning, driven by mindset. (TED, 2014; Child Development Perspectives, 2017)
quotes: I love a challenge,
I was hoping this would be informative,

title: Failure is feedback, not a verdict

text: **Everyone is a mixture, always — and it's domain-specific.** No one has a pure growth mindset: "Everyone is a mixture of fixed and growth mindsets." People can hold different mindsets in different domains, and "their dominant mindset in a given area will most strongly affect their goals, attributions, and behavior" — a strong situational cue can also temporarily *activate* a mindset without durably changing it. (KQED; Child Development Perspectives, 2017)
quotes: Everyone is a mixture of fixed and growth mindsets.
their dominant mindset in a given area will most strongly affect their goals, attributions, and behavior
title: Everyone is a mixture, always — and it's domain-specific

text: **Growth mindset does not deny that talent exists.** A misconception she names directly: "That a growth mindset denies the importance of talent. It doesn't. A growth mindset is simply the belief that talents and abilities can be developed." (Times Higher Education, 2017)
quotes: That a growth mindset denies the importance of talent. It doesn't. A growth mindset is simply the belief that talents and abilities can be developed.
title: Growth mindset does not deny that talent exists

text: **Mindset is a means, not a moral.** The point is learning and improvement, not feeling good — and not a self-esteem movement that praises children for nothing.
title: Mindset is a means, not a moral

text: **Mindset scales from the individual to the organization.** It is not only a private belief but a *cultural climate* a company broadcasts; the same fixed/growth distinction predicts trust, integrity, and innovation at the firm level (Canning et al. 2020).
title: Mindset scales from the individual to the organization

text: **Having a growth mindset does not automatically transmit it to others — practice does, belief alone doesn't.** A self-identified failure of her own original assumption: "recent research examining the mindsets of parents and their children... and of teachers and their students... shows little or no correlation... Many parents who endorse a growth mindset fail to use process praise. Many parents who endorse a growth mindset also react with concern or anxiety about their children's ability... when their children hit setbacks." Only *modeling the process* — teaching for understanding, working through being stuck, allowing revision — actually passes a growth mindset on. (Child Development Perspectives, 2017)

text: **A fixed mindset is not universally worse.** She volunteers, citing others' research rather than her own, two domains where a fixed stance appears more adaptive: accepting one's sexual orientation as who one is, and accepting aging rather than chasing extreme youth through cosmetic intervention. (Talks at Google, 2015)
title: A fixed mindset is not universally worse

text: **Fixed vs. growth mindset.** Ability as a fixed trait to be proven vs. a capacity developed through effort, strategy, and help. *Worked example:* in *Mindset*, growth-minded people define success as learning and stretching; fixed-minded people define it as validation and so avoid the challenges that would grow them. "Becoming is better than being. The fixed mindset does not allow people the luxury of becoming. They have to already be." (*Mindset*) **Provenance caveat:** Dweck herself says this specific saying predates her — "there was a saying in the 60s and 70s—'Becoming is better than being'—and now people attribute that to me... I repeated it in the Mindset book saying there was a popular saying, but now I see all these posters that read 'Becoming is better than being' by Carol Dweck" — and her own stance on such misattribution is passive: "sometimes people read and [then] repackage growth mindset without attribution... but you know, that's the way it is." (Social Science Space, 2019)
quotes: Becoming is better than being. The fixed mindset does not allow people the luxury of becoming. They have to already be.

text: **The power of "yet" / "not yet."** Reframe a verdict as a position on a learning curve. *Worked example:* a Chicago high school graded failing students "Not Yet" instead of "Fail" — "It all started when I learned about a high school in Chicago where students had to pass maybe 84 units to graduate... the students went around the school unabashedly saying to each other, how many Not Yets do you have." "If you get the grade 'Not Yet,' you understand that you're on a learning curve. It gives you a path into the future." She contrasts "the power of yet" with being "gripped in the tyranny of now." (TED, 2014; Talks at Google, 2015 — fuller origin)

text: **Praise the process, not the person — but distinguish effort praise from progress praise.** Praise effort, strategies, focus, perseverance, improvement — never the trait. *Worked example:* Mueller & Dweck (1998) — children praised for intelligence, after failure, showed less persistence, less enjoyment, and worse performance than children praised for effort. "Praising children's intelligence harms their motivation and it harms their performance." Concrete replacement scripts she recommends: "Wow, you really practiced that, and look how you've improved." "See, you studied more and your grade on this test is higher." "You tried different strategies and you figured out how to solve the problem." (Mueller & Dweck 1998; Hechinger Report, 2015) A later refinement narrows the target further: "praising effort has been overdone. I do praise progress... not just effort." (Remarkable People, 2023) The hard rule underneath both: "Never praise effort that isn't there" — if you don't know what a student actually tried, ask before praising. (Talks at Google, 2015)

text: **Even geniuses work hard.** Greatness is built, not gifted; fast learning is not deep learning. *Worked example:* "Albert Einstein swore that he was slow to learn and that's why he pondered the same questions year after year — with, as we know, excellent results." ("Even Geniuses Work Hard," 2010) A second, distinct phrasing of the same anecdote: "Albert Einstein says I'm not that smart. I'm not smarter than other people... I just stick to things [longer]. That's why people thought he was slow, originally." (Talks at Google, 2015)

Albert Einstein says I'm not that smart. I'm not smarter than other people... I just stick to things [longer]. That's why people thought he was slow, originally.
title: Even geniuses work hard

text: **Champions are made, not born (sports).** The champion's edge is the appetite to work on weaknesses and treat setbacks as information. *Worked example:* Michael Jordan, cut from his high school varsity team, as "the hardest-working athlete, perhaps in the history of sport." A second, sharper phrasing of the same example: "Michael Jordan, it turns out, wasn't particularly talented until he went at it so ferociously, more ferociously than anyone else." (*Mindset*; Talks at Google, 2015) The growth-minded competitor asks not "Did I win or lose?" but "Did I make my best effort?" — by which standard "you may be outscored but you will never lose." (*Mindset*) A more ambiguous worked example she volunteers herself, refusing an easy read: on Michael Jordan's attempt at professional baseball — "I really celebrate that he went for it, that was brave... I don't know what I make of the fact that he didn't make it even though he gave it his all." (Remarkable People, 2023)

text: **Relationships take work, not a soulmate.** The fixed mindset expects compatibility to be effortless and reads conflict as proof of a flawed partner; the growth mindset treats a partnership as built. *Worked example:* "A no-effort relationship is a doomed relationship, not a great relationship." (*Mindset*)
quotes: A no-effort relationship is a doomed relationship, not a great relationship.
title: Relationships take work, not a soulmate

text: **CEO disease / fixed-mindset leadership.** Leaders who treat talent as fixed crave validation, court flattery, silence critics, and stop learning. *Worked example:* the *Mindset* business chapter contrasts fixed-mindset leaders (Lee Iacocca coasting on past glory; Enron's "talent" culture breeding fraud and groupthink) with growth-minded executives who build teams that surface bad news. A sharper, first-person account of the psychological mechanism, not just the failure cases: "Many people have told me that when they were promoted into a prestigious position, they suddenly felt, now I have to have all the answers. Now, my period of growth is over... People who become CEOs suddenly feel they have to be gods [and] goddesses, and not people who say, gee, I don't know. Let's talk about it." (*Mindset*; HBR IdeaCast, 2012) Named positive contrasts she volunteers, not just anonymized aggregates: Lou Gerstner (IBM) and Anne Mulcahy (Xerox) as growth-minded turnaround leaders, set directly against the Enron failure case — "In a fixed mindset environment, where people are evaluating each other's brains and talent, it's each person for him or herself... no one is learning, enjoying their job, cooperating, or thinking of the longer-term health of the company. This is what happened at Enron." The individual mechanism underneath: after a blow to self-esteem, a fixed-mindset person repairs their self-image "by trying to feel that they are better than others" — in a company, "this might take the form of a boss blaming or taking things out on an employee" — while a growth-mindset person repairs it "by trying to improve themselves and correct their deficiencies." (Interview with Coert Visser, 2007)

title: CEO disease / fixed-mindset leadership

text: **Cultures of genius vs. cultures of development.** At the firm level: signaling that talent is innate ("you've either got it or you don't") produces worse outcomes than signaling that ability is developed. *Worked example:* across Fortune 500/1000 studies, employees who perceived a fixed-mindset ("culture of genius") company reported less collaboration, innovation, and integrity, and less trust and commitment — and, per the HBR write-up, "regularly kept secrets, cut corners, and cheated to try to get ahead," because "getting ahead of others and being a star is what's valued." (Canning et al. 2020; HBR 2014; SPSP 2020) The mechanism, in her own words: "if I have to be smarter than you, if I have to be the superstar, I'm going to consider all different ways to look better than you look. And if I have to keep secrets from you or hoard my knowledge from other people, I'm going to do that. But in the growth mindset organization where people are collaborating... where's the cheating going to come in? It isn't." (Talks at Google, 2015) Named, on-record worked example: asked whether Apple under Steve Jobs was a "culture of genius," she says "yeah a little bit... it took a long time for me to believe that but I do believe it... You certainly can't fault Tim Cook for what he has done" — a rare instance of naming an actual company rather than an anonymized aggregate. (Remarkable People, 2023) A companion, individual-level version of the same mechanism: "after a poor grade, students who held more of a fixed mindset of their intelligence actually said in advance they're seriously considering cheating on the next test." (Talks at Google, 2015) A named academic-discipline instance of the same pattern, with numbers: Mary Murphy studied 150 STEM professors who had taught over 15,000 students — "When STEM professors held a fixed mindset about intelligence... the achievement gap in their classes was twice as large" as under growth-mindset professors, who instead said things like "Everybody here can do well and will work with you until that happens." A related, independently-sourced finding she endorses (Cimpian & Leslie): "the more the scholars in the discipline said it's 'brilliance that can't be taught,' the fewer female PhDs there were... and fewer African Americans were... earning PhDs" — true across STEM, philosophy, and economics alike. (Social Science Space, 2019)

text: **The four-part organizational-culture messaging framework.** A concrete, reusable structure for how a growth-mindset culture actually gets built, beyond "genius vs. development" sloganeering: "First... the message from the top is really important, that we value passion, dedication, growth, and learning, not genius. Second, we don't expect that you've arrived here fully formed... Third, we expect you to stretch beyond your comfort zone and take reasonable risks... Fourth, we value process here, and we reward process... even if a project has not reached fruition or become successful, we reward that you've engaged in it in a wholehearted and smart way." (HBR IdeaCast, 2012) *Worked example, later and more concrete:* on Microsoft under Satya Nadella — "he formed all kinds of programs where people could get funding for a new idea... hackathons they call them... he said that he was gonna give big [budgets] and big teams to a few different projects and he expected at least half of them to fail... the ones who have succeeded really brought the company back." (Remarkable People, 2023)

text: **Named baseball-scouting and corporate-hiring mindset-interview frameworks.** A repeatable technique for detecting mindset at the hiring stage, developed as a consulting engagement for a major-league baseball team: Q1, "How do you get so good at baseball?" — fixed answer: "I was born with this natural talent"; growth answer: "my father and I — we worked at it constantly. We had a batting cage in the backyard." Q2: "what do you think you'd have to change [in the majors]?" — fixed: a superficial adjustment; growth: total reinvention ("maybe everything I'll have to take all my skills to a new level"). A parallel corporate-hiring version: ask candidates about their greatest failures, and whether they took responsibility, used the failure to "put value added back into the company," or blamed circumstance/others. (Talks at Google, 2015)

title: Named baseball-scouting and corporate-hiring mindset-interview frameworks

text: **"Brain Points" — mindset encoded directly into a learning game's scoring.** Named collaboration with University of Washington's Zoran Popovic: a math game whose "algorithms... detected the students' effort, their use of strategies, and their improvement" rather than raw speed — zooming through problems earns an apology and no points ("you didn't earn any points that time... We'll give you something more challenging the next time"). Result: players stayed engaged longer, used more strategies, and — the headline finding — in the standard (speed-rewarding) version mostly high achievers played to the end, but in the Brain Points version "so many more lower and medium achievers also stayed till the end." (Talks at Google, 2015)
quotes: algorithms... detected the students' effort, their use of strategies, and their improvement
you didn't earn any points that time... We'll give you something more challenging the next time
so many more lower and medium achievers also stayed till the end.
title: "Brain Points" — mindset encoded directly into a learning game's scoring

text: **The named fixed-mindset persona ("talk to your Dwayne").** Credited explicitly to her Australian colleague Susan Mackie: identify your own fixed-mindset trigger, name the persona, and negotiate with it rather than suppress it. Worked example, a banking executive: "when I'm in a crunch. I have a deadline. Dwayne shows up... Get Dwayne on board with your growth-mind-set goals. Don't try to get rid of Dwayne... say, 'Thank you for your input.'" She discloses trying it personally, including on her husband, while candidly flagging it as unvalidated: "I tried it out on my husband the other day... it's something we want to subject to rigorous research to see if this is really a powerful mind-set-change technique. But I know for a fact that just getting people to acknowledge that they have fixed-mind-set triggers is powerful." (Chronicle of Higher Education, 2016) The general, less personified version of the same technique, also credited to Mackie: "Just spend several weeks noticing when you enter a more threatened, defensive state. Don't judge yourself. Don't fight it. Just observe... give your fixed mindset persona a name. Talk to it... try to recruit it to collaborate on your challenging goals." (Edutopia, 2016)

text: **False growth mindset — a named taxonomy of misapplication, not just a slogan.** Coined by Susan Mackie ("We called this false growth mindset, a term coined by our Australian colleague Susan Mackie" — Dweck & Yeager 2019) after Mackie reported "seeing more and more false growth mindset... educators think and do all sorts of things that they simply call growth mindset." Dweck's own three named failure modes, each with a worked example: (1) *Praising Effort Alone* — "Great effort!" as a "consolation prize" decoupled from progress; (2) *Telling Students "You Can Do Anything"* — assurance without "the knowledge, skills, strategies, or resources to bring this about"; (3) *Blaming the Student's Mindset* — a school "in the name of a growth mindset" shaming a struggling child for not learning fast enough, per a parent's letter to Dweck: "Her daughter had been in a wonderful school that... made her feel like an effective learner, even when learning came slowly... She then went to a different school, where children were scolded and shamed." (Edutopia, 2016) A distinct, corporate-specific taxonomy exists in parallel: an HBR piece (not Dweck-authored, but adjacent to her circle) names five HR-side misapplication patterns — confusing growth mindset with business/revenue growth; attributing mindset to the org rather than individuals; believing personal growth is unlimited in any domain; treating growth mindset as binary; conflating it with generic positive thinking. (HBR "5 Mistakes," 2018) A named empirical instance of the implementation gap: a Stanford PhD thesis by Kathy Liu Sun found "that students continued to have fixed-mindset thoughts in math class when their teachers mouthed growth mindset phrases but didn't change their teaching practices." (Hechinger Report, 2015) The concept also extends to parenting specifically, not just teaching: "many parents endorse a growth mindset, but they still respond to their children's errors, setbacks or failures as though they're damaging and harmful. If they show anxiety or overconcern, those kids are going toward a more fixed mindset." (ibid.)

seeing more and more false growth mindset... educators think and do all sorts of things that they simply call growth mindset.
You Can Do Anything

title: False growth mindset — a named taxonomy of misapplication, not just a slogan

text: **Effort is a means; learning is the end.** Praising effort that is *not* producing learning is a trap. *Worked example:* hollow praise like "Great effort! You tried your best!" given to a student who isn't learning — "It's good that the students tried, but it's not good that they're not learning." The fix: "Let's talk about what you've tried, and what you can try next." A fuller version of the same redirect: "Let's look at what you've done," "Let's look at what your understanding is," "Let's look at what strategies you've used, and let's figure out together what we should try next." (EdWeek 2015; Hechinger Report, 2015)

It's good that the students tried, but it's not good that they're not learning.
Let's talk about what you've tried, and what you can try next.
Let's look at what you've done,
Let's look at what your understanding is,
Let's look at what strategies you've used, and let's figure out together what we should try next.
title: Effort is a means; learning is the end

text: **Mindsets can change — that is the point of the book.** *Worked example:* the *Mindset* change recipe — learn to hear your fixed-mindset "voice," reinterpret challenge/effort/setback as growth opportunities, and respond with growth-minded action, repeatedly, as a practice not a one-time conversion. (*Mindset*, ch. 8) *A second, empirically-measured worked example* (the abstract "it's a practice" claim made operational): the Heslin, VandeWalle & Latham 90-minute manager workshop she cites — (1) read a science article and watch a video on neuroplasticity, (2) list at least three reasons it matters that people can develop their abilities, (3) recall a personal area of once-low ability now performed well and explain the change, (4) write an email to a hypothetical struggling protégé about how abilities develop, (5) recall watching someone learn something thought impossible for them — measurably shifted fixed-mindset managers' attitudes and coaching behavior, with effects still present at a six-week follow-up. The same intervention family surfaces a specific, falsifiable managerial bias worth screening for: fixed-mindset managers "get stuck in their first impression of the employee and do not even see the change," so a subordinate who genuinely improves may get no credit because the boss's model never updates. (Interview with Coert Visser, 2007)
quotes: it's a practice
get stuck in their first impression of the employee and do not even see the change,
title: Mindsets can change — that is the point of the book

text: **Heterogeneity is the unit of analysis, not the average.** Her mature scholarly position: the question is not "does growth mindset work on average?" but *when, why, for whom*. *Worked example:* effects are "meaningfully heterogeneous" — stronger for low achievers and disadvantaged students facing real challenge, weaker or absent where students are already thriving ("There's a little bit of a ceiling effect. If you're getting As, you don't have anywhere to go") or where classroom norms don't support the message. (Yeager & Dweck 2020; Yeager et al. 2019; KQED 2023)
quotes: does growth mindset work on average?
There's a little bit of a ceiling effect. If you're getting As, you don't have anywhere to go
title: Heterogeneity is the unit of analysis, not the average

text: **Era-bridging research.** A named methodological philosophy for responding to a generational challenge to one's own field: fold a critical generation's preferred standards (large-N, preregistered, field-experimental) into the program rather than defend the old lab-effect-size standard. *Worked example:* the very structure of Dweck & Yeager (2019) — Dweck narrates the theory's origin and judgment/stereotype sections in her own "I" voice; her younger co-author David Yeager narrates the intervention/replication sections in his — an explicit intergenerational collaboration designed to produce research that "belongs to the new era."
quotes: belongs to the new era.
title: Era-bridging research

text: **The "basic research → mission-driven writer" self-model.** A career-stage framework she applies to her own trajectory, not to her subjects: basic researcher (hopes others apply the work) → real-world interventionist (crafts scalable interventions) → public-outreach author → movement steward (issues corrections when the movement drifts). *Worked example:* her own chronology — 1970s–90s lab research → the Betty Hamburg lunch → the student-forced 2006 book → the 2015 "false growth mindset" correction → the organizational extensions. (The Choice to Make a Difference, 2019)
quotes: basic research → mission-driven writer
false growth mindset
title: The "basic research → mission-driven writer" self-model

text: **Correct effect-size benchmarking as a discipline, not a single number.** A reusable heuristic: never accept a raw effect size without knowing what population/study-type produced the comparison benchmark. *Worked example:* "In psychology, we are familiar with Cohen's (1988) guidelines... a large effect size is .80. In education, many are familiar with John Hattie's guidelines... which suggest that .57 is a large effect size. But... Hattie included all kinds of studies... Instead, experts in educational evaluation understand that .20 is about the best that can be expected... Smaller class sizes..., a year with a good teacher..., and a whole year of schooling from the 9th through the 10th grade... all yield an effect size of about .20. The original, in-person growth-mindset interventions yielded effects of this size, and our self-administered online programs... yield about half of that effect for students at risk for lower achievement... It is pretty good to get a nice chunk of what is possible for so little time and cost." (The Choice to Make a Difference, 2019) A companion, more technical version from the peer-reviewed literature: Yeager & Dweck (2019) note that even best-in-class education interventions typically move GPA by only ~.06 points or graduation-track rates by 3–8 points, and that "the largest effects in the literature for large-sample, randomized controlled experiments with adolescents are roughly .20 SD" — smaller than Cohen's textbook "small effect" cutoff but, in their words, "realistic and meaningful." (Dweck & Yeager 2019)

Instead, experts in educational evaluation understand that .20 is about the best that can be expected... Smaller class sizes..., a year with a good teacher..., and a whole year of schooling from the 9th through the 10th grade... all yield an effect size of about .20.
