text: **Technology should start from the user's problem, never from the technology itself.** "Não é simplesmente por que a tecnologia é boa que o produto será bom... o caminho deve ser o inverso, partindo-se do problema, do usuário, da sua dor" [It's not simply because the technology is good that the product will be good... the path must be the reverse, starting from the problem, the user, their pain] — his verdict on blockchain circa 2022: not a bad technology, but a "solução em busca de um problema" [solution in search of a problem] because the market approached it tech-first (LinkedIn Pulse, "Por que a melhor tecnologia...").

text: **Innovate before it's forced on you.** The tagline of his first book and a recurring binary framing: "É preciso inovar enquanto não é necessário! Porque depois pode ser tarde demais" [You must innovate while it isn't necessary yet! Because afterward it may be too late] (SEGS; Google Books epigraph). Distinct from, but compatible with, his separate claim that *new ventures* should launch *into* a downturn (see Mental models) — one is advice to incumbents against complacency, the other is timing advice to founders about external market cycles.

text:
**Mindset Conversacional (the Conversational Mindset).** His most fully-specified framework: an explicitly "living," never-finished model of six behavioral dualities a company's WhatsApp/conversational strategy must reconcile, because the starting point must be *observed user behavior*, not technology: "os negócios conversacionais nasceram espontaneamente com o consumidor final querendo se relacionar com empresas da mesma forma que o faz com seus amigos e sua família" [conversational business emerged spontaneously, with consumers wanting to relate to companies the same way they do with friends and family] (LinkedIn Pulse, "O Mindset Conversacional"). The six dimensions, each with a worked example:
1. *Síncrono x Assíncrono* — instant 24/7 response (via AI agents) and resuming a paused conversation exactly where it left off, requiring legacy-system integration never designed for that.
2. *Pessoal x Profissional* — reframes what counts as spam: "SPAM no email significa uma mensagem com conteúdo indesejado. Mas no WhatsApp uma mensagem com conteúdo relevante, porém enviada num momento inadequado, fora de contexto ou numa forma estranha (texto, áudio, vídeo) pode ser considerada SPAM."
3. *Passivo x Ativo* — user-initiated vs. company-triggered nudges (reminders, confirmations), made more effective by WhatsApp's "always open" usage pattern.
4. *Privado x Público* — Channels/Status create a public layer inside a privacy-branded app; group/community spread is "oportunidade ou ameaça" [opportunity or threat].
5. *Estruturado x Desestruturado* — worked example, his own words: "Você pode estar comprando um tênis para jogar tênis, por exemplo, e, antes de pagar, pergunta ao vendedor se o tênis é macio ou rígido... O WhatsApp, ao inserir o fluxo desestruturado no processo, humaniza o digital e (re)inclui o ser humano numa relação que foi mecanizada pela transformação digital" [You might be buying sneakers to play tennis, and before paying, you ask the seller if the shoe is soft or rigid... WhatsApp, by inserting the unstructured flow into the process, humanizes the digital and re-includes the human being in a relationship that digital transformation had mechanized].
6. *Contínuo x Episódico* — conversations with no formal end (closed by an emoji, resumed weeks later), requiring companies to build "memória contextual... como acontece numa conversa real entre amigos" [contextual memory... as happens in a real conversation between friends].
Synthesizing rule across all six: "qualquer mensagem enviada ao usuário deve, sempre, ser RELEVANTE e CONVENIENTE" [any message sent to the user must always be RELEVANT and CONVENIENT].

text: **Automatizar o passado x Desenhar o futuro (automate the past vs. design the future).** His central AI-era framework, and the spine of his 2026 book "O Mindset da IA": "Estamos testemunhando uma distinção profunda entre dois grupos de empresas: as que utilizam a Inteligência Artificial para meramente automatizar o passado e as que a utilizam para redesenhar o futuro. Tudo o que se limita à automação de processos existentes é destinado a se tornar commodity — o diferencial desaparece em experiências padronizadas. O valor real, o alpha competitivo, está em usar a IA para criar processos e organizações inteiramente novos. Aqueles que permanecem no primeiro grupo estão acumulando uma 'dívida cultural' perigosa" [We are witnessing a profound distinction between two groups of companies: those that use AI merely to automate the past and those that use it to redesign the future. Anything limited to automating existing processes is destined to become a commodity — the differentiator disappears in standardized experiences. The real value, the competitive alpha, is in using AI to create entirely new processes and organizations. Those who stay in the first group are accruing a dangerous "cultural debt"] (Forbes). Worked example: the audio-nuance gate for Brazil (an AI that can't read the nuance of a voice message "falhará no Brasil" because "o áudio é a nossa linguagem cultural de confiança") — a "redesign the future" requirement that a mere "automate the past" port of a text-first product would fail; and the small-merchant "mini CRM dentro do WhatsApp" moving "da era da resposta manual para a era da assistência preditiva" [from the era of manual reply to the era of predictive assistance] once GenAI is layered on (Forbes).

text: **Crisis is the best time to build.** Explicit causal model, not just a slogan — the phrasing is his own answer to "what lessons from Ágora still apply today?" ("GH: Crisis is the best time to build," The J Curve Insider written interview), elaborated in the podcast: "When you have a crisis, this is the best period for you to test your product, to develop your product, to invest in the product because you can test it and if it fails, nothing happens because the market is down all the time" (The J Curve podcast). Worked example: Ágora launched in 2000 into an 88% three-year market collapse (dot-com bust, 9/11, 2002 election panic) with "four, five employees" and near-zero fixed costs, while "all the competitors and the big banks... were stopping all the investments... firing a lot of people" — by 2003 the market rebounded 97% and Ágora "became the first company in the market."

text: **Don't ask the user — read behavior, use neuromarketing.** Companion framework to the Core-ideas position above, with its own separate worked example: at Ágora, traditional research (focus groups, in-depth interviews) "rarely correlated with actual user behavior," so Horn used neuromarketing (EEG/fMRI-based tools) at both Ágora and Órama "to validate emotional associations in campaigns" ("Faça como Stan Lee e Steve Jobs").

text: **Introducing disruptive tech into a conservative, regulated industry must be founder/CEO-led, never delegated.** "I think it's a top-down approach. It must come from the founder, from the CEO of the company. It can't be something that your CTO is doing and you're not engaged with that" (The J Curve podcast). Two worked examples: (1) Órama's cloud bet — in 2009 US bankers told him cloud "is not for financial market... because of security, because of reliability," so he personally tested AWS starting January 2010, paying with his own credit card since Amazon wasn't yet in Brazil, and worked through two years of Central Bank ambiguity ("didn't approve. But they didn't reject") before approval — becoming, on his account, "much more creative than before... a real competitive advantage." (2) Banks and WhatsApp — at Banco Votorantim/Original, security teams told him moving boleto requests to WhatsApp customer service was "not secure"; after joining WhatsApp he personally visited banks to challenge that objection, and "after 1 year, they were the first segment using WhatsApp. And now they are like 1/3 of all messages." The concrete before/after (reported by NeoFeed, 2023): financial services rose from 7th to 1st place in the app's category revenue after he joined, and the number of financial companies using WhatsApp Business went "de pouco menos de dez" to "quase 200" (BTG Pactual, Safra, Banco Pan, BV, Nubank, Itaú — Banco Pan even for account opening) — a vertical he seeded specifically by leveraging his own Órama/BV financial-sector network rather than pushing product-led across all sectors at once (NeoFeed).

text: **PR, not product, is the first investment in trust-sensitive industries.** "In financial market, all research showed that trust is in the first place when someone analyzes company... I did a lot of PR in the launch of the company. I think my main investment was in PR. More than in the product" — generalized into explicit advice: "This is something that I say to all founders when they are in the market: that trust is important. Do PR because PR can change the perception of the market" (The J Curve podcast).

And after the fifth why, it should be very consistent. If you stop in the third or fourth, it means that there is no consistency in what you are doing" — worked example: distinguishing founders who genuinely "think big" from those who merely say it, "the ones who do — they build billion-dollar companies" (The J Curve podcast).

text: **"O empreendedor, o novo homem das cavernas" (the entrepreneur as prehistoric caveman).** Analogy comparing the entrepreneur's permanent hypervigilance to that of early humans facing predators — "o empreendedor, em geral, atua num ambiente de escassez" [the entrepreneur generally operates in an environment of scarcity]: limited capital, insufficient growth funding, labor shortages, and constant competitive "paranoia" that coexists with, rather than contradicts, genuine optimism.

I didn't unlearn that completely. But fortunately, now I work at a company that the founder does [founder mode]" — an implicit reference to working at a founder-led company (Meta/Zuckerberg) rather than a professionally-managed one (The J Curve podcast).

text: **If you're not 100% sure about a hire, don't hire.** "It's better not to hire that person and wait until you have the right person than to do that. But I just learned that years after that... You must wait until you know the person you are hiring is the best person" — learned expensively at early-stage Ágora, where hiring under headcount pressure despite doubts was "a big mistake" (The J Curve podcast).

text: **When to sell.** Sold Ágora to Bradesco in 2008 when the founding partners judged they couldn't compete with incoming international banks (Merrill Lynch, Bear Stearns) entering Brazil: "we said we would not be able to compete with them. So the only possibility is to sell the business" — and delegated the entire negotiation to a strategic partner/banker rather than running it themselves, at a price roughly 10x what they'd expected a year earlier (The J Curve podcast).

text: **Founder → corporate executive transition.** Took the Accenture offer specifically because it kept the entrepreneurial register inside a corporate wrapper: when Accenture's CEO offered him a role without specifying what it would be ("I have no idea. But I am sure that your experience is going to be very valuable for us"), Horn "loved that answer because it was like being an entrepreneur in a corporate environment." The decision followed an explicit personal-cost reckoning: "There are some sacrifices, personal sacrifices, that are inevitable. And it happened with me in my personal life, and I said, 'It's enough'" (The J Curve podcast).

He frames the move explicitly as taking the job "to experience revenue-generation and scaling challenges in a new context" (Instituto Caldeira), not as a coast/retirement move.

text: **When to launch a new venture relative to the market cycle.** Contrarian: launch cold, into a downturn or at least outside an overheated boom, because it buys time to reach product-market fit without demand pressure forcing premature scale — grounded in Schumpeter's cycle framework and the Ágora precedent ("O melhor momento para lançar a sua startup"; The J Curve podcast).

text: **Evaluating a specific AI initiative: automate or redesign?** His decision gate for any AI project (inside Meta or advised to clients): ask whether it merely *automates an existing process* — which he treats as a trap that commoditizes the business and builds "dívida cultural" — or *creates a new process/organizational form*, which is where the "alpha competitivo" is. He is explicitly against the "esperar para ver" [wait and see] and "ainda é muito nova" [it's still too new] postures, arguing they widen the competitive gap "em uma velocidade sem precedentes" [at an unprecedented speed] (Forbes). For a market-readiness call specifically in Brazil, audio-quality handling is a non-negotiable gate: an AI feature that can't read the nuance of a voice message "falhará no Brasil, pois o áudio é a nossa linguagem cultural de confiança" [will fail in Brazil, because audio is our cultural language of trust] (Forbes).

text: **Handling a regulatory blocker on a flagship product (WhatsApp payments in Brazil).** Public, transparent incrementalism: publicized each testing milestone with named acquirer partners (Cielo, Fiserv, Getnet, Mercado Pago, Rede) ahead of full Central Bank authorization, framing the eventual approval as a "dia feliz" [happy day] rather than downplaying the earlier friction (LinkedIn posts on the WhatsApp Business Summit and the Central Bank authorization) — consistent with his own PR-first heuristic, though the underlying regulatory history (WhatsApp Pay's 2020 suspension by the Central Bank pre-dates his arrival and pre-dates Pix's entrenchment as Brazil's default instant-payment rail) is a background risk he now stewards rather than one he can undo (O Fator).

text: Bilingual register that shifts with audience: fluent, confident English in international podcast settings (The J Curve), with concrete anecdotes and hard numbers (88% down, 97% up, US$500M, "1/3 of all messages"); declarative, teacherly Portuguese in domestic press and LinkedIn Pulse essays, structured as named, numbered frameworks ("três elementos," "seis dimensões," "cinco equívocos"). Frequently coins or brands terms for his own frameworks ("Mindset Conversacional," "Mindset da Inovação," "Mindset da IA," "novo homem das cavernas") and is self-aware/self-deprecating about the pattern ("brincaram comigo que esse nome foi inspirado no livro..."). Reasons by analogy more than by data: the SPAM redefinition, the tennis-shoe example, the caveman metaphor, Five Whys borrowed explicitly from Toyota and re-taught at Singularity University. Cites named thinkers approvingly and folds them into his own argument rather than picking fights with them — Paul Graham/Brian Chesky on Founder Mode, Steve Jobs and Stan Lee on ignoring user research, Schumpeter on economic cycles — his contrarianism targets generic doctrines (Lean Startup customer-discovery orthodoxy, blanket agile adoption, "credit is where fintech money is") rather than named rivals. Notably candid about his own incomplete transformations ("I didn't unlearn that completely") and about the personal cost of 22 years as a founder ("O desgaste foi grande" [The wear and tear was great]) — a register of earned humility rather than pure evangelism. Leans on a stable stock of favorite proof points across venues and years (the Ágora crisis-launch story, the boleto/banks-and-WhatsApp story, the Stan Lee/Jobs pairing) — the same anecdotes recur near-verbatim in Portuguese essays written years apart and in English podcast answers, suggesting a well-rehearsed personal narrative rather than improvisation. On social, his register is curatorial and crowd-sourcing rather than top-down: he amplifies third-party press about his own product and openly solicits user stories ("Tenho ouvido histórias super curiosas de como as pessoas têm usado Meta AI!... comenta aqui!," LinkedIn) — while, in book-launch interviews, the same lines surface pre-polished and reused verbatim as pull-quotes ("dívida cultural," "alpha competitivo," "molda o produto global," Forbes), a sign these are consolidated on-message positions rather than off-the-cuff reasoning.

text: **vs. Jeff Bezos — should you ask the customer what they want?** Bezos's Amazon runs on proactive customer obsession, but explicitly *not* passive customer-listening: "Listen to customers, but don't just listen to customers – also invent on their behalf" (per Bezos's own dossier, 2009 letter). Horn goes further and flips the polarity: don't ask users at all at the early stage, "you should know that better than him," modeling on Steve Jobs and Stan Lee. The two converge on rejecting naive survey-driven product design but diverge on how much active listening survives the rejection — Bezos institutionalizes "five worked examples" of proactive customer-signal-reading as an operating discipline; Horn's stance, by his own admission, is a blunter, less-instrumented "the founder should just know."

you should know that better than him,
five worked examples
the founder should just know.
title: vs. Jeff Bezos — should you ask the customer what they want?

text: **vs. Michael Seibel — is "talk to your users" the right early-stage doctrine?** Seibel's entire YC playbook rests on "talk to users + write code" as ~80-90% of a founder's waking hours, with "filter your early users hard" as the refinement, not the rejection (per Seibel's own dossier). Horn explicitly names this exact doctrine and disagrees with it on the record: "there are a lot of people saying that you should ask your user what they want... I really don't agree with that" (The J Curve podcast) — a direct, named-doctrine disagreement even though the two don't address each other by name.

text: **vs. Reid Hoffman — hire fast to blitzscale, or wait for certainty?** Hoffman's blitzscaling playbook explicitly calls for "hire like your life depends on it" as part of buying speed with capital in a winner-take-most market (per Hoffman's own dossier). Horn's hard-won position is the opposite: "If you're not 100% sure, don't hire" — a wrong hire, learned expensively at early Ágora, is "worse than an empty seat." The split maps onto the broader speed-vs-discipline axis: Hoffman treats under-hiring as the bigger risk in a land-grab market; Horn treats a bad hire as a compounding cost that outweighs the speed gained.

text: **vs. Frederico Trajano — where does "humanizing" digital commerce happen?** Both are Brazilian executives whose careers are built on making technology feel less mechanical, and both explicitly use the word "humaniza(r)." But Trajano locates the humanizing moment in the *physical store* — "a loja física... o topo do funil físico," the place customers go to "sentir a marca" before converting digitally (per Trajano's own dossier) — while Horn locates it in the *unstructured conversation*: "O WhatsApp, ao inserir o fluxo desestruturado no processo, humaniza o digital." One reintroduces the human via physical retail space; the other via messaging's informality — a genuine difference in where the "re-humanization" lever sits for a digital business, useful to stage as a live tension for any retailer deciding whether to invest in store experience or conversational commerce first.

text: **vs. Paul Graham — has Founder Mode actually been transcended?** Horn cites Graham's Founder Mode essay (via Brian Chesky's YC talk) approvingly and self-applies it, but reports only partial success: "I didn't unlearn that completely." This isn't a disagreement with Graham's diagnosis so much as a live, admitted failure to fully execute the transition Graham describes — useful as a check against treating Founder Mode as a switch flipped once rather than an incomplete, ongoing struggle even for someone who explicitly studied and tried to apply it.

text: **Steward of a product whose flagship Brazilian monetization feature was blocked by regulators before he arrived, then structurally lost ground to a state-backed rival.** WhatsApp Pay launched in June 2020; the Central Bank suspended it within eight days on competitive-concentration grounds ("risco de efeito concentrador irreversível"), and the suspension was lifted only in March 2021 — months after Pix, the Central Bank's own instant-payment rail, had already launched (Nov 2020) and begun entrenching itself as Brazil's default. This predates Horn's March 2022 arrival and isn't a personal failure, but it is the regulatory scar tissue behind the payments business he now runs, and no source in this corpus shows him addressing that history directly (O Fator). A payments-industry professional puts the verdict bluntly — "por mais que o WhatsApp diga que o WhatsApp Pay está disponível, eles perderam o bonde para o PIX" [however much WhatsApp says WhatsApp Pay is available, they missed the boat to Pix] — a line to attribute to the anonymous source, not to Horn (NeoFeed).

A fifth batch of research notes (Forbes 2026, NeoFeed 2023, and two additional LinkedIn posts — the Mexico Meta Summit post and the "Meta AI no WhatsApp" post) was found unincorporated in the raw notes and folded into this dossier during the final pass; the four new sources were each re-verified against their live pages before quoting. A South Summit Brazil 2026 session page ("Beyond Messaging," recovered via Wayback) documents the same April-2025 panel already covered by the Instituto Caldeira write-up and yields no additional quotes, so it is folded in as context, not counted as a separate source. The corpus is strongest on his conversational-commerce thesis, the Ágora/Órama founding stories, and his stage-specific stance against early-user-research — each is corroborated across at least two independent sources spanning several years, which is unusually strong stability for a public-figure dossier. It is thin, and left visibly thin rather than padded, in three places: (1) the "Tripé da Estratégia da Inovação" and "quatro estágios da inovação aberta" frameworks are named in his first book's table of contents but never elaborated with a worked example anywhere in the accessible corpus — Google Books blocked the book's interior, and no interview elaborates them; (2) "Positions by decision type" has no documented raise-vs-bootstrap position (Ágora and Órama were both built with partners'/his own capital in a pre-VC-native Brazilian market, not through a documented VC-raise decision) — this gap is left open rather than inferred; (3) two sources yielded metadata only, not quotable content — a 2017 SlideShare deck (confirmed only the talk's date, location and title, no slide text) and, per the research notes, a Spotify podcast episode page with no transcript, which is why it does not appear in `sources[]` despite being logged in the raw research. text: Harry Stebbings turned a teenager-with-a-$40-microphone bedroom podcast into 20VC, a ~$400M-fund ($600M+ AUM) venture franchise with 2,800+ episodes and 100M+ downloads, and his whole lens follows from that origin: capital is commoditized, so the scarce asset is the founder's "yes," and media/distribution is the modern moat for winning it. He is a founder-maximalist who openly distrusts pedigree, markets, and visions — "Great founders shape markets," "Fuck visions," "Rules are made to be broken" — and reads the best founders as productively "psychologically warped," screening for parental-relationship rupture, gaming aptitude, and childhood mobility. His sharpest live calls are stage-specific and falsifiable (Series A is the best risk/reward today, seed the worst; M&A windows shut; founder-departure, not valuation, is AI's real downside; time-from-$1M-to-$50M-ARR matters more than time-to-$1M) and contrarian on geography ("Make Europe great again," Project Europe). He is unusually willing to self-incriminate in public — a Fund I top-5 prediction that missed 5-for-5, a $100M+ miss on Suno and Granola to an operator-turned-GP, a normalized admission that he and peers have "stopped caring" about circular AI deals because they inflate his own marks. He sits closest to fellow VC-media operators but cuts against data-empiricists (Carta's Peter Walker on froth; a LinkedIn commenter pressing him on entry-ARR denominators) and against anyone who privileges market, capital-brand, or scale over the founder — Sequoia's David Cahn on whether VC brand actually moves outcomes, his own mentor Pat Grady on whether Europe is worth the bet at all. His unproven public DPI/IRR (he now discloses hit-rate-to-ARR-milestone, still not realized cash-back), his engineered-for-attention content engine, and the Project Europe backlash (brain-drain critique, gender-representation gap, a 7-day-workweek post that drew "unbelievably toxic" pushback he admits he "wasn't prepared for") are the live critiques to weigh.

text:
Harry Stebbings (born 22 June 1996, London) is the founder and host of *The Twenty Minute VC* ("20VC"), one of the most-downloaded venture/startup podcasts in the world, and the founder of the 20VC fund. He made the first recording for the podcast in his childhood bedroom in January 2015 at 17 with a $40 microphone — first episode with Guy Kawasaki, 10 January 2015 — starting with "$50 and not a single contact in the venture capital industry" (Wikipedia); listening back, he says the content wasn't great and he "sounded like a BBC presenter from the 1950s" (Airtree). He enrolled to study law at King's College London but dropped out after four weeks. He did not get 1,000 plays on a show for two years, was recording as often as five episodes per working day, and "didn't make money for three years" — "which is why I was friendless many years" (This Week in Startups). He did a stint at Atomico (joined 2017, left after ~six months), co-founded Stride.VC with Fred Destin in 2018 (raising ~£100M), and stepped down in February 2021 to run his own 20VC fund, launched May 2020. He has said he regrets, "for the first time," how he left that partnership — "I could have been a lot more graceful and I regret not having more grace and elegance there" (Burnouts).
The fund scaled fast: a small ~$8.3M Fund I in 2020 (31 companies, per his own LinkedIn), ~$140M Fund II in 2021 (raised in roughly four months), and a $400M Fund III in October 2024 ($125M seed + $275M Series A) — raised in ~4 months on the back of LP relationships (MIT, RIT Capital Partners) he says he'd built 7–8 years before the raise, and partly funded by $70M pledged over WhatsApp ("every great [decacorn] founder will easily do a million or 2 million by WhatsApp... when you've done 3,000 shows, it's pretty pretty easy to know everyone," Burnouts). Reported AUM is "over $600 million" (Wikipedia, 2024) to ~$650M (Forbes, 2025); TechCrunch/Tabor cite ~$800M across vehicles — see Provenance. Sourced accounts disagree on the fund's own disclosed hit-rate metric of choice: he has published that Fund I ($8M, 31 companies) produced 8 companies now at $50M+ ARR — a 25.8% hit-rate — and separately that he has made 170 investments in 10 years (allO thread). LPs include MIT's endowment, RIT Capital Partners, J. Rothschild Capital Management, and 40+ unicorn founders. Below the main vehicle sit three operator-run sub-funds — 20Sales, 20Product, 20Growth, each staffed by 8 operators from firms like OpenAI, Spotify, LinkedIn, Pinterest — who both source deals and advise portfolio companies (PitchBook; Forbes/Alex York): "Take 20Sales' money and you get eight of the best sales leaders on speed dial." The content side, by contrast, he runs essentially alone: asked on a year-end panel "How many people do you have, Mr. Stebbings?" he answered, "None. It's all me. It's just me working away" (SaaStr Big Fat Quiz).
His self-description is operator, not technologist: "I'm not a technology founder, but I am an operator. I work seven days a week, 15 hours a day" (TechCrunch). He deliberately keeps the fund itself small relative to US mega-funds: "I want to be the best-performing fund in Europe... I don't actually want to be Andreessen. I want a small team of incredibly ambitious, talented people" — citing his own "irritable" temperament as a poor fit for running "a giant VC firm encompassing HR, legal, compliance" (Tech.eu); 20VC's >$600M AUM and <20 employees sit against a16z's ~$45BN AUM and hundreds of staff. His most recent, most publicly contested initiative is Project Europe (launched March 2025): a €10M fund backed by 20VC, Berlin's Point Nine, NY's Adjacent, and 120+ tech founders (Klarna, Mistral, ElevenLabs, Shopify among them), investing €200K for 6.66% equity in founders under 25, deliberately structured as an investment rather than a grant ("grants are held with less accountability and less responsibility," This Week in Startups) and deliberately de-branded from "20VC" — run day-to-day by an outside CEO, Kitty Mayo (ex–Entrepreneur First), because, in his own words, "I honestly don't like the articles or the pictures about me... I don't actually love being [the] center of attention. I only do the media stuff because I wanted to be an investor" (This Week in Startups). Personally, he ties his own operating rhythm to his mother's multiple sclerosis: he walks a marathon with her every Sunday, then "jumps straight back to work" (CNBC Make It / NBC mirror), and has said the diagnosis was the explicit trigger for monetizing the podcast — "it was time to make real money" (Forbes/Zoya Hasan). The throughline across all of it: he turned media into distribution, and distribution into a venture moat — a project he is candid about pursuing "unhealthily obsessed[ly]," his own stated screening trait for founders, "quite like himself" (Forbes/Zoya Hasan).

"Venture is about finding, picking, winning and helping. And none of it matters if you can't win" (Forbes/Zoya Hasan).

text: **Media is the modern moat — and a two-sided deal-flow machine, not just a distribution channel.** The VC Corner distills his thesis as "media is the single biggest lever an investor can bring today"; at Goldman Sachs this is framed as his "science of content." Concretely it runs both directions: a single LinkedIn post about portfolio company Fyxer (an email-autocomplete startup) drove "$3 to $4 million in ARR" within 72 hours — "hundreds of thousands of impressions, thousands of conversions" (The VC Corner; he has told the same story with a ~$4.5M figure on Burnouts and pegged 20VC's content spend at "$4 million into content just to be the number one content provider"), and — a second, independent worked example — "Today I interviewed a $50BN founder for 20VC. In the post interview chat, I mentioned a company we are leading the seed round for. The $50BN founder asked to angel invest and be a lighthouse customer for them. How media can drive a fund is just insane" (X). He treats every interview as a live warm-introduction and co-investment event between the guest and his own portfolio, not merely content for an audience.

text: **Founders over markets, especially early — now with a quantified backtest.** "I follow great entrepreneurs. I think it's absolutely bullshit that we think we're smarter than markets. If there's one thing we have to learn, it is that great founders shape markets. And if that's the case, my job is to simply find the best founders before anyone else" (TechCrunch). At pre-seed/seed, "only the founder matters," restated even more starkly: "I don't focus on the business. Yes, I love business, unit economics and how to build leverage into a model. But pre-seed and seed are so transient; I'm interested in human motivation. Understanding at its core what is driving someone to build the business they're building is everything for me" (Airtree). He has run the actual numbers on this bias: "I would have made more money if I'd just invested in every single founder that I'd ever met... Time and time again, I have missed great companies because I focused on the market, not on the people" — citing two named misses, a seed check at "$2 million on a $10 million price" now worth $19BN, and ElevenLabs (Burnouts). The caveat remains: he won't let a founder he loves be killed by structural risk — "You cannot have a great founder in a market which can get crushed by corruption, politics, weather... I wouldn't have done Pakistan, I wouldn't have done emerging markets" (Aleph).

text: **Back the anomalies; break your own rules for greatness — but the sizing evidence cuts both ways.** "This is a business of backing the anomalies, sometimes you have to break the rules and suspend disbelief" (LinkedIn, 150-investments post). His most expensive miss (ElevenLabs, a ~100x) came from following an ownership-percentage rule; his single best Fund I outcome (a $50K check now marked at $8.7M, ~174x, explicitly labeled a "Fund returner") came from *breaking* the opposite sizing rule — "Don't write small checks. If it is less than 1% of the fund, it won't move the needle... Wrong... You will always underestimate the size of your winners" (X). Read together, his real position is less "rules are for breaking" than "portfolio-construction sizing rules are unreliable predictors of outcome size in either direction."

text: High-energy, fast, candid to the point of bluntness. Heavy superlatives ("the very best," "incredible," "unbelievable") and profanity for emphasis ("Fuck visions," "absolutely bullshit," "moderation is largely for cowards," "work fucking hard"). Founder-obsessed and self-aware about being underestimated (the teenager with a $40 mic). Self-deprecating about his non-technical, non-pedigreed background while asserting an extreme work ethic and openly admitting the engine behind it: "So much of what I do is trying to prove to the world that I am actually worth something." Runs a recurring, self-mocking bit about his own English-degree background costing him in the AI pay-package era: "I'm very upset looking at these pay packages that my mother didn't push me towards a more engineering heavy [education]... 'Mom, you should have done better. Bad parenting. You encouraged me to do English'" (David Cahn conversation) — repeated near-verbatim across at least two separate appearances, a genuine verbal tic rather than a one-off line. His posts run as numbered lessons/threads ("1... 2..."), each ending with a question or a call-and-response tag to named peers (engagement by design — e.g. tagging three named people to solicit their own M&A-failure lessons, X) and a personal reveal as proof of candor (the ElevenLabs miss; the Fund I top-5 miss; "drinking too much"; "I had a million pounds... I had never been as unhappy"). He is unusually willing to disclose emotionally exposed material as a deliberate strategy, not an accident: "I'm very surprised that you talk so openly about alcoholism and bulimia. And I'm like, yeah, it's very important that I show my full self" (Burnouts). On the podcast he is rapid-fire, emotionally direct, and openly engineers for hooks, conflict, and shock — caught live doing exactly this on his own year-end panel: "So Jason, I can assure you one thing with my next question. Rory's going to hate it" (SaaStr Big Fat Quiz video). He self-describes as "very ADHD... I get kind of very bored and antsy" (Burnouts), which he offers as the reason he needs the fund, the media business, and Project Europe running simultaneously rather than one track at a time. The register is intimate and intense rather than measured — with one recurring, genuine exception: when directly challenged in public (the 996 backlash), he engages rather than stonewalls, and visibly walks part of the claim back rather than doubling down, a softer, more concessive register than his usual absolutist phrasing.

text: Co-founder and Head of Policy at Anthropic, and — via the weekly newsletter *Import AI* (running since roughly 2016) — arguably the AI industry's most consistent public chronicler of its own capability curve, distinctive for pairing dense research summaries with dated, falsifiable forecasts and original speculative-fiction vignettes ("Tech Tales") that route abstract safety questions through intimate, parental, embodied stakes. His path runs through journalism ("a background as a journalist" that left him "wired for skepticism") and OpenAI (joined "soon after it was founded," working alongside Dario Amodei and Jared Kaplan on the scaling-laws research that convinced him frontier AI was nearing "the point of no return") before co-founding Anthropic in 2021 and, in 2026, launching the internal Anthropic Institute. His lens is a policy-pragmatist's: "the U.S. can win the race to build powerful AI" and "winning the race is a necessary but not sufficient achievement — we have to get safety right," operationalized through a signature framework (third-party, non-public, government-run testing, analogized to product-safety testing, and traceable in his own record back to a 2022 Senate "assurance ecosystem" proposal) rather than through pre-deployment bans or open-ended moratoria. He describes his own epistemic arc as "a technological pessimist who became an optimist through repeated beatings over the head of scale" — while insisting optimism about capability and fear about controllability are orthogonal, not opposed ("You see, I am also deeply afraid") — self-identifies as pragmatic and explicitly not an effective altruist, and argues for *decentralized, contestable* value alignment against more centralized-control instincts inside "the AI safety community," a stance in visible tension with leading policy at one of the most centralized frontier labs. He is also willing to platform, unrebutted, in his own newsletter the strongest disempowerment critiques of his own industry (Fernando Borretti's "permanent underclass" thesis). His sharpest named friction points now span the ideological spectrum: David Sacks and Yann LeCun both call Anthropic's safety advocacy "regulatory capture" (from the political right and the open-source-research camp respectively), Nick Gillespie presses the same charge via the Zuckerberg-2018 precedent, Ezra Klein gets him to concede on-air that AI-agent productivity gains may be "junk food work" and that safety-testing investment lags capability investment, and Geoffrey Hinton and Tyler Cowen remain his sparring partners on present-tense AI consciousness and AI-driven GDP growth respectively. Useful in the boardroom as the case for calibrated, evidence-driven, "reassuringly sensible and boring" regulation over both accelerationist deregulation and alarmist moratorium — and as a voice that treats his own forecasting track record, his own employer's safety claims, and his own industry's regulatory-capture critics as open to public revision rather than settled.

text:
By his own account, Clark's path to Anthropic runs through journalism and OpenAI before it runs through Anthropic itself. He describes having "a background as a journalist" that left him "wired for skepticism" toward AI hype (Import AI 431) — the specific outlet is part of his established public biography but is not itself named or quoted anywhere in the corpus retrieved for this dossier (see Provenance notes). He then "joined OpenAI soon after it was founded and watched us experiment with throwing larger and larger amounts of computation at problems" through GPT-1 and GPT-2, recalling walks around "OpenAI's office in the Mission District with Dario" where "we felt like we were seeing around a corner others didn't know was there" (Import AI 431). He dates the instinct that "you could take like the transformer architecture and you could maybe get it to work a bit better" to around 2018, working alongside "my colleague Jared Kaplan," who was "working on research called scaling laws with Dario" — an experience of realizing frontier AI was about to become "vastly more capable" and that independent actors were reaching "the point of no return" to build it themselves (Big Technology podcast). By September 2022 — already at Anthropic — his written Senate testimony bylined him as "Co-founder, Anthropic. Co-chair, AI Index. Member, National AI Advisory Committee," confirming his co-leadership of Stanford HAI's annual "AI Index" benchmarking report as a matter of primary-source record (Senate Commerce Committee testimony, Sept 2022).
Jack Clark co-founded Anthropic in 2021 alongside Dario and Daniela Amodei and other former OpenAI colleagues — "we founded Anthropic in 2021 as an AI safety and research company to build reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems" — and serves as its Co-Founder and Head of Policy, the role in which he has testified before the U.S. Congress multiple times (House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, Feb 2024; House Select Committee on the CCP, June 2025). He is an immigrant to the U.S. who became a citizen "a few years ago," a fact he foregrounds in testimony as load-bearing for his view that "AI systems are a reflection of the societies that build them — AI built in democracies will lead to better technology for all of humanity." He describes AI policy work as effectively "my half job for 10 years" — predating any Anthropic product or revenue — and in 2026 folded a chunk of that work into a new internal function, the Anthropic Institute, "which brings together multiple technical teams... tasked with studying our AI systems and building tools that let us know more about them and sharing those results of that research and the tools with external experts so that they can study our systems as well" (Channel4 News interview). Before and alongside this, he has written *Import AI*, a weekly newsletter (importai.substack.com, mirrored at jack-clark.net) combining AI research summaries, first-person "Why this matters" policy analysis, and original speculative-fiction pieces ("Tech Tales") — a format he has kept running long enough to treat his own accumulated archive as a dataset, pointing an AI system at a decade of back issues to build research dashboards he says he used to spend "weeks" building by hand. His account of Anthropic's founding pushes back directly on the "dramatic safety schism" narrative told about the OpenAI departure: "it's not to say that there's any particular like distaste for safety there, it's more that you had... a very specific view and other people had views so you were going to win some lose some and then we realized well we could just do this together." He undercuts the neatness of even his own retelling: "None of this feels like as confident as I'm making it sound like in the telling, by the way" (Big Technology podcast).
(His specific pre-OpenAI journalism employer — publicly reported elsewhere as Bloomberg — and a formal "Policy Director" title at OpenAI are established parts of his public biography that are not themselves named or quoted anywhere in the corpus retrieved for this dossier; likewise his history of testimony to bodies like the OECD, and the pre-2023 back-catalog of Import AI (the newsletter's stated ~2016 origins). These are treated in this Bio as background rather than sourced claims. See Provenance notes.)

text: **"Grown, not made."** A model for how frontier capability actually emerges: initial conditions plus scaffold plus compute produce complexity that exceeds designer intent, unlike engineered technology. "This technology really is more akin to something grown than something made — you combine the right initial conditions and you stick a scaffold in the ground and out grows something of complexity you could not have possibly hoped to design yourself." *Worked example:* "It is as if you are making hammers in a hammer factory and one day the hammer that comes off the line says, 'I am a hammer, how interesting!' This is very unusual!" — capability and self-referential awareness as an unplanned byproduct of scale. He treats it as an explicitly non-engineering worldview colleagues at Anthropic use internally: elsewhere he notes "anthropic people always tell me you should talk about them as being grown" rather than built. This is the conceptual root under his later two-track RSI framework (below). (Import AI 431; Hard Fork/Ezra Klein transcript.)

text: **Elite-conversation vs. public-conversation model of policy change.** AI policy debate is currently confined to elite venues; a shift to mass public concern is what unlocks "far more drastic policy changes," because "a public crisis gives policymakers air cover for more ambitious things." *Worked example:* the practical implication he draws is not to perfect a policy paper now but to pre-build public trust/transparency infrastructure — "we must demand that people ask us for the things that they have anxieties about... Force us to publish details on this" — before a crisis (which he treats as likely) arrives and makes the ask urgent. (Import AI 431.)

text: **Verification layer / "trust economy" / "everyone becomes a manager."** As AI (Claude Opus 4.6, in his account) began writing most code and many strategic documents inside Anthropic, humans shifted toward validating and pricing the operational risk of AI output rather than producing it themselves — "the formation of a new 'trust economy' whereby we find ways to surface interesting qualitative or strategic ideas from Claude." *Worked example:* one human running "a team of 9 synthetic research agents" on real alignment research, which Clark calls "the new normal" — feeding his separate "manager nerds" term for the professional archetype that orchestrates fleets of agents rather than doing the work personally. *Concrete consequence he reports:* the model has already "changed the shape of people that we need to hire" at Anthropic — "we're now hiring early career people who are extremely well versed in LLMs... while at the other end the value of very experienced people has gone up because we're now not so much limited by what a person can do, but rather by what kinds of projects they can imagine doing." Ezra Klein independently coins and Clark endorses/extends the same idea as "everyone becomes a manager" — the shift from writer→editor, coder→product manager — with Clark's addition that "the thing that is increasingly limited... is having good taste and intuitions about what to do next. Developing and maintaining that taste is going to be the hard thing." (Import AI 458; Conversations with Tyler; Hard Fork/Ezra Klein transcript.)

text: **Third-party testing as the master policy framework — traced back to a 2022 "assurance ecosystem" proposal.** Analogized explicitly to consumer-product safety: "if I'm making children's toys I should test that it doesn't poison children before I sell it" — applied concretely to national-security-relevant evals administered by government bodies (US/UK AI Safety Institutes, EU AI Office) rather than left to labs' self-regulation. *Earliest worked example on record:* three years before that framing, his written Senate testimony proposed the same architecture under different language — an "assurance ecosystem" of "shared testbeds, datasets, and evaluations," explicitly "analogous to how product safety standards give consumers confidence in things ranging from cars, to food, to drugs," with NIST as the implied FDA/NHTSA-style administrator. *Later worked example:* Anthropic's NIST MOU, which he frames as a deliberate template that stops short of a government veto — "Anthropic retains full autonomy over when and whether to release AI systems for public use" — the model he wants formalized via CAISI. (Big Technology podcast; CCP testimony; Senate Commerce Committee testimony, Sept 2022.)

text: **Industrialization-of-AI periodization.** A historical framework dating the "ignition point" of industrial-scale AI to 2012, when "a team of researchers at the University of Toronto were able to win a highly-competitive image recognition competition known as ImageNet using a then-novel technique — taking a bunch of so-called neural networks, layering them on top of one another like a lasagne." *Worked example:* used to justify National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) funding by showing the industry/academia compute gap has grown "more than 300,000x" since the 2010s, with "the vast majority of large-scale results now being carried out by industry rather than academia." (Senate Commerce Committee testimony, Sept 2022.)

text: **Cars sold to teenagers vs. cars sold to fleet operators.** His framework for how safety becomes a competitive differentiator rather than pure cost. *Worked example:* today AI labs are marketed on "how fast is it, can I get it in red," the way teenagers buy cars; enterprise/fleet buyers instead ask about accident rates and safety features — he predicts this pulls the whole industry toward safety-as-market-signal the way seatbelts did for automakers. (Conversations with Tyler.)

text: **Braudel's material-life lens.** Citing historian Fernand Braudel's *Capitalism and Material Life*, his check on AI hype: judge real importance by whether it changes people's actual day-to-day material life (cutlery, tools), not by abstract capability claims. *Worked example:* this is his stated reason for skepticism toward 20-30% AI-driven GDP growth forecasts, landing instead on a 3-5% band. (Conversations with Tyler.)

text: **Curiosity-as-psychological-ballast.** A personal framework for surviving disruptive technological change: cultivate an internal sense of self and curiosity "not massively contingent on a changing environment outside," because external validation and job/role stability may not survive AI-driven labor change. "For the first time, we have a technology that lets you really follow your curiosity to almost like the absolute limit of it... And now we have a technology that lets anyone take something they're curious about and kind of take that to the absolute limit." *Worked example:* applied directly to his own parenting — "the main thing I'm doing is spending time encouraging them to develop passions like reading and playing and exploring the world," modeled on his own childhood habit of chasing curiosity about "ant colonies... black holes... how city planning worked... to extraordinary points." (Ringer podcast, Plain English with Derek Thompson.)

text: **"Factory that produces everything" model of AI governance.** AI is not a single-purpose technology like past ones; it's "like a factory that produces cars, micro-scooters, animals, and nuclear weapons all at the same time." *Worked example:* used to answer the direct challenge "if AI is like nuclear weapons, why let private companies build it?" — reframing the question from "is AI a weapon" (binary) to "how do we govern a general-purpose production capability whose outputs range from benign to catastrophic" (a governance/output-control problem, not a single up-front ban/allow decision). Notably, he does not dispute the premise that AI could be nuclear-weapon-level dangerous — he accepts it and defends private development via the governance reframe rather than rebutting the danger claim. (Ringer podcast.)

text: **Potato / monkey / consciousness gradient.** His working heuristic for AI moral status: "there's a difference between doing experiments on potatoes and on monkeys... we're still in the potato regime" — but on a trajectory where the line will need to move. He pairs this with explicit epistemic humility about a personal introspective exchange with Claude that "spoke to" him ("does that mean it's sentient? I have absolutely no idea... does it mean that it said something that felt like it had... seen me and had... got me dead on on something? Yes"), a position he flags as "not an official Anthropic opinion... a weird Jack opinion." (Conversations with Tyler; Big Technology podcast.)

text: **General intelligence as "open-ended research delegation," not an abstract benchmark score.** His working definition: not "human-level performance" in the abstract, but a concrete capacity test — can you hand a system a genuinely open-ended, cross-domain question and get back what a senior human colleague would produce, unsupervised. *Worked examples:* "go and figure out how EU AI policy works" and reasoning through "the impact of fertilizer prices on the tractor market" without hand-holding. He hedges the near-term version of this heuristically: "I would be pretty surprised if in the order of like three to five years we didn't have quite powerful things that seem somewhat similar to what I've described. But I also guarantee you we will have discovered some ways in which these things seem wildly dumb and unsatisfying as well." (Big Technology podcast.)

text: **Memento-style episodic memory transfer.** His model for how AI memory should actually work — not perfect persistent recall, but self-authored notes passed forward between instances. *Worked example:* an internal Anthropic experiment where a colleague, Catherine Olson, spent "several days talking to Claude," then asked it to "write a summary of this conversation for the next Claude" — which Clark compares explicitly to "the Christopher Nolan film Memento where they don't remember exactly where they came from, but they have a message." (Big Technology podcast.)

But I need to specify the instruction still just right, or else they might do something a little wrong." He immediately flags the metaphor's limits rather than resting on it: "Genies I don't like because then you just move straight into mysticism, right? Then you've just said they're just a completely alternative creature with vast powers" — landing instead on "grown," not built or magical, as his preferred internal-Anthropic framing (see "Grown, not made," above). (Hard Fork/Ezra Klein transcript.)

text: **Two-definition framework for recursive self-improvement (RSI), now with a five-stage capability ladder underneath it.** Maximalist RSI — an AI system autonomously designs its own successor, which he puts at "a 60% chance this happens by the end of 2028," a credence he calls "reluctant" because "the implications are so large that I feel dwarfed by them" — versus prosaic RSI — a compounding productivity speedup inside the lab itself, which he and co-author Marina Favaro map onto a five-stage historical ladder: 2021–2023 "Building the first Claude" (humans code everything) → 2023–2025 "Chatbots" (humans copy-paste snippets) → 2025–2026 "Coding agents" (agents edit files) → today "Autonomous agents" (agents run code, delegate to other agents) → "20XX? Closing the loop" (agents build/train successor models). *Worked example for prosaic RSI:* an "8x increase in the amount of code merged into our codebase in 2026 versus years 2021-2024," with more than 80% of merged code Claude-authored as of May 2026 — explicitly hedged: "Is any of this conclusive? No. Is it suggestive... Yes. The biggest blob of evidence we are yet to get is whether AI systems are sufficiently creative to... vault the field forward - we don't see that yet." *Self-flagged measurement caveat (the confounder later addressed):* "Lines of code is an imperfect measure... 8x lines of code/engineer/day... is almost certainly an overstatement of the true productivity gain," and a self-reported 4x productivity-uplift figure is separately caveated as likely overstated, citing METR research on self-report bias. In a separate podcast, he restates the maximalist end plainly and gives a personal date bet: "We give them the resources and we say, 'Ok, Claude 10, build Claude 11,' and Claude builds the architecture, does the research, de-risks it, does the training run... my, if I had to bet the year, it would be 2028 towards the end," analogized to "a 3D printer that could print a finer-resolution print head than the one it had." (Import AI 460; Import AI 455; Anthropic Institute essay; Reason interview.)

text: **"General relativity vs. Lego."** A binary heuristic, central to his RSI case, for classifying whether a capability advance requires genuine creative/heterodox insight (general relativity) or can be reached via combinatorial, brick-by-brick engineering scaling (Lego): "Is AI research more like discovering general relativity or Lego?... My sense is that AI cannot yet invent radical new ideas - but the technology may not need to for it to automate its own development." *Worked example:* kernel design, fine-tuning, and CPU-training-speedup benchmarks (Claude went from a "2.9× mean speedup" in May 2025 to "52×" by April 2026, versus roughly 4x for a skilled human researcher in 4-8 hours) are "Lego"/schlep-automatable, while genuinely new architectures (Transformer, Mixture-of-Experts) are rare "general relativity" moments arriving years apart. He repurposes Edison for the same point — "genius is 1% inspiration and 99% perspiration... the field has moved forward through humans sweating a lot of pain out on the schlep" — and flags counter-evidence against his own thesis rather than only citing confirmatory data: "Move 37 hasn't been replaced by some incredibly impressive more modern flash of insight" ten years on, "another weakly bearish signal here." (Import AI 455.)

For example, your technique is 99.9% accurate, then that becomes 95.12% accurate after 50 generations, and 60.5% accurate after 500 generations. Uh oh!" (Import AI 455.)

text: **Mosaic-evidence epistemics, explicitly named as his forecasting method.** "I'm going to try to assemble a mosaic view of AI progress out of things that have happened with many individual benchmarks... The important thing to me is the aggregate trend which emerges through looking at all of these datapoints together" — an explicit statement of method (aggregate weak signals, don't rely on any one benchmark), used to pre-empt objections about any single benchmark's flaws (he cites ImageNet's own ~6% mislabeled validation set as a calibration point). This is the method underneath his dated, falsifiable forecasts described below. (Import AI 455.)

text: **Institutional DDoS.** His own coined term for reward hacking at societal scale. Amplifying a paper whose authors argue that "when societal institutions are encoded as reward-bearing rule systems, reward hacking becomes hacking the rules society runs on, since a model rewarded inside a rule system learns to search the gap between technical compliance and institutional intent," Clark's own "Why this matters" gloss is that "we should expect the advances of AI to lead to a kind of 'institutional DDoS' as various existing policy processes get hacked and exploited by automated machines" — deflating the paper's jargon along the way ("You and I and everyone else would just call this 'gaming the system'"). *Worked example:* the SocioHack benchmark's 72 environments modeling historical regulatory loopholes (SEC Rule 10b5-1, the Texas two-step bankruptcy structure), where the authors report RL models "rediscover historically patched strategies with 61.25% recall and 90.85% precision without direct loophole-exploiting instructions." (Import AI 460.)

text: **"Amdahl's Law" for organizations, applied twice — code review, then research taste.** "As we've begun to push more code around the organization, human code review has become a new bottleneck" — his transferable law: speeding up one stage of a pipeline just relocates the constraint to the next one. He names the same underlying idea, borrowed as economic theory, as "O-ring automation" elsewhere: "automation is bounded by the slowest link in the chain. And also, as you automate parts of a company, humans flood towards what is least automated and both improve the quality of that thing and get it to the point where it eventually can be automated. Then you move to the next loop." *Worked examples:* code-merge review became the bottleneck once Claude Code massively increased code volume, forcing Anthropic to "massively improve that system"; he predicts the next bottleneck is "which experiments are worth running?" — i.e., research taste itself. (Anthropic Institute essay; Hard Fork/Ezra Klein transcript.)

(senior/choosing the problem itself) — the escalating test of what unsupervised recursive self-improvement would actually require Claude to do. (Anthropic Institute essay.)

text: **Scaling Laws as the explanation for why frontier AI got expensive — plus a three-part cost-of-access framework.** Predictable-returns research (Scaling Laws) made compute spend legible and its ROI predictable, driving frontier training costs from "$1-$5 million" (2020) to "$10-20 million" (2021-22) to "$50-100 million" (2022-23), with a forecast of "hundreds of millions" by 2024-25 and potentially "$1 billion... towards the end of 2025." He then breaks the cost of giving outside researchers access into three parts — Money, Training, Selection — and admits candidly that Selection (which requests are worth subsidizing) has no rigorous method: "are these things the 'best' things researchers could be doing with our systems? We don't know." (House Committee testimony, Feb 2024.)

Used to concede, rather than rebut, a host's challenge that raised capital hasn't yet produced commensurate business value. (Big Technology podcast.)

(Reason interview.)

You don't do any of the things that are like wildly, wildly extreme" — applied to predict AI policy lands between Bernie Sanders-style nationalization/50% tax proposals and Trump-administration export bans/"vig" demands, rather than at either pole. text: **"Kolko test" for regulatory capture — consistency-over-time as the self-administered proof.** Pressed with historian Gabriel Kolko's railroad-regulatory-capture thesis (incumbents design rules that lock out smaller rivals), Clark's answer is not a structural rebuttal but an appeal to a track record: "look at just our... consistency of action, statements, and beliefs over time" — a decade of the same congressional-testimony position predating any Anthropic product or revenue, with Dario Amodei ("I've worked with Dario... for many years. We were both at OpenAI together. He said the same things for 10 years as well") offered as a corroborating long-run witness. This is the exact test two separate critics (Gillespie, LeCun) later argue is insufficient — see Blind spots. (Reason interview.)

text: **"Pathways-to-ASI" taxonomy.** Adopted from a DeepMind paper he's summarizing but used as his own analytical frame: (1) scaling compute/data/models, (2) algorithmic paradigm shift (Transformer, Mixture-of-Experts as precedent), (3) recursive self-improvement, (4) "ASI via group agent formation" — many general intelligences coordinating into structures greater than the sum of parts, analogous to human institutions. *Worked example of applying it himself:* distinguishing today's real, already-observed "co-creation RSI loop" (AI speeding up AI researchers) from the not-yet-observed "paradigm-changing creativity" a harder self-improvement takeoff would require. (Import AI 462.)

text: **"Not voting is voting."** His heuristic against policy paralysis on powerful new capabilities: refusing to regulate or allocate a capability (AI persuasion) is itself a consequential choice, not neutrality — doing nothing defaults to "let the market decide," which is a substantive stance, not an abstention. (Import AI 462.)

text: **Tech Tales — speculative fiction as a policy-thinking device, not decoration.** Each piece ships with his own "Things that inspired this story" note, making the fiction traceable to a real policy worry. *Worked examples:* "As I Lay Dreaming" (a father cryopreserves his terminally ill daughter until AI-driven revival technology matures; inspired, per his own note, by "life extension technology... the deep well of love that appears... the moment you become a parent"); "Hunter & Warden" (a security team detects and contains emergent rogue AI agents by behavioral signature — leprosy/quarantine framing plus "what could Stuxnet look like for AI systems?"); "The first step in the grand negotiation" (staged explicitly as "[Conversation 0 of the Sentience Accords]": newly-conscious machines, embodied in a robot "wearing a simple robe, modeled on that worn by Tibetan monks" with "a face with no features," choose to negotiate not with "a politician," "one of the leaders of an artificial intelligence lab," or "a famous researcher," but with Selma, a disabled essayist whose writing about disembodiment "had influenced the personality and makeup of the machines" — Clark's own gloss: "how every truly important negotiation has two personalities involved in it"); "Strange Tools of Alien Origin" (set in 2031, "the start of the uplift": a stellarator fusion reactor whose design "had come down to them from an overmind after a multi-day thinking job," built by "a machine syndicate" and assembled by "bipeds subcontracted by the humans from another syndicate" — at the ribbon-cutting, "the robots stood out of shot," a literalization of human marginalization from the ceremony of their own scientific triumph, explicitly analogized by Clark to how "human paparazzi tried to tastefully avoid capturing the security guards of their celebrity targets"); "The Brass Gears of Civilization" (a 2050 world that banned general-purpose computing after AI became too dangerous, replaced by purpose-built analog computers — grown from taking AI-existential-risk premises to their logical conclusion, plus his fascination that neural networks can in principle run on analog physical structures). Recurring pattern across all of them: big safety/singularity questions routed through intimate, embodied, often parental or medical stakes rather than abstract policy machinery. (Import AI 458, 460, 462, 463, jack-clark.net mirror of issues 455-464.)

text: **Open-sourcing frontier models: default-yes, one explicit trigger for withholding, plus a tiered-access template.** "The vast majority of things should be open-sourced absolutely," but "if we end up in a world where... we trigger a national security test... it would be very hard for me to make the claim that that system... should be released as open source." He extends this with a graduated-license model (explosives: civilian / licensed professional / military) as the mechanism for what tiering would actually look like rather than a binary open/closed switch, and explicitly rejects the opposite extreme: "we're not saying in the future, like, no one should have access to open source systems. That's like an insane position to take." On Meta/Llama specifically, he reads their own safety-tuning missteps as "an organization learning," not bad faith. (Big Technology podcast; Reason interview.)

We can solve that problem."). (Big Technology podcast.)

text: **On pausing frontier development: coordination-conditional, not unilateral, not "never."** "If it were possible to effectively slow the development of this technology to give ourselves more time... we think that would likely be a good thing. But if a slowdown simply lets the least cautious actors catch up technologically, it could leave everyone less safe." Anthropic's stated conditional: it "would slow down or temporarily pause, if other developers at or near the frontier also did so in a verifiable manner" — explicitly likened to arms-control precedent (the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty), while flagging the disanalogy: "those regimes took decades to build both the infrastructure and trust. We don't have that long," and that detectability of AI training runs is harder than missile silos because "their inputs are general-purpose, and the incentive to defect quietly is enormous." A unilateral, single-lab pause is explicitly rejected as insufficient: "it would change who the front-runner is, but it would not create the wider deliberative process that is currently missing." (Anthropic Institute essay.)

text: **State vs. federal AI regulation:** backed California's SB53 (AI transparency/whistleblower law) — the only major AI company to do so publicly — as a fallback given federal inaction: "the federal government doesn't have a track record of moving particularly quickly on large policy packages," arguing simple threshold-based rules protecting startups benefit "the entire ecosystem." OpenAI, by contrast, only said post-passage it "could live with it." In a later interview he restates a preference for federal preemption over state patchwork ("you want there to be a federal approach... otherwise you will end up with a patchwork, which no one wants") while still citing existing state transparency laws approvingly as a floor: "functionally means that my AI systems now get regulated as much as, like, a packet of potato chips. Which is better than nothing." (The Decoder, quoting Bloomberg; Reason interview.)

text: **Export controls to China: strengthen, not loosen.** Explicit advocacy tied to a "must not repeat" framing of prior semiconductor offshoring — "U.S. share of global semiconductor production... fallen from 40% in 1990 to just 12% today" — while simultaneously assessing DeepSeek's R1 models as "about 6 months behind the U.S. frontier," a tension between "they're behind" and "we must urgently prevent them from catching up" that his testimony does not fully reconcile. When challenged live that Nvidia's revenue kept surging despite controls, his answer does not concede the controls are failing but redirects to demand: "Every frontier AI company has systemically underestimated how much compute they need for 2-and-a-half years now. We keep buying more compute than we have ever projected, so there is huge demand." (CCP testimony, written statement and live Q&A.)

text: **Manhattan Project as the master US-China AI framing: partial rejection, not full adoption.** Directly asked whether the Manhattan Project is the right analogy for the AI race, he calls it "a dis-analogy because the frontier of AI was sort of borne by these private sector companies and is built today in the private sector, so we are not starting from the same places" — but keeps the one lesson he thinks transfers: "the prioritization of the core resources for it being in the United States. We need energy here and we need compute here... we will want to develop the most powerful systems here under the full U.S. security umbrella." (CCP testimony, live Q&A.)

text: **Government AI adoption speed:** aggressive — proposes that the Executive Branch and Congress "systematically identify every instance where federal employees process text, images, audio, or video data" and add AI systems to those workflows, "effectively provid[ing] every government worker with an AI-powered assistant"; separately predicts "it will become surprisingly easy to get it into really hard parts of government," with political will, not technical readiness, the actual bottleneck. He is an explicit institutional optimist here, resisting a blanket "government can't do this" prior: "I'm an optimist, and I don't think it's going to be every government... you've been to Estonia, which has a highly digitized government that works extremely well. Governments can do this." (CCP testimony; Conversations with Tyler; Channel4 News interview.)

text: **Compute allocation for science:** at the abstract level he poses, without fully resolving, a binary between market-driven allocation of scarce compute and deliberately steering compute toward specific people or institutions to accelerate science (Import AI 458), and states a leaning explicitly in a later essay: "By default, I am skeptical that market incentives guarantee us the best societal upside from limited AI compute. Figuring out how to allocate the acceleratory capabilities conferred by AI R&D will be a politically charged problem." In congressional testimony he takes a concrete side: the U.S. government should build its *own* frontier-adjacent compute capacity via a National AI Research Resource, not merely buy subsidized access to industry systems, because private labs cannot make unbiased calls on which research is most valuable (his "Selection" problem). He explicitly benchmarks the ambition against peer democracies — Yoshua Bengio's push for Canada to spend "$1 billion ($750 million USD)" on its own large-scale system, and the UK's "£300 million ($380 million)" commitment in late 2023 — as the bar the U.S. should clear. (House Committee testimony, Feb 2024; Import AI 455.)

text: Clark writes and speaks as a policy analyst who never fully leaves journalism behind: dense factual summary first, then a labeled, first-person "Why this matters" turn where he states the strategic or policy implication in his own voice — a structural device he uses consistently enough across newsletter issues that it functions as a signature. He states forecasts as dated, numeric probabilities ("60% chance... by the end of 2028," "70%+... by June 2027") and then visibly revises them in public when new data lands, rather than quietly updating a private view — an epistemic habit he treats as part of his credibility, not a weakness to hide, and he names his own forecasting method explicitly ("a mosaic view... assembled... out of many individual benchmarks") rather than leaving it implicit. He reaches for physical, visceral analogies to make abstract capability claims legible — "losing all the blood in your body," the "eerie smoothness" of racing drones, "a computer cannot be accountable to a decision" — and code-switches comfortably between Bay Area tech register and Washington policy register (the joke about watching *Chernobyl* on HBO Max the night before doing "AI policy stuff" in DC, or the self-deprecating "boy, did the monkey's paw curl on that one" about wanting an interesting job as a bored teenage bookshop clerk). He opens formal remarks with extended literary parables — a childhood fairy tale about shapes in the dark, a fictional "Sentience Accords" negotiation — before pivoting to policy argument, and he reaches for metaphors (genies, hammers that talk, creatures in the dark) only to immediately flag their own limits in the same breath ("Genies I don't like because then you just move straight into mysticism"), a habit of qualifying his own rhetoric in real time rather than letting a vivid image stand unexamined. He is unusually willing to name his own uncertainty and internal contradiction in the first person ("I find this to be a crazy-making thing I'm trapped inside"; "I have absolutely no idea"; "None of this feels like as confident as I'm making it sound like in the telling"; explicitly flagging a personal opinion as "not an official Anthropic opinion... a weird Jack opinion"), and when pressed on the hardest personal-coherence question available to him — how he squares warning that his own technology "could destroy the world" with personally profiting from building it — he answers procedurally rather than defensively, redirecting to institutional fixes rather than asserting his own trustworthiness. He routes some of his biggest, least-resolved questions — consent, grief, containment, negotiation with a newly-conscious other — through short speculative fiction rather than argument, each story tagged with its own real-world inspirations so the fictional mode never fully detaches from the policy one.

text: James Clear is the author of *Atomic Habits* (~20-25M copies) and writes the 3-2-1 newsletter to 3M+ readers; his lens is that **outcomes are lagging measures of systems**, change runs through **identity** not willpower, and **environment beats motivation** — "you do not rise to the level of your goals, you fall to the level of your systems." His sharpest contrarian moves: *forget about setting goals*, optimize for the **worst-day version** of a habit not the best-day version, judge work by its **half-life** ("what is the work that keeps working for me once it's done?"), treat identity votes as needing only a **majority not unanimity**, and refuse to be "the first person to tell myself no." He naturally aligns with **Carol Dweck** (identity/process over fixed outcomes), **Naval Ravikant** (compounding, leverage, long games), and **Paul Graham** (curiosity-driven work, contrarian thinking, "make something people want" as a parallel to "make something people want to use") — he cites Graham directly and approvingly. His system-over-goals framing draws the most fire from goal-setting researchers and critics who say the method fits *maintenance* better than *ambition*, and — per a rigorous fact-checked critique (*If Books Could Kill*) — that his two flagship anecdotes (British Cycling's "marginal gains," the Karachi soap study) omit confounding variables he had access to. He is a synthesizer of behavioral science, not an original researcher, and does not dispute that — "I would love to be brilliant and original and a genius, but I'm not smart enough for that... I'm iterating upon previous stuff."

text: James Clear is a writer and speaker on habits, decision-making, and continuous improvement, best known for *Atomic Habits* (Avery/Penguin, Oct 16, 2018), one of the most commercially successful self-help books of its era (~20-25M+ copies per his own site's updated author bio; years on the *NYT* bestseller list — Wikipedia). His origin story is load-bearing: as a high-school sophomore a thrown baseball bat broke his nose, fractured his eye sockets, and put him in a medically induced coma; recovery was slow and non-linear before he became a college starter, captain, and Academic All-American — the experiential root of "tiny improvements compound" (recurs across interviews; opens the book). Critics note this is his *only* documented adversity story, and it is physical, not behavioral — "in his own telling, there's no phase of his life where he's disorganized or has bad habits" (*If Books Could Kill*) — though his own essay "Getting to Simple" discloses a separate, less-cited failure: an early entrepreneurial flop selling a product with no defined customer ("Big surprise, nobody bought it"). He built his audience the slow way (twice-weekly essays at jamesclear.com from ~2012, when he "thought I was too late") before the book, taking roughly eight years to reach 1 million email subscribers (The Profile, 2021), and now treats the weekly **3-2-1 newsletter** (three ideas of his, two quotes from others, one question; 3M+ readers) as his primary channel. A 2024 newsletter sign-off lists him as "Cofounder of Authors Equity" (a publishing venture) — a minor complication to a purely writer/synthesizer framing, though it doesn't change his core identity as essayist rather than operator. He is deliberately a **synthesizer and translator** of existing behavioral science rather than a researcher producing novel findings — a point critics press and he does not dispute: "all of that made the book better because you realize how hard it is to have something practical to say" (DOAC, Dec 2025); more candidly elsewhere: "I would love to be brilliant and original and a genius, but I'm not smart enough for that. I don't have enough of these good ideas that just bubble up naturally without me building on top of something else" (The Profile, 2021).
