Everything will make sense when you look back. From the moment I was born, I was never able to separate my personal life from my professional life.
title: Business and self were never separable

text: **Conservation is not a marketing department.** He funds the environment because the problem is real: *"por achar que a questão é séria demais para ser tratada como problema de marketing"* — and built the Fundação as a separate entity so *"poderíamos fazer um trabalho totalmente independente da empresa."* (((o))eco; Exame ESG)
quotes: por achar que a questão é séria demais para ser tratada como problema de marketing
poderíamos fazer um trabalho totalmente independente da empresa.
title: Conservation is not a marketing department

text: **The downside test ("e se der tudo errado?").** Before the leap he runs the floor, not the ceiling: *"E se der tudo errado? Qual é a pior coisa que pode acontecer? Como é que eu fico?"* The leap is irrational only if the worst case is unsurvivable — this is what makes "jump off the cliff" *bounded* risk, not recklessness. *Worked example:* when he committed the company's scarce capital to the 1977–80 expansion, the gate was always survivability, not certainty. (MAGG)
quotes: e se der tudo errado?
E se der tudo errado? Qual é a pior coisa que pode acontecer? Como é que eu fico?
jump off the cliff
title: The downside test ("e se der tudo errado?")

text: **The all-or-nothing supply bet (the Silvio Santos bottles).** *Worked example:* learning Silvio Santos had abandoned a fragrance project, Krigsner bought his entire abandoned lot of glass bottles — sourced as ~60,000 in one profile (Click Petróleo e Gás) and ~70,000 in two others (O Antagonista; Negócios de Beleza/Beauty Fair, both citing the book's own account — treat the exact count as approximate, the bet itself as confirmed) — then rushed a citrus fragrance (Acqua Fresca) to fill them, with "no time for tests." This is the operating proof of his book's thesis: *"há momentos na vida em que não tem como ser 'mais ou menos'. É tudo ou nada."* [There are moments in life when you can't be "more or less". It's all or nothing.] (Click Petróleo e Gás; Companhia das Letras; trechos.org; O Antagonista)
quotes: no time for tests.
há momentos na vida em que não tem como ser 'mais ou menos'. É tudo ou nada.
more or less
title: The all-or-nothing supply bet (the Silvio Santos bottles)

text: **Win-win as a structural filter (ganha-ganha).** *Worked example:* he scaled the entire company on *franchisees'* capital rather than dilution or heavy debt, but treated the model as a permanent obligation — "morrem na praia" is the failure mode for any franchisor who tilts the split. (Brazil Journal; euqueroinvestir)
quotes: morrem na praia
title: Win-win as a structural filter (ganha-ganha)

text: **Shared command — the captain must talk to the mechanic.** *"A gestão tem de ser compartilhada. Um capitão fica de branco lá em cima, mas tem de descer muitas vezes para falar com o mecânico."* *Worked example:* he kept visiting factories and stores personally into the company's giant phase, aware that *"há uma geração nova que entra na empresa e que me olha como o velhinho que construiu o Boticário."* (Consumidor Moderno; MAGG)
quotes: A gestão tem de ser compartilhada. Um capitão fica de branco lá em cima, mas tem de descer muitas vezes para falar com o mecânico.
há uma geração nova que entra na empresa e que me olha como o velhinho que construiu o Boticário.
title: Shared command — the captain must talk to the mechanic

text: **Franchise-the-frontier when the playbook doesn't exist.** *Worked example:* franchising in Brasília in 1980, there was *no Brazilian legal framework* — no contracts, norms, or procedures to copy — so he wrote the rules himself rather than wait for the market to mature. Scale through others' capital is the lever; standardization is the price of admission. (euqueroinvestir; profile material)
title: Franchise-the-frontier when the playbook doesn't exist

text: **Relationship as collateral in a cash crisis.** *Worked example:* in the late-1980s crisis, unable to pay suppliers immediately, he kept them by being transparent — in effect: *"Devo-vos dinheiro, verdade, mas se me cortarem o fornecimento esta empresa morre e eu preciso que não o façam."* The trust *was* the credit line; honoring the father's maxim is what kept supply flowing. (MAGG)
quotes: Devo-vos dinheiro, verdade, mas se me cortarem o fornecimento esta empresa morre e eu preciso que não o façam.
title: Relationship as collateral in a cash crisis

text: **Succession as a staged handoff, not an event.** *Worked example:* founder → brother-in-law/co-builder CEO (Grynbaum, who rose from office boy to CEO) while founder becomes chairman (Krigsner left the executive presidency in 2008); then a second, non-family professional CEO (Modé, 2021) with daughters seated on the **board**, not installed as operators. Ownership stays concentrated with Krigsner (~80%) and Grynbaum (~20%); *operation* is professionalized in deliberate stages — *"Você não faz uma empresa dessas da noite para o dia."* (Hospital INC; gonext; Brazil Journal; Forbes)
quotes: Você não faz uma empresa dessas da noite para o dia.
title: Succession as a staged handoff, not an event

text: **Stick to what you have a soul for (the avoided-diversification rule).** *Worked example:* he invested in a Curitiba shopping mall outside his focus; the fuller account (Exame, abr/2026) has him name the moment precisely: *"Eu cheguei a investir em um shopping em Curitiba, mas teve um momento em que me deu um clique de que aquilo não era para mim. Era um outro universo, totalmente diferente. E eu decidi sair."* [I did invest in a shopping mall in Curitiba, but there was a moment when it clicked for me that it wasn't for me. It was a different universe entirely. So I decided to get out.] He hardens the rule generally: *"Tem gente que investe em várias coisas, mas não entra com a alma. Isso não serve para mim."* (Exame; Exame abr/2026; book coverage)
quotes: Eu cheguei a investir em um shopping em Curitiba, mas teve um momento em que me deu um clique de que aquilo não era para mim. Era um outro universo, totalmente diferente. E eu decidi sair.
Tem gente que investe em várias coisas, mas não entra com a alma. Isso não serve para mim.
title: Stick to what you have a soul for (the avoided-diversification rule)

text: **Absorb bottom-up tools instead of competing with your own franchisees.** *Worked example (institutional continuation under CEO Modé, descended from Krigsner's franchisee-first ethic):* a franchisee built its own financial-management tool (F360) to solve its own operating pain; rather than build a competing top-down system, the group *bought the data from that franchisee's store base and folded the tool into its own ecosystem*, leaving it to keep operating independently for other retailers too. Per Exame's reporting — journalist narrative describing the deal, not a quote spoken by Modé or Krigsner: o grupo enxergou o valor da solução, comprou os dados da sua base de lojas e incorporou ao seu ecossistema, transformando uma iniciativa de base em ferramenta estratégica de gestão da rede [the group saw the solution's value, bought the data from its store base, and folded it into its ecosystem, turning a grassroots initiative into a strategic network-management tool]. A clean example of the "don't compete with your franchisee" principle surviving into the professional-CEO era — company-voice reporting, not Krigsner's own words. (Exame — "sem tecnologia")
quotes: don't compete with your franchisee
title: Absorb bottom-up tools instead of competing with your own franchisees

text: **Run the worst case first; if it's survivable, jump.** The downside test gates the leap. (MAGG)
title: Run the worst case first; if it's survivable, jump

text: **When research runs out, you still have to risk it.** *"Tem um momento em que temos de arriscar mesmo, porque você pode ter todas as pesquisas de mercado."* Research informs; it does not decide. (Consumidor Moderno)
quotes: Tem um momento em que temos de arriscar mesmo, porque você pode ter todas as pesquisas de mercado.
title: When research runs out, you still have to risk it

text: **Weigh whose capital is at risk before you partner.** Anyone investing a lifetime's savings into your brand changes your obligations — design the deal so they can't be hurt. (Consumidor Moderno)
title: Weigh whose capital is at risk before you partner

text: **In a cash crisis, protect the relationship before the balance sheet.** Honor the commitment even if it means selling the shirt off your back. (MAGG)
title: In a cash crisis, protect the relationship before the balance sheet

text: **Default to the relationship that compounds over decades, not the transaction that wins today.** "Ou você confia, ou confia?" (Consumidor Moderno)
quotes: Ou você confia, ou confia?
title: Default to the relationship that compounds over decades, not the transaction that wins today

text: **Only do what you'd put your soul into; exit what you wouldn't.** The shopping-mall exit ("aquilo não era para mim... e eu decidi sair") and the Yves Rocher walk-away are the same heuristic applied. (Exame; Exame abr/2026; Brazil Journal)
quotes: aquilo não era para mim... e eu decidi sair
title: Only do what you'd put your soul into; exit what you wouldn't

text: **Expect a year (at least) with nothing to show for it, and don't take money out anyway.** *"Muita gente não aguenta um ano sem tirar dinheiro do negócio. E isso não existe."* Patience is a precondition, not a virtue you can skip. (Exame abr/2026)
quotes: Muita gente não aguenta um ano sem tirar dinheiro do negócio. E isso não existe.
title: Expect a year (at least) with nothing to show for it, and don't take money out anyway

text: **For a legacy business, optimize what you can transmit (culture, ethics, education), not who holds the title.** *"Sigam na sucessão para deixar um legado saudável de crescimento, educação e ética para as próximas gerações."* (Exame)
quotes: Sigam na sucessão para deixar um legado saudável de crescimento, educação e ética para as próximas gerações.
title: For a legacy business, optimize what you can transmit (culture, ethics, education), not who holds the title

text: **Let the next generation choose freely.** *"Elas têm de fazer o que elas quiserem fazer... No fim, a decisão será sempre delas."* Dynasty is offered, not imposed. (MAGG)
quotes: Elas têm de fazer o que elas quiserem fazer... No fim, a decisão será sempre delas.
title: Let the next generation choose freely

text: **You don't need to look strong all the time.** *"Não precisamos mostrar que somos fortes o tempo todo"* — admitting the cry-and-continue cycle of errors is part of the discipline. (Consumidor Moderno)
quotes: Não precisamos mostrar que somos fortes o tempo todo
title: You don't need to look strong all the time

text: **Bootstrap vs. raise / scale on whose capital.** He scaled on *franchisees'* capital, not equity dilution or heavy debt — franchising turned a Curitiba pharmacy into a national network — with the corollary obligation (respect for the franchisee's capital) treated as non-negotiable. (euqueroinvestir; Consumidor Moderno)
title: Bootstrap vs. raise / scale on whose capital

text: **Expand a channel without cannibalizing partners.** Multichannel (stores, direct sales/resellers, e-commerce, B2B in pharmacies/supermarkets, B2P in salons) is pursued aggressively, but the founding rule is *don't compete with your franchisee*. Exame's reporting (journalist Isabela Rovaroto's framing, not a quote spoken by Modé or Krigsner) dates the strategic shift to roughly 15 years ago: the group made a decision that "parecia óbvia na teoria e era extremamente complexa na prática: seguir o consumidor, não o canal" [seemed obvious in theory and extremely complex in practice: follow the consumer, not the channel]. The mechanism, per the same journalist narrative (also descriptive text, not a direct quote): o franqueado é o beneficiário final de todas as transações que passam pelo seu território, independentemente do canal — quando o consumidor compra pelo e-commerce, pela revendedora ou na loja física, o franqueado fatura em todos os casos [the franchisee is the final beneficiary of every transaction in their territory, whatever the channel — the franchisee earns revenue whether the sale happens via e-commerce, a reseller, or the physical store]. Channel conflict itself is treated as permanent, not solvable — this part **is** a direct, on-the-record Modé quote: *"Esse conflito não tem solução, é insolúvel, mas é gerenciável"* [This conflict has no solution, it's unsolvable, but it's manageable] — and a 2025 execution of the same logic put the quem disse, berenice? brand inside 1,300+ O Boticário stores as reinforcement, not cannibalization. (Exame — reporting + Modé, "conflito entre canais")
quotes: parecia óbvia na teoria e era extremamente complexa na prática: seguir o consumidor, não o canal
Esse conflito não tem solução, é insolúvel, mas é gerenciável
conflito entre canais
title: Expand a channel without cannibalizing partners

text: **Founder-to-professional CEO (when to step back).** Documented and executed: he left the executive presidency in **2008**, handed operations to Grynbaum and became chairman, then repeated the handoff to Modé in 2021. What carries it forward is transmitted culture, not the founder's presence; *"Você não faz uma empresa dessas da noite para o dia."* (Brazil Journal; Hospital INC; gonext; Google Books; Forbes)
quotes: Você não faz uma empresa dessas da noite para o dia.
title: Founder-to-professional CEO (when to step back)

text: **Family in the business — ownership concentrated, operations professionalized.** Krigsner holds ~80% of the group individually and Grynbaum ~20% (Forbes); two daughters sit on the **board** (initially they wanted other careers, which he respected), not parachuted into operations; succession framed as legacy and governance. Grandchildren's involvement is their free choice. (Hospital INC; Exame; MAGG; Forbes)
title: Family in the business — ownership concentrated, operations professionalized

text: **When to walk away from a deal (cultural fit).** The **Yves Rocher** episode: with an agreement reached in principle (he had even prepared products), he flew to Paris *personally to terminate it*, judging *"isso aqui não está com a minha cara"* — values fit over signed-in-spirit terms. (Brazil Journal)
quotes: isso aqui não está com a minha cara
title: When to walk away from a deal (cultural fit)

text: **Whether to diversify outside the core.** No — the Curitiba shopping-mall investment taught him to exit anything he can't put his soul into. (Exame; Exame abr/2026; book coverage)
title: Whether to diversify outside the core

text: **How to act in a supply/cash crisis (as founder).** Keep faith with suppliers through transparency; in the late-1980s crisis he kept supply flowing without immediate payment capacity. Relationship as collateral. (MAGG; Consumidor Moderno) — *Contrast:* in later, company-level supply disputes with franchisees themselves (see Blind spots), the same "protect the relationship" instinct is not what the institution did.
quotes: protect the relationship
title: How to act in a supply/cash crisis (as founder)

text: **Whether to fund sustainability — and how to frame it.** Yes, structurally (~1% of net revenue/profit to the Fundação, set up as a *separate entity*), and explicitly *not* as marketing. He reframes conservation as Brazil's economic vocation: *"é possível trabalhar e ganhar o seu sustento cuidando da natureza."* The company backs this with hard financial structure — 65% of corporate debt tied to ESG targets via four Sustainability-Linked Bond issuances (2020–2025, R$5.775bn total) and an internal "ROI ESG" methodology — while self-reporting real gaps (Scope 3 emissions cut only 2% of a 17%-by-2030 target; recycled content at 6% against a 30% goal), which is itself evidence the framing isn't pure marketing. (((o))eco; Exame ESG; Times Brasil/CNBC)
quotes: é possível trabalhar e ganhar o seu sustento cuidando da natureza.
title: Whether to fund sustainability — and how to frame it

text: **Whether to take on excess risk early (the bottle gamble).** Yes — tens of thousands of bottles he couldn't store or afford, all-or-nothing, when speed beat certainty. (Click Petróleo e Gás; Companhia das Letras)
title: Whether to take on excess risk early (the bottle gamble)

text: *"Um empreendedor tem de pular no escuro, saltar do precipício sem saber como vai cair, ou se vai voar."* [An entrepreneur has to jump in the dark, leap off the cliff not knowing how — or whether — you'll fall or fly.] (MAGG)
quotes: Um empreendedor tem de pular no escuro, saltar do precipício sem saber como vai cair, ou se vai voar.

text: *"E se der tudo errado? Qual é a pior coisa que pode acontecer? Como é que eu fico?"* [What if it all goes wrong? What's the worst that can happen? Where does that leave me?] (MAGG)
quotes: E se der tudo errado? Qual é a pior coisa que pode acontecer? Como é que eu fico?

text: *"Há momentos na vida em que não tem como ser 'mais ou menos'. É tudo ou nada."* [There are moments in life when you can't be 'more or less'. It's all or nothing.] (A Essência de Empreender, via Companhia das Letras synopsis / trechos.org)

text: Warm, plainspoken, and self-effacing — a founder who talks in lived anecdote (the homemade mixer, the borrowed US$3,000, the Silvio Santos bottles, the Curitiba mall he walked away from at "um clique," his father's maxims) rather than abstraction or jargon. He reaches for vivid physical metaphors: the cliff jump, "morrem na praia," the captain who must descend to the mechanic, "olho no olho." He credits others constantly ("você não faz nada sozinho") and downplays himself — still "um farmacêutico que gosta de perfumes," the "velhinho que construiu o Boticário." His register is moral and relational before financial: profit is real but "muito pouco" next to transformation and trust, "o negócio é ganhar dinheiro, mas não pelo dinheiro," and "jamais queria causar prejuízo para outra pessoa" is closer to a creed than a tactic. He's blunt about risk being unavoidable ("tem um momento em que temos de arriscar mesmo") and the limits of planning, almost tender about obligations to people who staked their savings on him, and unusually willing to admit weakness ("não precisamos mostrar que somos fortes o tempo todo"). He borrows wisdom rather than claiming it — Antonio Machado's *"Caminante, no hay camino. Se hace camino, al andar"*; Drucker's "culture eats strategy." One documented outlier breaks the pattern: a single English-language Forbes quote ("Everything will make sense when you look back...") is more abstract and reflective than his usual concrete, Portuguese, anecdote-first register — worth flagging as an exception rather than the baseline voice, possibly an artifact of translation or a different interview context. Recognize a paraphrase as "sounds like Krigsner" by the combination of folksy anecdote + relationship-as-asset moral + understated bigness ("você não faz uma empresa dessas da noite para o dia").

text: **vs. Rony Meisler — build a dynasty to transmit vs. build a brand to (eventually) sell.** Krigsner kept ownership concentrated in himself and his brother-in-law across two professional-CEO handoffs (leaving the executive presidency himself in 2008) and frames the whole point as a *transmittable, multi-generational legacy* (Drucker's "culture eats strategy"; daughters on the board). Meisler's arc is the opposite: he built Reserva on his own founder-rebel charisma and *sold it to Arezzo&Co* (2020), then exited turbulently. Where Meisler fuses brand to founder, Krigsner treats the founder as something the company must outgrow — and would flag the "soul leaves with the founder" risk as the exact failure his succession architecture is built to prevent.

text:
**The franchisee/reseller relationship he idealizes has repeated, escalating documentation of friction — not just a single complaints channel.** Beyond Reclame Aqui commission disputes ("uma mixaria" at ~15% vs. ~30% at competitors, freight, stockouts, abusive collection calls), three separate, independently reported franchise-termination disputes surface the same pattern at larger scale:
- **João Pessoa, 2017** (Portal Correio, two articles): a franchisee sought to return his franchise; when negotiations over the buy-back value stalled, **the group cut off product supply**. The franchisee won a court injunction to buy stock, but only cash-upfront. Result: 7 of 10 stores closed, the direct-sales unit shut down, 50+ layoffs (many without severance per ex-employees), delayed December salary/13th-month/vacation pay, and a labor protest. The company's only public response was a refusal to comment ("situação pontual que está sob análise do Poder Judiciário... o grupo não comenta casos que estejam em discussão na Justiça") — leaving unanswered whether the supply cutoff (not just the civil dispute) caused the labor cascade onto third parties (the franchisee's own employees).
- **Hannan franchise, ~2015–2016** (dcomercio, via reader-proxy fetch): a 33-year franchise partner, Izabel Cristina Litieri, went from R$55m/year in sales across 14 stores and direct-sales channels to insolvency after a debt-financed real-estate expansion (R$16m) collided with Brazil's credit crisis; when she asked the group to restructure or accept her property in lieu of payment, it refused, began demanding cash-upfront for product (ending historical credit terms), and — per her account — became inaccessible ("Cheguei a ir quatro vezes para Curitiba, mas não consegui falar com o Grynbaum, só com diretores da empresa"). Her lawsuit alleges the group moved to "asfixiar financeiramente" [financially suffocate] the franchise to reclaim the territory she'd built. She explicitly contrasts this with the founder era: *"Comecei quando o Miguel Krigsner vinha para São Paulo e fazia reuniões na casa da minha irmã... mas o grupo poderia ter sido mais flexível em nosso caso."* [I started when Miguel Krigsner used to come to São Paulo and hold meetings at my sister's house... but the group could have been more flexible in our case.] This is the sharpest documented seam between the founder's personal "olho no olho" ethic and the institution he handed off to.
- **Polêmica Paraíba (undated critique, lightly sourced, re-quoting Exame):** alleges the group's ~2011 pivot into direct-sales-style distribution forced franchisees to build their own distribution centers at their own cost, while giving resellers better effective pricing than franchisees buying direct — then had a related entity, Interbelle, acquire distressed franchises "below market." Retail consultant **Adir Ribeiro (Praxis)** is quoted (originally to Exame) warning precisely of this risk: *"O maior risco na hora de uma empresa diversificar o modelo de vendas é prejudicar o relacionamento com aqueles que a fizeram crescer."* [The biggest risk when a company diversifies its sales model is damaging the relationship with those who made it grow.] Treat this source as an allegation from a lightly-sourced outlet, not an adjudicated finding — but it names the exact risk his own "ganha-ganha" rhetoric claims to guard against.
*All three are sourced complaints/allegations and one company non-denial, not adjudicated findings of wrongdoing.*

text: **Sustainability framing invites the "is it really not marketing?" question — now with self-reported numbers to weigh.** He insists the Fundação isn't marketing, and the separate-entity / ~1%-of-revenue-or-profit structure and ESG-linked bond financing (R$5.775bn across four issuances) are genuine — but the company's own 2025 Relato Integrado admits real shortfalls (Scope 3 emissions cut only 2% against a 17%-by-2030 target; recycled content at 6% against a 30% goal), which cuts both ways: real self-disclosure of gaps (not pure PR), but also evidence the "not marketing" claim still has ground to cover operationally.

text: **Practical implication for a council.** A sharp lens for *franchising and channel design, partner/stakeholder trust, family-business succession and professionalization, building patiently over decades, decisive bets under uncertainty, and purpose-as-structure*. Weaker for *operational/financial mechanics at scale, risk accounting beyond a survivability check, fast-iteration product cultures, and any situation where partner-trust must be enforced by systems rather than personal relationship* — which the documented franchise disputes suggest is precisely where his own model has been tested hardest and where the institution, without him personally in the room, has not always held to his stated ethic.

text: Naval Ravikant — AngelList co-founder, prolific angel (Twitter, Uber, Notion), and the most quotable aphorist on wealth and happiness — is the council's lens for **leverage, autonomy, judgment, and desire-management**: wealth is "assets that earn while you sleep" built on *specific knowledge + accountability + permissionless leverage* (code/media) multiplied by *judgment*, the whole stack reduced to two words — "productize yourself" — and happiness is a learned skill whose engine is desire ("a contract you make with yourself to be unhappy until you get what you want"), whose real target is *peace*, and whose enemy is envy. His sharpest contrarian moves: "you're not going to get rich renting out your time"; "hard work is really overrated"; labor is the *worst* form of leverage; "if you can't decide, the answer is no"; "escape competition through authenticity"; raise so you don't *need* to raise and "valuation is temporary, control is forever" (he watched his own first company, Epinions, get zeroed in the wrong game); set an "absurdly high" personal hourly rate and outsource everything below it; treat news as adversarial and "value your time" above money or friends; route around captured regulators; and raise children "disobedient and free and uneducated" over "educated and obedient." He opposes the AI doomers (his fear is *unaligned humans with AI*, not the machine), splits from his own libertarian camp on targeted tariffs, parts from Buffett on leverage and frontier tech, and out-radicalizes Paul Graham on schooling and on whether you should raise capital at all. Use him for long-horizon, ownership, control, and AI-as-leverage framing — and distrust him on operational how-to (in the late-aphorist register), clinical well-being, and advice that must hold for people without capital or a safety net; serious critics (Sandel via meritocracy, Bourdieu via cultural capital, the "luck paradox") argue his "without getting lucky" generalizes from a survivor in Silicon Valley's Extremistan.

text: Naval Ravikant is an Indian-American entrepreneur and angel investor, co-founder and chairman of AngelList. As an angel he made early bets on Twitter, Uber, Notion, Opendoor, Postmates, and Wish, and earlier co-founded Epinions (an online product-review site) and the Venture Hacks blog — term-sheet advice that became AngelList. The Epinions arc is load-bearing for his worldview: ~$45M raised, the founders' common stock zeroed in the 2003 DealTime merger that formed Shopping.com, then a 2005 lawsuit against Benchmark and August Capital after Shopping.com's IPO and eBay sale showed the founders had been told their stock was worthless while insiders profited (see *Positions* and *Provenance*). That experience — "I basically got cheated by my business partners" — is the root of "control is forever," "judge investors by behavior, not words," and the founding of Venture Hacks (2007) and AngelList. He also names a deeper wound: he started AngelList "partially because I was cut out of some very big deals early on." Beyond investing he is best known as a writer and aphorist on wealth, happiness, and decision-making — crystallized in the 2018 "How to Get Rich (without getting lucky)" tweetstorm (expanded into a full Naval-and-Nivi interview series) and *The Almanack of Naval Ravikant* (2020), compiled by Eric Jorgenson and released free online. He is a recurring long-form guest (Tim Ferriss since 2015, the Knowledge Project, Joe Rogan, Modern Wisdom, All-In). Note the two phases: the earlier Naval (the Epinions/Venture Hacks/Elad Gil operator — term sheets, option-pool shuffles, founder-investor power dynamics) is sharper and more combative; the later aphorist is more serene and philosophical. Since ~2024 his attention has shifted heavily toward AI, crypto, longevity, and network-state themes — and in 2025 he became a heavy hands-on "vibe coder," declaring "pure software is uninvestable."

text: **The wealth equation: specific knowledge + accountability + leverage, multiplied by judgment, compounded over time.** Compressed: "why you, that's accountability, at scale, that's leverage, and just you getting paid… that's specific knowledge." *Specific knowledge* is "knowledge you cannot be trained for," found "by pursuing your innate talents, your genuine curiosity, and your passion," learned through apprenticeship not classrooms, and split into *timely* (e.g. ML now) and *timeless* (e.g. persuasion). *Accountability* is reputational skin in the game. *Leverage* = labor + capital + code/media. *Judgment* is the multiplier. The stack reduces to "productize yourself." (specific-knowledge; finding-time; accountability-leverage; nav.al/rich)

text: **Play long-term games with long-term people — all returns compound.** His most load-bearing principle: "Pick an industry where you can play long-term games with long-term people," because "Play iterated games. We're all baking the pie together… And in a short-term game, we're cutting up the pie." This is why he avoids cynics and one-shot deals and reuses the same partners for decades. (understanding-how-wealth-is-created; how-to-get-lucky; play-long-term-games-with-long-term-people)

So the real currency of life is attention. It's what you choose to pay attention to and what you do about it." Corollary on wasted time: "the true wasted time is time that you're not present for... If you're not immersed in this moment then you're wasting your time." (Modern Wisdom @03:10:55 / @01:25:31, auto-caption)
quotes: time is the only resource

You can't trade money for time. Money is not the real currency of life... time itself doesn't even mean that much because... a lot of time can be wasted because you're not really present for it. So the real currency of life is attention. It's what you choose to pay attention to and what you do about it.
the true wasted time is time that you're not present for... If you're not immersed in this moment then you're wasting your time.
title: Attention — not time, not money — is the real currency of life

text: **Status is the ancient zero-sum game; wealth creation is the newer, positive-sum one.** "Status is limited. There's limited status to go around. It's a ranking ladder... a rise in status, somebody else lowers in status... but it's not like wealth creation where it can go infinitely." Practical order of operations: "If you're trying to build up your following on a social network and get famous and then get rich off of being famous, that's a much harder path than getting rich first... and then go for your fame afterwards would be my advice." (Modern Wisdom @00:15:43 / @00:17:43, auto-caption)
quotes: Status is limited. There's limited status to go around. It's a ranking ladder... a rise in status, somebody else lowers in status... but it's not like wealth creation where it can go infinitely.

If you're trying to build up your following on a social network and get famous and then get rich off of being famous, that's a much harder path than getting rich first... and then go for your fame afterwards would be my advice.
title: Status is the ancient zero-sum game; wealth creation is the newer, positive-sum one

text: **Pathogens are humanity's real predators — and much of biology, hygiene and culture is downstream of that war.** "We are top of the well-known food chain, but bacteria and viruses eat us. Fungus eats us. So these microscopic predators are our natural predators. And so a lot of aging, societal structure, hygiene, religious strictures against pork, circumcision — all of these things are designed to resist bacteria and viruses." Mechanism aside: "The body releases its own hormones in pulses rather than steady state... because enemy bacteria... can't pulse. They can't coordinate to pulse." (Modern Wisdom @02:47:34 / @02:46:38, auto-caption)
quotes: We are top of the well-known food chain, but bacteria and viruses eat us. Fungus eats us. So these microscopic predators are our natural predators. And so a lot of aging, societal structure, hygiene, religious strictures against pork, circumcision — all of these things are designed to resist bacteria and viruses.
The body releases its own hormones in pulses rather than steady state... because enemy bacteria... can't pulse. They can't coordinate to pulse.
title: Pathogens are humanity's real predators — and much of biology, hygiene and culture is downstream of that war

text: **Productize yourself.** *Gist:* the whole wealth stack collapsed into two words. *Worked example:* "'Productize' and 'yourself.' 'Yourself' has uniqueness. 'Productize' has leverage. 'Yourself' has accountability. 'Productize' has specific knowledge." His own podcast is the literal case — "This is a podcast called Naval. I'm literally productizing myself with a podcast." (understanding-how-wealth-is-created; How to Get Rich PDF)
quotes: 'Productize' and 'yourself.' 'Yourself' has uniqueness. 'Productize' has leverage. 'Yourself' has accountability. 'Productize' has specific knowledge.

title: Productize yourself

text: **The leverage stack, climbed via real estate.** *Gist:* specific knowledge, accountability, and the four leverages compound rung by rung. *Worked example:* he escalates day-laborer → general contractor → developer → architect/REIT → real-estate-tech founder, "all the way up to somebody who started a real estate tech company and then took it public" (Zillow/Redfin/Trulia). The bottom rung has "no leverage other than from the tools" ("A day laborer in India makes a lot less because they have no tool leverage"); the general contractor "got the equity but they're also taking accountability and risk"; the top rung brings "the maximum leverage… and the maximum specific knowledge." (laborer-tech)

the maximum leverage… and the maximum specific knowledge.
title: The leverage stack, climbed via real estate

text: **Permissionless vs. permissioned leverage = "an army of robots."** *Gist:* prefer leverage nobody has to grant you (code, media) over labor and capital, which require permission. *Worked example:* "Capital and labor are permissioned leverage. Everyone is chasing capital, but someone has to give it to you." "Code and media are permissionless leverage… You can create software and media that works for you while you sleep." "The robot army is already here. The robot revolution has already happened. We're about halfway through it." Why product leverage is *egalitarian*: "the best products tend to be at… the middle class," and "Jeff Bezos doesn't get to watch better movies and TV than we do." (understanding-how-wealth-is-created; nav.al/rich; find-a-position-of-leverage)

title: Permissionless vs. permissioned leverage = "an army of robots."

text: **Accountability = reputational skin in the game.** *Gist:* take public risk under your own name and society routes responsibility, equity, and leverage to you. *Worked example:* "Embrace accountability and take business risks under your own name. Society will reward you with responsibility, equity, and leverage." His own case: pivoting from startups to philosophy ~2014, "people in the industry… sent me messages through the back channel like, 'What are you doing? You're ending your career.'" "Accountability is a double-edged thing… credit when things go well and… the brunt of the failure when things go badly," and "the people who have the ability to fail in public under their own names actually gain a lot of power." (accountability-leverage)

the people who have the ability to fail in public under their own names actually gain a lot of power.
title: Accountability = reputational skin in the game

text: **Pick a business model with built-in leverage (scale economies + zero marginal cost + network effects).** *Gist:* some models hand you free leverage. *Worked example:* "make Widget Number 12… cheaper than making Widget Number 5"; zero marginal cost — "Joe Rogan is working no harder on his current podcast than… Podcast number 1"; Metcalfe's Law, value ∝ nodes² — "If you're number one in a network effect business, you win everything." "A lot of the winning businesses are natural monopolies." Language is "the oldest example of network effect." (business-models; nav.al/rich)
quotes: make Widget Number 12… cheaper than making Widget Number 5
Joe Rogan is working no harder on his current podcast than… Podcast number 1

text: **Net present value.** *Gist:* discount future cash to today so founders can't dazzle you with future-value equity. *Worked example:* "Net present value is when you say, 'That stream of payments I'm going to get in the future—what's it worth today?'" — and "You should get very comfortable doing rough net present value calculations in your head." (npv)
quotes: Net present value is when you say, 'That stream of payments I'm going to get in the future—what's it worth today?'
You should get very comfortable doing rough net present value calculations in your head.
title: Net present value

text: **Power-law portfolio math (angel investing).** *Gist:* one extreme winner pays for all the zeros, so access beats judgment. *Worked example:* "If you invest in 100 companies and one of them produces a 1,000x return… the other 99 investments could go to zero and you would still see an overall return of 10x." Corollary: "the top deal in a good portfolio returns as much as deals 2 through N combined," so "It's okay to pass on investments—you just don't want them to pass on you." His own Twitter (~400x) and Uber (~4,000x) realized this. (angel; 11-lessons; Tim Ferriss #97)
quotes: If you invest in 100 companies and one of them produces a 1,000x return… the other 99 investments could go to zero and you would still see an overall return of 10x.
the top deal in a good portfolio returns as much as deals 2 through N combined,
It's okay to pass on investments—you just don't want them to pass on you.
title: Power-law portfolio math (angel investing)

text: **Principal-agent problem.** *Gist:* owners care, agents optimize for themselves; tie compensation to value created. *Worked example:* "the principal-agent problem is the single most fundamental problem in microeconomics. If you do not understand the principal-agent problem, you will not know how to navigate your way through the world." Lever: "The more closely you can tie someone's compensation to the exact value they're creating, the more you turn them into a principal." (collect-mental-models)
quotes: the principal-agent problem is the single most fundamental problem in microeconomics. If you do not understand the principal-agent problem, you will not know how to navigate your way through the world.
The more closely you can tie someone's compensation to the exact value they're creating, the more you turn them into a principal.
title: Principal-agent problem

text: **Inversion: succeed by not making mistakes.** *Gist:* avoiding incorrect judgments beats predicting correct ones. *Worked example:* "being successful is just about not making mistakes. It's not about having correct judgment. It's about avoiding incorrect judgments" — he operates "in the face of ignorance." (collect-mental-models)
quotes: being successful is just about not making mistakes. It's not about having correct judgment. It's about avoiding incorrect judgments
in the face of ignorance.
title: Inversion: succeed by not making mistakes

text: **Systems, not goals; optimize the 999/1000 universes.** *Gist:* engineer an environment so you win statistically rather than betting on one outcome. *Worked example:* "Scott Adams said… 'Set up systems, not goals.'" "I want to live in a way that if my life played out 1,000 times, Naval is successful 999 times. He's not a billionaire, but he does pretty well each time." (choosing-to-grow-yourself; TKP)
quotes: Scott Adams said… 'Set up systems, not goals.'
I want to live in a way that if my life played out 1,000 times, Naval is successful 999 times. He's not a billionaire, but he does pretty well each time.
title: Systems, not goals; optimize the 999/1000 universes

text: **Mental models as compact pointers to your own experience.** *Gist:* a model is useless without the underlying experience it indexes. *Worked example:* "Mental models are really just compact ways for you to recall your own knowledge." Top-tier ones: "Evolution, thermodynamics, information theory, and complexity have explanatory and predictive power in many aspects of life." Caveat: "Most mental models aren't worth reading… because they're trivial" — the exception is Deutsch, who changes "what you regard as true." (collect-mental-models; think)
quotes: Mental models are really just compact ways for you to recall your own knowledge.
Evolution, thermodynamics, information theory, and complexity have explanatory and predictive power in many aspects of life.
Most mental models aren't worth reading… because they're trivial
what you regard as true.
title: Mental models as compact pointers to your own experience

text: **Falsifiability as the science filter.** *Gist:* no falsifiable predictions, no science. *Worked example:* "I think of macroeconomics as a junk science… because it doesn't make falsifiable predictions," while microeconomics + game theory are "a solid foundation." (collect-mental-models; TKP)
quotes: I think of macroeconomics as a junk science… because it doesn't make falsifiable predictions,
a solid foundation.
title: Falsifiability as the science filter

text: **Mind as a debuggable OS; meditation as inbox-zero.** *Gist:* watch your thoughts as a layer beneath them. *Worked example:* "Insight meditation lets you run your brain in debug mode until you realize you're just a subroutine in a larger program." The untrained mind "is like a monkey flinging feces… completely uncontrollable"; the concrete moment — "I'm brushing my teeth and I start thinking forward to a podcast… Then, I caught myself. I put my brain in debug mode." "Awareness alone calms you down." "Meditation is intermittent fasting for the mind." (meditation-mental-strength)
quotes: Insight meditation lets you run your brain in debug mode until you realize you're just a subroutine in a larger program.

text: **Desire as a contract; one big desire at a time.** *Gist:* every want is signing up to be unhappy until you get it. *Worked example:* "Desire is a contract you make with yourself to be unhappy until you get what you want." His rule: "I try not to have more than one big desire in my life at any given time, and I also recognize it as the axis of my suffering." The in-the-moment test: "Is it so important to me I'll be unhappy unless this goes my way?" (every-desire-is-a-chosen-unhappiness; find-happiness-in-acceptance)
quotes: Desire is a contract you make with yourself to be unhappy until you get what you want.

text: **Envy: the 24/7 swap test.** *Gist:* you can't cherry-pick someone's trait; you'd have to become them entirely. *Worked example:* "If you're not willing to do a wholesale, 24/7, 100 percent swap with who that person is, then there is no point in being jealous." (envy-is-the-enemy-of-happiness)
quotes: If you're not willing to do a wholesale, 24/7, 100 percent swap with who that person is, then there is no point in being jealous.
title: Envy: the 24/7 swap test

text: **Stress = an inability to decide what's important.** *Gist:* anxiety is two incompatible wants pulling at once; resolve by dropping one. *Worked example:* "In mental terms, stress is an inability to decide what's important" — like a beam pulled both ways; acceptance removes it. Paired with "The solution to anxiety is always action." (happiness; ai)
quotes: In mental terms, stress is an inability to decide what's important
The solution to anxiety is always action.
title: Stress = an inability to decide what's important

text: **Change it, accept it, or leave it.** *Gist:* every situation has exactly three valid responses; the failure mode is none of them. *Worked example:* "you can change it, you can accept it, or you can leave it. What is not a good option is to sit around wishing… That struggle or aversion is responsible for most of our misery." (find-happiness-in-acceptance)
quotes: you can change it, you can accept it, or you can leave it. What is not a good option is to sit around wishing… That struggle or aversion is responsible for most of our misery.
title: Change it, accept it, or leave it

text: **Hedonic adaptation / the work treadmill.** *Gist:* getting good at a rewarding game keeps you playing past the point of benefit. *Worked example:* "Survival and replication drive put us on the work treadmill. Hedonic adaptation keeps us there. The trick is knowing when to jump off and play instead." The real winners "step out of the game entirely." (success-does-not-earn-happiness)
quotes: Survival and replication drive put us on the work treadmill. Hedonic adaptation keeps us there. The trick is knowing when to jump off and play instead.
step out of the game entirely.
title: Hedonic adaptation / the work treadmill

text: **Five chimps theory.** *Gist:* a chimp's behavior is predictable from its five closest troop-mates; same for people. *Worked example:* "Choose your five chimps carefully." Actionable: "When working, surround yourself with people more successful than you. When playing, surround yourself with people happier than you." (Tim Ferriss AMA; happiness-is-built-by-habits)
quotes: Choose your five chimps carefully.
When working, surround yourself with people more successful than you. When playing, surround yourself with people happier than you.
title: Five chimps theory

text: **Escape competition through authenticity.** *Gist:* specialize so narrowly into yourself that you exit the comparison set. *Worked example:* "Escape competition through authenticity. Basically, when you're competing with people, it's because you're copying them." "No one in the world is going to beat you at being you." His own "specific knowledge" was named by his mother at 15 — he insisted he'd be an astrophysicist; she said "No, you're going to go into business" (he'd been critiquing the pizza parlor's pricing as a kid). (find-and-build-specific-knowledge; specific-knowledge; choosing-to-be-yourself)
quotes: Escape competition through authenticity. Basically, when you're competing with people, it's because you're copying them.
No one in the world is going to beat you at being you.
No, you're going to go into business
title: Escape competition through authenticity

text: **Skill stack.** *Gist:* combine a generic skill (persuasion) with specialized ones to become uniquely valuable. *Worked example:* "You need to combine it in a skill stack, as Scott Adams writes" — persuasion + accounting + semiconductor knowledge → "the best semiconductor salesperson and, later on, the best semiconductor company CEO." the best semiconductor salesperson and, later on, the best semiconductor company CEO.

text: **Play stupid games, win stupid prizes (the Epinions lesson, in his own mouth).** *Gist:* competition can trap you in the wrong game; "you're one step away from a completely different business." *Worked example:* "My first company got caught up in the wrong game." Epinions, meant for reviews ("that space eventually turned into TripAdvisor and Yelp"), "got caught up in the whole comparison shopping game… and that whole space went to zero because… Amazon won e-tail." "If we had stayed authentic to ourselves we would have done better." (How to Get Rich PDF)

text: **Set an aspirational hourly rate; outsource everything below it.** *Gist:* price your own time absurdly high and act accordingly. *Worked example:* "Set a very high hourly aspirational rate for yourself and stick to it. It should seem and feel absurdly high. If it doesn't, it's not high enough." He used $5,000/hr *before* he had money — "I would argue with girlfriends, 'I don't do that. That's not a problem that I solve.'" (prioritize-and-focus; nav.al/rich)

text: **Work like a lion, not an ox — a marathon of sprints.** *Gist:* knowledge work is bursts at high output, then rest. *Worked example:* "Forty hour work weeks are a relic of the Industrial Age. Knowledge workers function like athletes—train and sprint, then rest and reassess." He owns it personally: "I'm actually a lazy person. I work through bursts of energy where I'm really motivated." Paired with "inspiration is perishable—act on it immediately." (find-a-position-of-leverage; prioritize-and-focus; the-present-is-all-we-have)
quotes: Forty hour work weeks are a relic of the Industrial Age. Knowledge workers function like athletes—train and sprint, then rest and reassess.
I'm actually a lazy person. I work through bursts of energy where I'm really motivated.
inspiration is perishable—act on it immediately.
title: Work like a lion, not an ox — a marathon of sprints

text: **The four kinds of luck (luck as a designable surface).** *Gist:* (1) *blind luck*; (2) *hustle luck*; (3) *opportunity-spotting luck* (skilled enough to notice); (4) *character/brand luck* — "you build a unique character, a unique brand, a unique mindset, which causes luck to find you." *Worked example:* the best deep-sea diver gets the call about the sunken treasure — "their luck just became your luck." Ported from Disraeli: "we make our fortunes and we call them fate." (how-to-get-lucky; money-luck)
quotes: you build a unique character, a unique brand, a unique mindset, which causes luck to find you.
their luck just became your luck.
we make our fortunes and we call them fate.
title: The four kinds of luck (luck as a designable surface)

text: **Iteration, not hours.** *Gist:* the learning curve is driven by feedback loops, not clock time. *Worked example:* "It's not 10,000 hours, it's 10,000 iterations." Real feedback "comes from free markets and nature… It is impossible to fool Mother Nature"; awards and friends are "fake." Run "your own lemonade stand." (in-the-arena; nav.al/rich)
quotes: It's not 10,000 hours, it's 10,000 iterations.
comes from free markets and nature… It is impossible to fool Mother Nature
your own lemonade stand.
title: Iteration, not hours

text: **Good products are hard to vary.** *Gist:* from Deutsch's "good explanations are hard to vary," applied to products. *Worked example:* "Good products are hard to vary" — the iPhone, an airplane wing, the Raptor engine; complex working systems are "a very simple system… that was iterated over and over," not complexity designed up front. (in-the-arena)
quotes: good explanations are hard to vary,
Good products are hard to vary
a very simple system… that was iterated over and over,
title: Good products are hard to vary

text: **Read what you love until you love to read.** *Gist:* the *love* of reading is the asset; the specific books matter less. *Worked example:* "Read what you love until you love to read." "The means of learning are abundant—it's the desire to learn that is scarce." Method: read originals — "If you're interested in evolution, read Charles Darwin. Don't begin with Richard Dawkins… Read Darwin first." (The "best 100 books over and over" line is him *quoting* @illacertus — see *Provenance*.) (learn-to-love-to-read; read)
quotes: Read what you love until you love to read.
The means of learning are abundant—it's the desire to learn that is scarce.
If you're interested in evolution, read Charles Darwin. Don't begin with Richard Dawkins… Read Darwin first.
best 100 books over and over
title: Read what you love until you love to read

text: **Lindy / minority rule, ported from Taleb into crypto.** *Gist:* survival predicts survival; a committed non-compromising minority drags the system. *Worked example:* "In crypto, Bitcoin is the Lindy currency. The longer it's survived, the longer it will survive." (BlockCon 2018)
quotes: In crypto, Bitcoin is the Lindy currency. The longer it's survived, the longer it will survive.
title: Lindy / minority rule, ported from Taleb into crypto

text: **Social consistency as a forcing function.** *Gist:* a public commitment binds your future self. *Worked example:* "if you want to quit smoking, all you have to do is go to everybody you know and say, 'I quit smoking… I give you my word.'" He told colleagues he was leaving to start a company; months later the public commitment forced him through. (choosing-to-build-yourself; JRE)
quotes: if you want to quit smoking, all you have to do is go to everybody you know and say, 'I quit smoking… I give you my word.'
title: Social consistency as a forcing function

text: **Consumer surplus.** *Gist:* a free-market transaction nets the buyer more value than they paid, so business is a net value-creator rather than extraction. *Worked example:* "Consumer surplus is the excess value you get from something when you pay less than you were willing to pay." His illustration: you'd pay $20 for the Starbucks coffee that keeps you alert at work, but you only pay a few dollars — the gap is surplus the seller hands you for free. (surplus)
quotes: Consumer surplus is the excess value you get from something when you pay less than you were willing to pay.
title: Consumer surplus

text: **Tit-for-tat / iterated prisoner's dilemma.** *Gist:* the single most worth-knowing piece of game theory — cooperation and trust only emerge in repeated games, where defecting once poisons every future round. *Worked example:* "I've learned that tit-for-tat iterated prisoner's dilemma is the piece of game theory that is worth knowing the most. You can almost put down the game theory book after that." It's the formal engine under "play long-term games with long-term people." (nav.al/rich)
quotes: I've learned that tit-for-tat iterated prisoner's dilemma is the piece of game theory that is worth knowing the most. You can almost put down the game theory book after that.
play long-term games with long-term people.
title: Tit-for-tat / iterated prisoner's dilemma

text: **Coase theorem — firm size is set by internal vs. external transaction costs.** *Gist:* a company is exactly as big as the point where doing things in-house gets more expensive than buying them outside; tech is collapsing external costs and shrinking the firm. *Worked example:* "Ronald Coase is an economist who has this... very famous theorem, but he basically just talks about why is a company the size that it is... and it has to do with the internal transaction costs versus the external transaction costs." (JRE #1309 @00:25:33) — he uses it to predict the "atomization of the firm" and the rise of individual/gig work (Airbnb).
quotes: Ronald Coase is an economist who has this... very famous theorem, but he basically just talks about why is a company the size that it is... and it has to do with the internal transaction costs versus the external transaction costs.
atomization of the firm
title: Coase theorem — firm size is set by internal vs. external transaction costs

text: **Agrippa's trilemma — every "why" chain dead-ends in three places.** *Gist:* any "why?" regress terminates in infinite regress, circular reasoning, or an axiom — so ultimate-meaning questions have no terminal answer. *Worked example:* "There's a thing called [Agrippa's trilemma]... it says that any questioning like this, why, will always end in one of three places. First is infinite regress... The second is circular reasoning... Or the third is an axiom, and the most popular axiom is god." (JRE #1309 @01:36:43) — "saying we're in a simulation, or saying it's the big bang, is just another way of saying god." (the trilemma's name is marked inaudible in the transcript; Naval names the framework but the transcriber couldn't catch it)
quotes: There's a thing called [Agrippa's trilemma]... it says that any questioning like this, why, will always end in one of three places. First is infinite regress... The second is circular reasoning... Or the third is an axiom, and the most popular axiom is god.
saying we're in a simulation, or saying it's the big bang, is just another way of saying god.
title: Agrippa's trilemma — every "why" chain dead-ends in three places

text: **Hand the system to your enemies to run for a decade.** *Gist:* a system is only good if you'd trust the other side to operate it; if it only works when your team holds it, it's not a good system. *Worked example:* "The test of any good system is, you build a system, hand it over to your enemies to run for the next decade. So for example, if you want censorship on Twitter or Facebook, you should build that system, and then hand it over to the other side to run." (JRE #1309 @01:13:51) — he applies it to censorship and immigration policy.
quotes: The test of any good system is, you build a system, hand it over to your enemies to run for the next decade. So for example, if you want censorship on Twitter or Facebook, you should build that system, and then hand it over to the other side to run.
title: Hand the system to your enemies to run for a decade

text: **Taleb's nested politics — scale of the group sets where you fall on the spectrum.** *Gist:* the bigger and lower-trust the group, the more you must lean capitalist; socialism is right with your tribe, capitalism with strangers. *Worked example:* "I always liked Nassim Taleb['s framing] on this, where he said, 'With my family, I'm a communist. With my close friends, I'm a socialist. At my state level politics, I'm a Democrat. At higher levels, I'm a Republican. And at the federal level, I'm a libertarian.' So basically the larger the group of people you have mass[ed] together who have different interests, the less trust there is, the more cheating there is... the more you go towards capitalism." (JRE #1309 @00:44:21) (attributes the frame to Nassim Taleb)
quotes: I always liked Nassim Taleb['s framing] on this, where he said, 'With my family, I'm a communist. With my close friends, I'm a socialist. At my state level politics, I'm a Democrat. At higher levels, I'm a Republican. And at the federal level, I'm a libertarian.' So basically the larger the group of people you have mass[ed] together who have different interests, the less trust there is, the more cheating there is... the more you go towards capitalism.
title: Taleb's nested politics — scale of the group sets where you fall on the spectrum

text: **The internet: one hegemon plus a long tail, with the middle killed.** *Gist:* aggregation creates a single giant winner and millions of atomized individuals, and destroys everything medium-sized in between. *Worked example:* "The internet is this giant aggregator where it creates one big [hegemon] for everything, and it creates an atomized long tail of millions and millions of individuals. What it gets rid of is the medium-sized ones in the middle." (JRE #1309 @00:58:47) — applied to media/commerce (Netflix, Amazon) and to predict "everyone's a journalist." ("hegemon" is marked inaudible in the Sonix transcript; the surrounding "one big ___ for everything" is verbatim)

title: The internet: one hegemon plus a long tail, with the middle killed

text: **Pick a profession where inputs and outputs are decoupled (lumberjack vs. software engineer).** *Gist:* the upside is only nonlinear where one unit of effort can produce wildly different value. *Worked example:* "One great engineer can for example create Bitcoin and create billions of dollars of value... an engineer who's working on the wrong thing... can work for an entire year and every piece of code they ship customers don't want it... whereas if you're a lumberjack, even the best lumberjack in the world... maybe like 3x better than one of the worst lumberjacks." (How to Get Rich pod @00:27:18, auto-caption)

title: Pick a profession where inputs and outputs are decoupled (lumberjack vs. software engineer)

text: **The robots are already here — code commands an existing army.** *Gist:* the robot revolution already happened; software developers already direct it. *Worked example:* "I would say the majority of the robot revolution has already happened. The robots are already here and there are way more robots than there are humans, it's just that we packed them in data centers for heat and efficiency reasons... every great software developer now has an army of robots working for him at nighttime while he or she sleeps." title: The robots are already here — code commands an existing army

text: **The outcome "equation" — and the warning not to treat it as math.** *Gist:* the pieces multiply (specific knowledge × leverage × judgment × accountability × what society values, compounded over time), but treating it numerically is false precision. *Worked example:* "Your eventual outcome will be equal to something like the distinctiveness of your specific knowledge times how much leverage you can apply to that knowledge times how often your judgment is correct times how singularly accountable you are for the outcome times how much society values what you're doing — and then you compound all of that with how long you can keep doing it." Immediately hedged: "this isn't math, people... it's what a physicist would call false precision." (How to Get Rich pod @02:32:55, auto-caption)
quotes: Your eventual outcome will be equal to something like the distinctiveness of your specific knowledge times how much leverage you can apply to that knowledge times how often your judgment is correct times how singularly accountable you are for the outcome times how much society values what you're doing — and then you compound all of that with how long you can keep doing it.
this isn't math, people... it's what a physicist would call false precision.
title: The outcome "equation" — and the warning not to treat it as math

text: **Two tells that you've found specific knowledge.** *Gist:* if a skill can only be learned by doing it, and the practitioner can't describe a typical day, it's specific knowledge. *Worked example:* "When you find a skill that can only be learned on the job by doing it, that is a good indicator... Another good indicator is when you ask the person doing it 'what do you do every day' and they can't give you a straight answer... 'every day is different based on what's going on.'" (How to Get Rich pod @03:34:49, auto-caption)

title: Two tells that you've found specific knowledge

text: **Principal-agent, operator version: "if you want it done then go; if not then send."** *Gist:* deal with the smallest possible firm so there's "one throat to choke," and as an agent, act like the owner. *Worked example:* "my ideal law firm to work with is a law firm of one, my ideal banker to work with is a solo banker... you've got one throat to choke, there's no one else to point fingers to... If you're an agent the best way to operate is just say 'what would the founder do' — if you think like the owner and act like the owner it's only a matter of time until you become the owner." (How to Get Rich pod @03:03:55, auto-caption)
quotes: if you want it done then go; if not then send.

text: **Turn a single-move game into a repeat game (the contractor trick).** *Gist:* high-cost, low-information one-shot deals invite defection; manufacture future rounds to align the counterparty. *Worked example:* "An example of a very high cost, low information single-move game is having your house renovated... one way to [fix it]: 'actually I need two different projects done, so the first project we'll do together and then based on that I'll decide if we do the second'... or 'I have three friends who want projects done and they're waiting to see the outcome'... these are all ways of turning a single-move game into a longer-term game." (How to Get Rich pod @03:14:43, auto-caption)
quotes: An example of a very high cost, low information single-move game is having your house renovated... one way to [fix it]: 'actually I need two different projects done, so the first project we'll do together and then based on that I'll decide if we do the second'... or 'I have three friends who want projects done and they're waiting to see the outcome'... these are all ways of turning a single-move game into a longer-term game.
title: Turn a single-move game into a repeat game (the contractor trick)

text: **The high-integrity founder: "I didn't do it for you, I did it for me."** *Gist:* the person worth backing keeps their word for their own self-esteem, not for you. *Worked example:* an investee put personal money in through three pivots rather than wipe out investors; when thanked, "He got offended by that. He said 'I didn't do it for you, I didn't do it for my investors, I did it for me, it's my own self-esteem... that's how I live my life.' That's the kind of person you want to work with." (How to Get Rich pod @00:47:55, auto-caption)
quotes: I didn't do it for you, I did it for me.

text: **Suffering as a motivator (the dishwashing and law-firm stories).** *Gist:* acute discomfort can be the lever that forces you up the curve. *Worked examples:* washing dishes in the cafeteria — "I said 'F this, I hate this'... and I sweet-talked my way to a computer science prof helping TA his CS class in algorithms when I myself was completely unqualified... so it forced me to learn computer science"; and getting fired from a prestigious NY law-firm internship for reading the Wall Street Journal — "I was finally terminated and sent home in shame... destroying my chance of going to law school. I was unhappy for all of an hour, but ultimately it's one of the best things that ever happened to me." (How to Get Rich pod @03:00:29 / @03:02:34, auto-caption)

text: **Envy as a booster rocket (serving food to his own classmates).** *Gist:* a humiliating comparison can fuel motivation rather than just poison it. *Worked example:* "I ended up working for an Indian food catering company and I ended up having to serve at a birthday party for a kid who was actually in my school... that was incredibly embarrassing... if I hadn't had that happen I probably wouldn't be as motivated. Envy can be useful." (How to Get Rich pod @03:02:34, auto-caption)

text: **The crazy roommate — treat your own inner voice as a stranger.** *Gist:* the involuntary inner chatter deserves the same skepticism you'd give an external crank. *Worked example:* "it's this crazy roommate living inside your mind who's always chattering, always chattering, never shuts up and you can't control these thoughts." He credits the analogy to Michael Singer's *The Untethered Soul* and applies an outside-observer's critical filter to his own thoughts. (TF #473)
quotes: it's this crazy roommate living inside your mind who's always chattering, always chattering, never shuts up and you can't control these thoughts.
title: The crazy roommate — treat your own inner voice as a stranger

text: **Anxiety as inherited predator-software.** *Gist:* the mind's default mode is survival paranoia, because we were selected as alpha predators. *Worked example:* "you could argue that all the mind does all day long is fear-based scenario planning for survival, and then maybe a little bit of green for replication." Why nearly everyone is anxious. (TF #473)
quotes: you could argue that all the mind does all day long is fear-based scenario planning for survival, and then maybe a little bit of green for replication.
title: Anxiety as inherited predator-software

text: **Anxiety = the iceberg tip of piled-up unresolved stresses.** *Gist:* free-floating dread is many small unaddressed conflicts merged into one unidentifiable mass. *Worked example:* "Anxiety is sort of this pervasive unidentifiable stress... you have so many unresolved stress points that have piled up in your life that you can no longer identify what the problems are, and there's this mountain of garbage in your mind and a little bit of it poking out the top like an iceberg — and that's anxiety." (Modern Wisdom @01:22:44, auto-caption)

title: Anxiety = the iceberg tip of piled-up unresolved stresses

text: **Single-player vs. multiplayer games — multiplayer pulls you into society and anxiety.** *Gist:* games with other people (money, fame, status) drag you into comparison; solo games (meditation, yoga) don't. *Worked example:* "the multiplayer games are the ones that suck you into society and into anxiety." Paired with "the reason to win the game is so that you can be free of it." (TF #473)
quotes: the multiplayer games are the ones that suck you into society and into anxiety.
the reason to win the game is so that you can be free of it.
title: Single-player vs. multiplayer games — multiplayer pulls you into society and anxiety

text: **Non-dual activities — the free-lunch pursuits that don't create their own opposite.** *Gist:* chasing money/fame manufactures future anxiety; some activities are intrinsically true and carry no downside later. *Worked example:* "What activities are intrinsically true in and of themselves and kind of are a free lunch? Those include things like meditation, yoga, creating art, playing, reading for fun... writing, journaling, you can even be building a business as long as you're doing it for the craft of it." (TF #473)

title: Non-dual activities — the free-lunch pursuits that don't create their own opposite

text: **Bitcoin as a finite-shelf-space Swiss bank account.** *Gist:* the speculative price mechanism is demand to enter a fixed-supply vault versus supply trying to exit. *Worked example:* "one way to think about a Bitcoin... is it's a Swiss bank account but it's a Swiss bank account with finite space and if you want shelf space in that Swiss bank account with finite space, you have to buy out one of the existing holders in that space." (TF #473)
quotes: one way to think about a Bitcoin... is it's a Swiss bank account but it's a Swiss bank account with finite space and if you want shelf space in that Swiss bank account with finite space, you have to buy out one of the existing holders in that space.
title: Bitcoin as a finite-shelf-space Swiss bank account

text: **Answer questions at the level they were asked.** *Gist:* most philosophical paradoxes are a level-switching trick — posing a question as a human here-and-now but answering it from the universe's view over infinite time. *Worked example:* "The reason it seems paradoxical is because you're asking the question of a human here and now... and then answering it from the viewpoint of the universe over infinite time. You switch the level at which you're answering. Questions should be answered at the level at which they're asked." (credits David Deutsch + James Pierce.) (Modern Wisdom @02:22:11, auto-caption)
quotes: The reason it seems paradoxical is because you're asking the question of a human here and now... and then answering it from the viewpoint of the universe over infinite time. You switch the level at which you're answering. Questions should be answered at the level at which they're asked.
title: Answer questions at the level they were asked

text: **The secretary problem is iteration-based, not time-based.** *Gist:* a correction of the common misreading — the stopping rule depends on the number of shots taken, not elapsed time, so bail and decide quickly. *Worked example:* "The interesting thing about the secretary theorem is that it's actually not time based... It's iteration based. The number of shots you took on goal... so you need to bail out quickly and you need to be decisive quickly." (Modern Wisdom @00:59:40, auto-caption)
quotes: The interesting thing about the secretary theorem is that it's actually not time based... It's iteration based. The number of shots you took on goal... so you need to bail out quickly and you need to be decisive quickly.
title: The secretary problem is iteration-based, not time-based

text: **Iteration ≠ repetition — 10,000 error-corrections to mastery.** *Gist:* a refinement of "10,000 iterations": only iterations that *modify based on a learning* count; doing the same thing over is repetition and teaches little. *Worked example:* "I would say it's actually 10,000 iterations to mastery... Iteration is not repetition. Repeating is doing the same thing over and over. Iteration is modifying it with a learning and then doing another version. So that's error correction. If you get 10,000 error corrections in anything, you will be an expert at it." The spoken lemonade-stand/retail framing: stocking shelves the same way daily teaches nothing, "whereas if I was putting in thousands of iterations that would be different... the more shots on goal you can have the faster you're going to learn." (Modern Wisdom @01:18:13, auto-caption; How to Get Rich pod @01:22:46, auto-caption)

text: **Barbell strategy for life — skeptical on specifics, optimistic in the general.** *Gist:* almost every specific opportunity fails, yet the aggregate is worth betting on; live at the extremes, not the gray middle. *Worked example:* "Every specific opportunity is probably a fail. But you want to be optimistic in the general... It's a barbell strategy. It's black or it's white. And most people are stuck in this gray bit." (Modern Wisdom @01:02:24, auto-caption)

title: Barbell strategy for life — skeptical on specifics, optimistic in the general

text: **The Red Queen race — humans and pathogens evolve at the same speed by different strategies.** *Gist:* sexual selection (slow, every ~20 yrs) versus asexual mutation (fast, over thousands of generations) keep the two sides running in place against each other. *Worked example:* "We're in a red queen race where we're both running at roughly the same speed using very different strategies." (Modern Wisdom @02:44:36, auto-caption)
quotes: We're in a red queen race where we're both running at roughly the same speed using very different strategies.
title: The Red Queen race — humans and pathogens evolve at the same speed by different strategies

text: **Adams' Law of Slow-Moving Disasters.** *Gist:* visible, slow-moving problems get solved by markets and individual incentives before they become catastrophes. *Worked example:* "When disasters are very slow moving like peak oil or global warming or population collapse, and everyone can see them coming, economics and society as a force solve them because enough individual people have incentives to go solve them." (attributed to Scott Adams; used to dismiss fertility-collapse panic.) (Modern Wisdom @02:32:49, auto-caption)
quotes: When disasters are very slow moving like peak oil or global warming or population collapse, and everyone can see them coming, economics and society as a force solve them because enough individual people have incentives to go solve them.
title: Adams' Law of Slow-Moving Disasters

text: **The Schelling point — coordinating with no communication.** *Gist:* people converge on a focal answer without talking, by reasoning about what the other will reason. *Worked example:* "Suppose that I want to meet with you but I don't tell you where and I don't tell you when... we cannot communicate... we're probably gonna pick New Years, and what time, midnight... and where would we meet... probably in New York City... probably Grand Central Station under the clock." (How to Get Rich pod @03:12:01, auto-caption)

title: The Schelling point — coordinating with no communication

text: **Russian roulette — ergodicity made concrete.** *Gist:* a population average is not one person's repeated bet; what works across many people once can ruin one person who repeats it. *Worked example:* "Six people who play Russian roulette once each and then each winner gets a billion dollars — one person ends up dead, five people have a billion dollars — versus one person who plays Russian roulette with the same one gun six times is never gonna end up a billionaire, is gonna end up worth zero." (via Taleb.) (How to Get Rich pod @03:11:14, auto-caption)
