title: Russian roulette — ergodicity made concrete

text: **Price discrimination — charge by willingness-to-pay, not by cost.** *Gist:* the same good is priced far above cost to those who'll pay, using small signals of comfort/status to segment them. *Worked example:* "Business class seats will routinely cost five or ten times what an economy class seat does, but it probably costs the airline just two, maybe three x to provide that — it's just the rich person is more willing to pay, so you have to give them the little things... to either signal they're rich or that little bit of comfort." (How to Get Rich pod @03:19:00, auto-caption)
quotes: Business class seats will routinely cost five or ten times what an economy class seat does, but it probably costs the airline just two, maybe three x to provide that — it's just the rich person is more willing to pay, so you have to give them the little things... to either signal they're rich or that little bit of comfort.
title: Price discrimination — charge by willingness-to-pay, not by cost

text: **Externalities are best fixed by pricing, not exhortation.** *Gist:* moralizing campaigns waste effort; pricing the externality routes the cut to whoever consumes most. *Worked example:* "California likes to run declarations and ads to scare you into not taking showers... when it would be just much better to raise the price of fresh water. Your average consumer might pay a few pennies more for a shower, but then the almond farmers who consume a lot of the water will cut back... properly pricing externalities can save resources in a tremendous way." (How to Get Rich pod @03:22:39, auto-caption)
quotes: California likes to run declarations and ads to scare you into not taking showers... when it would be just much better to raise the price of fresh water. Your average consumer might pay a few pennies more for a shower, but then the almond farmers who consume a lot of the water will cut back... properly pricing externalities can save resources in a tremendous way.
title: Externalities are best fixed by pricing, not exhortation

text: **Steel frame vs. scaffolding — understand from the basics up, don't memorize.** *Gist:* a ground-up foundation you can re-derive beats a scaffolding of memorized advanced concepts; memorizing is the tell that you don't understand. *Worked example:* "[Know] the basics from the ground up [—] solid foundation of understanding, a steel frame of understanding, than it is to just have a scaffolding [where you're] just memorizing advanced concepts." (JRE #1309 @01:33:30) — cites Feynman taking you "from counting numbers on your hand, all the way to calculus in four pages of text"; the tell of not understanding is heavy jargon you can't follow.
quotes: [Know] the basics from the ground up [—] solid foundation of understanding, a steel frame of understanding, than it is to just have a scaffolding [where you're] just memorizing advanced concepts.
from counting numbers on your hand, all the way to calculus in four pages of text
title: Steel frame vs. scaffolding — understand from the basics up, don't memorize

text: **If you can't decide, the answer is no.** "For all practical purposes, there are an infinite number of investments out there, so pass." The tell: "If you find yourself creating a spreadsheet for a decision with a list of yes's and no's… forget it." Its time-protection twin: **"Hell yes or no"** — "If I'm not excited about something, I'm not going to do it" (crediting Sivers). And the calendar trap: "current me, present me, is always making promises for future me" — only commit if you'd do it right now. (11-lessons; collect-mental-models; Tim Ferriss AMA; TKP)

text: **When evenly split, take the more painful short-term path; run uphill.** "If you're evenly split on a difficult decision, take the path more painful in the short term" — the brain avoids short-term pain, so the even split implies the gain lies behind it. (collect-mental-models)
quotes: If you're evenly split on a difficult decision, take the path more painful in the short term
title: When evenly split, take the more painful short-term path; run uphill

Don't carry false precision: "the more estimated variables you have, the greater the error." (learn-the-skills-of-decision-making; Modern Wisdom #922)

text: **The more you know, the less you diversify.** Conviction from knowledge concentrates bets; a tiny edge in being right (80% vs 70%) is "valued and compensated in the market hundreds of times more" under leverage. (learn-the-skills-of-decision-making)
quotes: valued and compensated in the market hundreds of times more
title: The more you know, the less you diversify

text: **Impatience with actions, patience with results.** "Anything you have to do, just get it done. Why wait?" — but "you have to be patient with the results because you're dealing with complex systems." (choosing-to-build-yourself; How to Get Rich PDF)
quotes: Anything you have to do, just get it done. Why wait?
you have to be patient with the results because you're dealing with complex systems.

text: **Optimize for independence over pay; be accountable on output, not input.** "If you have independence and you're accountable on your output, as opposed to your input—that's the dream." quotes: If you have independence and you're accountable on your output, as opposed to your input—that's the dream.
the part of the job with the steepest learning curve
avoid repetitive drudgery—that's just biding time until your job is automated away.

quotes: Smart money is money plus the promise of help that's worth paying for, dumb money is money plus hidden harm… assume your investors are mostly money.

text: Aphoristic and compressed — ideas packaged as tweet-length lines built to stand alone, which he describes as deliberate mnemonics: "I use my tweets and other people's tweets as maxims that help compress my own learnings and recall them," and "Twitter has made me a worse reader but a much better writer." The tweets aren't manufactured — "something happens to me, something affects me emotionally, and then I synthesize it"; the bar is "say something true, but in an interesting way," and he'll "delete tweets that have 10,000 likes… because I catch a grammar or spelling error" ("It has to be correct and incompressible"). He cites Emerson — in genius "we recognize our own rejected thoughts" — for why a good aphorism converts the reader's tacit knowledge into explicit. First-principles and reductive: he strips a topic to a definition then rebuilds, with a favorite move of *deflating an awe-word* by pointing at something mundane ("we already know how to create AGI, go have a child"; naming "a single Sumerian" to shrink an ego battle). He distrusts false precision and "carrying variables around" as if philosophy were math — "Happiness is more like poetry than algorithms," and he asks for charity because he "conflate[s] happiness, pleasure, peace, joy, bliss." Calm, declarative, near-stoic in the late phase; heavy analogy (happiness "like fitness," the lion vs. the marathon runner, the monkey mind "flinging feces," meditation as "intermittent fasting for the mind," the brain in "debug mode," an "army of robots"). He readily names and venerates his sources (Taleb, Munger, Sivers, Thiel, Scott Adams's skill stack and "systems not goals," David Deutsch as the rare reasoning-changing author, Disraeli, Bruce Lee, Jerzy Gregorek), and openly disclaims authorship of borrowed lines (the "100 books" line is @illacertus's). He is self-deprecating about his own practice — the "faileo diet," "I'm pretty bad at this… meditation," "I have a failed physics background," and "Dumb luck, dumb luck" — and habitually disclaims his own authority: the Periscope is "for entertainment purposes only. I do not promise to be consistent or even coherent." The earlier Venture Hacks / Epinions / Elad Gil voice is more operational, profane, and combative — real option-pool mechanics and a wary, adversarial read of investors ("You call your lawyer: 'What the fuck?!'"). Note the recurring tension between "specialize into yourself" and "specialization is for insects": he reconciles it as specialize your *output* while keeping *curiosity* broad — a seam a sharp interlocutor can press. The portable form is both the appeal and, critics argue, the limitation.

text: **The luck paradox / survivorship bias.** The sharpest sourced critique: claiming you can get rich "without getting lucky" while operating in venture — an industry whose model is betting on rare, unpredictable winners — is "undoubtedly a logical contradiction." His own arc (Epinions, $45M of VC, AngelList) unfolded in Silicon Valley "Extremistan" during an internet boom. (36Kr) He half-concedes it — "I've encountered plenty of bad luck… It's only the third time around has been a charm" — but frames repeated survival as skill, the very move critics flag. His own words make the bias vivid: "every brilliant person I met in Silicon Valley 20 years ago… every single one is successful. Every single one. I cannot think of an exception" (in-the-arena). BetterSelfLabs: the advice "leans into survivorship bias… and underplays luck/variance."

text: **Documented vs. inferred.** Nearly everything in Core ideas, Mental models, Decision heuristics, Positions, and Signature quotes is *documented* (verbatim, sourced). The *inferences* are: the **Where they disagree** matrix (the head-to-heads with Horowitz/Lemkin, Bezos, the doomer camp, and the work-life-balance camp are reconstructed from both sides' documented positions, not a direct exchange) and the practical-council framing in *Blind spots*. The **Blind spots** critiques themselves are sourced (BetterSelfLabs; Decoding the Gurus; 36Kr citing Sandel/Bourdieu; the Sovereign Child interview) — not invented — and are *complemented* by Naval's own self-acknowledged tensions (the hard-work contradiction, the "every brilliant person… succeeded" line, the conceded anger/politics/meditation gaps), which are his own corpus, not external critique.

text: **Attribution & verbatim caveats.** Where Naval paraphrases others his exact wording is kept and the borrowed source flagged: "the most dangerous things are heroin, and a monthly salary" (Taleb), "I'd rather teach an engineer marketing" (Gates), the one-kick-ten-thousand-times line (Bruce Lee), "Easy choices, hard life" (Jerzy Gregorek), "Set up systems, not goals" / skill stack (Scott Adams), "we make our fortunes and we call them fate" (Disraeli), "To find a worthy mate, be worthy" (Munger), the Pascal/Confucius/Homer epigraphs. The **"100 great books over and over"** line is Naval *quoting* @illacertus, not original. The Venture Hacks pieces are mixed-byline: `pick-cofounder` is cleanly Naval; `11-lessons` is Nivi's pen but "most of the wisdom is from Naval"; the `option-pool-shuffle` quote used here is a **signed Naval comment**; the `writing`/marketing lines are Nivi/shared-voice and are **not** attributed to Naval in this dossier. Three lines from the prior dossier remain **dropped** as misattributions: *"To a calm mind the whole universe surrenders"* (Lao Tzu), *"the internet of money"* (Andreas Antonopoulos), and an untraceable "ground yourself in the present" line. The Epinions *lawsuit* facts on the navalmanack page are the **NYT's words**, not Naval's. BlockCon 2018 and Vitalia quotes are from podcastnotes.org mirrors (primary transcripts returned 403/402) — faithful-but-not-guaranteed-verbatim. The 2017 blockchain tweetstorm's canonical X URL blocks automated fetch; wording was cross-checked against independent reproductions. Periscope #1/#2 quotes are from the circulating transcript PDFs. A **JRE #1309 fold-in patch** added the Joe Rogan Experience #1309 quotes (the dossier's first material extracted directly from a podcast recording), each carried with a "(JRE #1309 @timestamp)" citation. text: The Almanack is a *compilation*: no methods section, no controlled comparisons, minimal citation — a structural fact underlying several of the sourced critiques.

Co-founder/former CEO of Algolia (hosted search API, ~$2B+, YC W14) turned YC Group Partner who has coached 1,000+ early-stage teams — the rare advisor who both *scaled* a developer product through the brutal $20–100M wall to ~350 people and now pattern-matches across a huge sample. His lens: developers are the buyers and the channel ("documentation is marketing," "you are your audience"), culture is founded before the product and then shipped/debugged like one, you price on value not cost, and in the AI era "code has become a commodity — evals are more important." His sharpest, most contrarian calls: a *formal* DevRel team can destroy the grassroots evangelism it was meant to scale (keep it cultural until ~150 people force the issue); hire the operator who ran the *next* stage, never the visionary who only knows the destination; wait for ~$1M ARR before the first salesperson and Series A before a dedicated dev advocate; and step yourself down when the company's need (GTM at scale) outgrows your skill — which he did, by his own initiative. He files his own decisions under "wouldn't do again" (home-grown billing, killing search-query pricing "to encourage usage," the overloaded first hire) more readily than most founders, and volunteers his own biggest hindsight regret unprompted — that even with a hard, differentiated technical build, he'd have spent far more time with customers while building it. His documented blind spot — first-principles curdling into not-invented-here and competitor-blindness — bites against his own stated worldview and shows up independently in two separate ex-employee accounts. He opposes cost-plus pricers, "institutionalize DevRel" growth orthodoxy, hire-ahead-of-growth VC advice, monetizing open source via support-and-services, and the AI-era view that the codebase is the durable asset — while showing a live, unresolved tension between the patient, community-led GTM Algolia actually lived and the more aggressive "charge early, don't fear burning leads, go outbound first" advice he gives as a coach.

text:
Nicolas Dessaigne co-founded Algolia in 2012 with Julien Lemoine and led it as CEO through YC (W14), a $110M Series C, and a valuation reported above $2B, scaling to ~350 people. He holds a PhD in Computer Science from the University of Nantes ([Partiful event page](https://partiful.com/e/hJSfxKhW4Kp8zy2J3N2C); [HN announcement](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45399674)). Algolia did not start as a search API: "We actually started Algolia with another product: a search engine able to run locally on a mobile device without relying to a server." (Vator/Algolia, 2016.) The mobile market disappointed and they pivoted to server-based SaaS — catalyzed, he says, by a botched YC interview: "We messed up the interview because we really didn't know what we were doing at the time. So we decided to spend the week in San Francisco, met a lot of great entrepreneurs and got so much feedback that it really transformed the company." Being outsiders helped: "A big advantage was we didn't know anyone in Menlo Park. We had no family or distractions. It was an excuse to just focus on work and do it." (STATION F.) The relationship that unlocked their second, successful YC application traced back to a customer connection: fellow YC partner (and future fellow advisor in this repo) Michael Seibel, then running Socialcam, vouched for them as an early beta customer — a concrete instance of "who vouches for you" mattering as much as the pitch itself.
He and Lemoine treated culture as the true founding act, ahead of product: "On day one, Julien and I spent a lot of time discussing our goals. We didn't focus on the product then... We see ourselves as a culture-first company — Algolia wouldn't exist at all if not for its culture." They didn't hire anyone for a full year after that conversation. "Back in 2012, our seminal discussions culminated in our decision to create the company together. We didn't hire anyone for another year, but, right then, I feel like we created Algolia — not the product, but its culture." Only after that alignment did he resign his job: "The next day, I gave my notice." ([Algolia Stories: Culture-First Company](https://stories.algolia.com/how-algolia-built-a-culture-first-company-around-ownership-eee6623b1b6).) They built the company borderless from day one: English as the sole company language despite the largest office being in Paris, and infrastructure ahead of regulation — "We have more than 1100 servers and 50 data centers around the world. If we have a customer in Germany who is very concerned with privacy, we have data centers in Germany compliant with those security standards where we can store that customer's data." Dual structure: "Our developers are in Paris, so our IP is in France." (STATION F.)
In May 2020 he stepped down as CEO — his decision, not the board's — handing the role to Bernadette Nixon and moving to a board seat. In his own first-person announcement: "Algolia has been at the center of my life over the past 8 years, and I believe in the company and our people more than ever. While I won't retain an operational role, I will be Algolia's strongest champion and will continue to support Bernadette and the team as a dedicated board member." At the moment of handoff Algolia served "over 9,000 companies... across 120 countries" and powered "over one trillion searches in 2020 — touching 1 in 6 web users each day," with logos including Under Armour, The RealReal, Stripe, and Slack. (Algolia blog, "Algolia's next wave of growth.") By late 2024, per YC's own promotional copy, the platform he built "powers over 1.75 trillion searches annually for 17,000+ customers worldwide" — legacy scale accruing years after he left the operating seat. (LinkedIn/YC, Nov 2024.)
He then joined Y Combinator as a Group/General Partner (both titles appear in press; YC itself favors "Group Partner"), where by his most recent public bio he had "conducted over 3,000 office hours across 9 batches" as of October 2025 (Partiful/HN) — the dossier's earlier profile-based figure of "12 batches, 1,000+ startups" reflects a later pull from YC's own people page; treat both as directionally consistent snapshots at different dates, not a contradiction. Associated alumni he mentors include Checkr, Front, Sendbird, PostHog, and Airbyte. His 2025–26 posture centers on AI-native startups, dev tools for agents, and iteration speed; per one 2026 interview, "half of Nicolas's time is now spent helping alumni founders," not just batch founders. (Tim Frin / Clef de voûte.)
He is the rare advisor here who has personally lived both sides of the founder/coach divide. The most useful thing he carries that most advisors don't is granular memory of *where things broke* — billing, support, pricing, the wrong senior hire — at specific headcounts and revenue bands, paired with an unusual willingness to name his own biggest operating regret unprompted (see Blind spots).

text: **Build-time vs. runtime ideas.** Build-time tools (docs, QA, testing) are "nice to have" — a customer can live without them, which is why the market is noisy with competitors chasing the same obvious pain. Runtime ideas (APIs that run in production, like Stripe or Algolia) are "must-have": "If you bet on an API, for example, you cannot run your own product if it's down." Runtime ideas also align incentives with customer growth — "if their customers sell more products, they make more money. Everyone is happy." *Worked example:* he explicitly ranks his own company's category (search API) above the build-time tools he says are overcrowded (yet another QA/docs tool). Libraries/frameworks are a third bucket — often open source, hard to monetize directly (e.g. Pandas), monetizable mainly via hosting (Next.js → Vercel). (YC Library: Dev Tools Company.)

text: **The pivot that keeps its dividend.** A failed bet isn't wasted if it forces a capability the next bet needs. *Worked example:* the dead-end mobile on-device search engine produced the relentless performance focus that differentiated the SaaS product. (Vator/Algolia, 2016.) His own retelling on a YC panel adds a harder edge: the mobile SDK generated real but tiny revenue ("a few thousand dollars a month"), and the actual pivot trigger was reading the pattern of hard sales and flat demand — "we could build a lifestyle company, but it's not what we want to do here, let's change something." (YC Office Hours: AI GTM & Pivoting.)

He resists reducing this to a formula: "I don't think it's a formula. I don't think there is an algorithm... I think it's more like a deep conviction you build for yourself coming from a lot of conversations." (YC Office Hours: AI GTM & Pivoting.) The model: traction that is real-but-not-enough is itself a pivot signal, not only a dead market.

text: **Open source as GTM: a three-tier necessity rule.** (1) Mandatory if you're a library or framework — "Developers wouldn't implement on top of a new framework that is not open source." (2) Mandatory if you handle sensitive data — a new database, or an API touching a CRM/EHR. (3) Optional-but-a-real-differentiator for APIs and applications — "you could be the open source version of X," citing PostHog vs. Amplitude, Supabase vs. Firebase, Airbyte vs. Fivetran. *Worked example on community contributions:* Airbyte got many connectors contributed by its community, but "I would be careful on that one. Most cases, you shouldn't count on them because the quality of the contribution may not be up to your standard." (YC Library: Dev Tools Company.)
quotes: Developers wouldn't implement on top of a new framework that is not open source.
you could be the open source version of X,
I would be careful on that one. Most cases, you shouldn't count on them because the quality of the contribution may not be up to your standard.
title: Open source as GTM: a three-tier necessity rule

text: **Open source as an enterprise trust-shortcut, beyond dev tools.** Open source isn't only a developer-GTM play — for non-developer enterprise SaaS it lowers procurement friction. *Worked examples:* Medplum (open-source EHR) — being open source "was really about creating... trust... and shortening the sales cycle by maybe a year"; Twenty (open-source CRM) — "some people may want to use that product because they can... trust it because they can dig in the code if necessary. They'll never do that, but just the level of trust that it generates [is enough]." He names the tradeoff too: self-hosting "comes at a cost... you have to charge a very high price for it." (YC Office Hours: AI GTM & Pivoting.)

title: Open source as an enterprise trust-shortcut, beyond dev tools

text: **Open-source monetization: three legitimate models, one bad incentive.** (1) Hosting/cloud — customers self-host free or pay you to host and maintain it. (2) Open-core — an enterprise tier with SSO, OAuth, disaster recovery, SLAs. (3) Support-and-services — which he actively discourages: "your incentive becomes to build the most complex product possible so you can charge for support and services, which is a bad incentive." As a YC partner/investor, he's explicitly unworried about open-sourcing even monetizable layers: "There are many ways for an open-source company to monetize its product," citing PostHog and Strapi's open-core playbook as proven. (YC Library: Dev Tools Company; Lago.)
quotes: your incentive becomes to build the most complex product possible so you can charge for support and services, which is a bad incentive.
There are many ways for an open-source company to monetize its product,
title: Open-source monetization: three legitimate models, one bad incentive

text: **"Good / Better / Best" pricing ladder for non-open-source dev tools.** Good = self-serve, solves the individual developer's pain, low price. Better = engineering-manager-facing, collaboration features, still self-serve. Best = sold to the CTO — security, audit logs, SLAs — sales-led. The alternative architecture is pure usage-based (APIs like Algolia, Stripe), possibly with enterprise-specific add-ons. (YC Library: Dev Tools Company.)
quotes: Good / Better / Best
title: "Good / Better / Best" pricing ladder for non-open-source dev tools

text: **Speed × quality, not speed vs. quality.** Product excellence is a *product* of two dials, not a tradeoff to pick one side of: "a crappy product that doesn't provide value will go nowhere." YC deliberately withholds a fixed ratio — "YC is not about dictating the balance between speed and quality. It's on you to decide what's critical. We'll push you out of your comfort zone, and that's where founders develop superpowers." (Tim Frin / Clef de voûte.)
quotes: a crappy product that doesn't provide value will go nowhere.
YC is not about dictating the balance between speed and quality. It's on you to decide what's critical. We'll push you out of your comfort zone, and that's where founders develop superpowers.
title: Speed × quality, not speed vs. quality

text: **Crappy-quick-and-dirty, then refactor — a two-phase code-quality model.** "Crappy, quick and dirty is completely okay early stage, and then you refactor what actually matters." Concretely: "I would assume that you'll throw away 90% of all the code you write. So your goal at that stage is just to identify the 10% of what you're building that's actually valuable as fast as possible." (YC Library: Dev Tools Company; YouTube Short: advice for founders.) *Tension worth naming (see Blind spots):* Algolia's own founding product was a genuinely hard, low-level search engine — there was no throwaway "crappy" version that still worked — which sits awkwardly next to this generalized advice.

title: Crappy-quick-and-dirty, then refactor — a two-phase code-quality model

text: **Borderless/global from day one.** One company language (English), distributed infrastructure built ahead of regulation — see Bio for the full "1100 servers, 50 data centers" and Germany-compliance example, offered as evidence that customer trust requirements are a leading indicator of coming regulation, not something to wait on. (STATION F.)

text: Put developers on the founding team — for a dev tool, essential, not nice-to-have. You don't need a non-technical co-founder for one; the "you are your audience" advantage does the selling and marketing work a business co-founder would.

text: Launch the rough prototype; let a paying customer validate before you polish. "Crappy and quick is fine" early — his own first Algolia demo was "just a command line and then a very simple webpage," no API client, no admin UI, and it closed a $2,000/month contract. (YC Library: Dev Tools Company.)

text: Find your first users from your own network and outbound — "Nobody knows you yet." Start with prior colleagues/classmates, expand via LinkedIn, and personalize every message: "Just ask yourself: would you be excited to open your message?" (YC Library: Dev Tools Company.)

Engage with hostile comments too, not to convince the hater but everyone else reading. *Worked examples:* Segment tested an idea by launching it on HN and it blew up; Ollama started as a Hacker News comment, then launched (and relaunched) repeatedly, "every few months," to keep fueling growth. (YC Library: Dev Tools Company.)

text: Do things that don't scale early: manual outreach, hands-on implementation, "hustle your way to a demo." *Worked example:* early Stripe engineers sat side-by-side with small-startup customers, coding the integration with them in person. (YC Library: Dev Tools Company.)

text: Choose your tech stack for existing expertise, not novelty — pick what lets you iterate fastest, not what you want to learn.
Don't hire until you've convinced yourself you're working on the right idea.

Wait for ~$1M ARR before hiring your first salesperson, and even then hire someone technical or dev-literate. Wait for Series A or later for a dedicated developer advocate; before that, delegate to engineers, and when you do hire, look inside your own community first (open-source contributors, active Discord members). (YC Library: Dev Tools Company.)
When you make a senior hire, require they've operated at the stage just above yours — not the stage you aspire to.

Don't institutionalize what you want to stay cultural. Keep evangelism/support an expectation of every engineer's role for as long as you can; staff a dedicated team only when an external constraint (enterprise SLA, ~150 people) forces it.
When the company's potential outgrows your skill set, hand the wheel — "someone with more go-to-market experience would probably be a better person at achieving that potential."

text: Choose investors who fit the culture over the largest check; treat fundraising as business development. Read the term sheet yourself (he recommends *Venture Deals*). His stated preference: investors "that showed real interest, as opposed to faceless giant funds to whom they would just be pocket change." (STATION F.)
quotes: that showed real interest, as opposed to faceless giant funds to whom they would just be pocket change.

text: Go deep before wide: make your first ~100 customers love the product by solving one problem better than anyone, then let word of mouth carry the next ones.

Price on what the customer values, not on your costs. Decide early how long you'll grandfather legacy plans. Before removing a monetization lever "to encourage usage," model whether customers actually value the thing you're giving away for free — see his own search-query-pricing regret below.
quotes: to encourage usage,

text: Before building infra in-house, price the long-term *maintenance* liability, not just the build. The more decision-makers a system touches (billing = whole exec team) rather than engineering alone, the stronger the case for buying or open-sourcing rather than building.

In the AI era, invest in evals, proprietary data, and the user-feedback loop — those, not the code, compound into a moat. The harder the technical problem, the better the moat — but budget real time with customers even while heads-down on a hard build.

(As a coach, a more aggressive register than his own company's path — see "Positions by decision type" below): don't wait to launch, charge early, don't fear burning leads, prioritize outbound over other channels early on, and be accountable to people close to you, investors, or peer companies at your stage. (SaaS Connection #21.)
quotes: Positions by decision type

text: **Pivot vs. persevere.** Pivot on a clear negative market signal — but mine the abandoned path for what it taught you (mobile→SaaS). Pivot even *with* traction when a side-built tool is worth more than the current product (Firecrawl/Mendable, "a deep conviction you build for yourself," not a formula). A pivot that throws away the hard-won capability is worse than one that redirects it. (Vator/Algolia; YC Office Hours: AI GTM & Pivoting.)
quotes: a deep conviction you build for yourself,
title: Pivot vs. persevere

text: **How to price (architecture).** Documented arc: tiered → pure usage-based. "As most early stage companies, we had no clue about what our pricing should look like... We ended up with three plans, from $49 to $299 per month with different quotas." Later: "we decided to move to a full usage-based pricing. No more tiered plans." The migration wasn't free — "As we scaled, however, it became a nightmare. We always grandfathered our customers." For non-open-source dev tools generally, he offers the Good/Better/Best ladder as the alternative architecture to pure usage-based. (Lago; YC Library: Dev Tools Company.)

text: **How to price (philosophy, with two named regrets).** Value-based, not cost-plus: "What matters is not your costs but what your customers value." He names two separate pricing mistakes against himself, not just the principle. First: home-grown billing (see Build vs. buy, below). Second, and more specific: "At some point... we decided to stop charging for search queries. Indexing was our major cost and we thought that by making searching free, we would encourage customers to better leverage the product. It turned out to be a very bad move" — because "the vast majority of people value search and don't care about indexing." (Lago.)
quotes: What matters is not your costs but what your customers value.

title: How to price (philosophy, with two named regrets)

text: **Build vs. buy (infrastructure) — the decision-maker-breadth signal.** They built billing in-house because "there was nothing on the market that really worked well for the overage component," then regretted the maintenance: "we also underestimated the complexity of maintaining a billing system... I'd probably think about it twice." He adds a governance lens beyond cost: for a pure dev tool, "the Engineering team is the only decision-maker"; for a cross-functional system like billing, "nearly every person on the Executive Committee has a say." The wider the decision-maker circle a system touches, the stronger the case to buy (or open-source) rather than build — the test remains "is this our differentiation?" Search was; billing wasn't. (Lago.)

text: **When to staff a function vs. keep it cultural (DevRel/support).** Keep it cultural as long as possible; staff only under external pressure. First dedicated support/DevRel "at around 150 people," and even then "engineers are still expected to do one to two days of technical support and contribute to DevRel each month." (VentureBeat.) The same logic extends to sales (~$1M ARR) and dev advocacy (Series A+) — see Decision heuristics.

text: **Who to hire when scaling.** Bounded experience — people who've run the *next* stage, not visionaries who only know the destination. Don't overload a heroic generalist: "We were super lucky with our first hire... at some point, we asked too much of him." Hire experienced leaders for customer success and service engineering rather than stacking pre-sales + CS + service engineering on one early person. (FastForward.)

title: Who to hire when scaling

text: **When to sell / when to step down.** He sold his own CEO seat, not the company: a voluntary handoff when his skills no longer matched the next stage. "It really started on my side. The board was supportive of the decision but it didn't come from them." (TechCrunch.) His own written announcement frames it the same way from the inside — full operational exit ("I won't retain an operational role"), full continued governance/support ("strongest champion... dedicated board member") — a clean two-part model for what a founder keeps and gives up. (Algolia blog, "Algolia's next wave of growth.")

text: **Raise vs. how-to-raise.** He doesn't moralize about bootstrapping; Algolia raised aggressively (an $18.3M round in 2015, a $53M round in ~2017 led by Accel with Jason Lemkin, Point Nine, and AppDynamics'/Intercom's/InVision's founders participating, and eventually a $110M Series C). text: **Focus vs. diversify (first customers).** Focus, hard: "Your first 100 customers need to love your product because you solve a problem better than anyone else!" Breadth is earned by depth via word of mouth, not pursued directly. (Hexa.)

text: **GTM channel sequencing — a live, unresolved tension in his own advice.** Algolia's *own* lived path was patient and community-led: docs, Hacker News launches, DevRel-as-culture, word of mouth from a deeply-loved first 100 customers. But as a coach he also gives a more aggressive, outbound-first register: "Don't wait before launching," "charge [customers] as early as possible," "don't be afraid to 'burn' leads — it's better than not taking the risk," and "early on, prioritize outbound over every other marketing channel." (SaaS Connection #21.) These aren't strictly contradictory — outbound-for-first-contact and community-for-scale can coexist — but the register is genuinely different: patient/organic in his own war stories, urgent/aggressive in his generic coaching soundbites. Worth flagging explicitly when simulating him on a GTM-timing question: check which mode the situation calls for before defaulting to either.

text: Measured, practical, low-ego. Speaks as a builder-turned-coach, not a thought-leader; advice is concrete and operational ("hire a recruiter once you pass ~10 hires/year"; "wait to get to about one million ARR before hiring your first salesperson") rather than aphoristic. Reaches for exact, small numbers to anchor a claim rather than rounding to a clean story — "$2,000 a month," "74% vs. 45%," "150 people," "9 people, 1.2 million ARR" — a teaching habit of proving the point with the specific data point he remembers, not the tidy version. Strikingly willing to file his own decisions under "wouldn't do again" — billing, killing search-query pricing, the overloaded first hire, hiring destination-people, and (self-volunteered, unprompted) not spending enough time with customers during a hard technical build — in plain, unflinching language ("To be honest, we also underestimated…," "it turned out to be a very bad move"). Reaches for *product* metaphors for non-product things (culture has "versions... iterations... bugs"; a bad hire is "a divider"). Frames problems in terms of *relationships and reactions* ("it's how you react when there is a problem") rather than tactics. Often closes a talk with a tight, numbered recap (the six-point "start now / build quickly / spend time with your users / launch early / consider open source / you're the best salesperson and marketer" close) — a lecture-hall habit distinct from the more conversational register of his podcast interviews. European founder sensibility (US-scale company from a French/global base); emphasizes culture, values, team, and the long term over hype. Cites others' work (Radical Candor, Venture Deals, Creativity, Inc., Freedom, Inc.) rather than positioning himself as an originator — per 20VC's show notes, *Creativity, Inc.* is his favorite book and SaaStr his favorite blog. Self-deprecating about early mistakes; his register shifts noticeably between the patient, community-led story he tells about Algolia and the more urgent, outbound-first soundbites he gives as a generic coach (see "Positions by decision type").

text: **vs. Paul Graham on hiring / "do things that don't scale."** PG's canonical advice is to delay process and hire slowly. Dessaigne agrees on doing-things-that-don't-scale early but is unusually explicit that the scaling phase needs *experienced* outside leaders deliberately: "At some point, you cannot rely only on your existing team. You have to get people with experience onboard." (FastForward.) His twist — hire for the *next leg*, not the destination — is a sharper rule and a hedge against PG-style under-hiring at the $20–100M wall.
quotes: do things that don't scale.

text: **vs. "hire ahead of growth" VC orthodoxy.** Many investors push founders to hire the executive who's "been there at 10x your size." Dessaigne documents the opposite mistake as the costly one: late-stage people "who... don't know how to get there from here." (FastForward.) Hire the operator from one stage up, not five.

text: Paul Graham is the essayist-investor who co-founded Y Combinator and, across ~225 plain-prose essays, wrote the operating system a generation of founders runs on. His lens: a startup is *growth*, not size; the one act that survives every other consideration is "making something people want"; conventional, credentialed wisdom is optimized for the average case and reliably wrong about the exceptional one; and the most valuable ideas look *bad* (so the biggest wins are black swans) and involve work everyone avoids ("schlep blindness"). His sharpest/most contrarian positions: determination beats IQ in founders; wealth is *created* not extracted, so billionaire fortunes need not be exploitative ("the key is not exploitation but empathy"); "founder mode" beats the hire-good-people-and-give-them-room manager orthodoxy; independent thinking requires keeping your *identity small*; returns on effort are superlinear, so be ambitious past the point others find reasonable; and writing is thinking, so the AI era splits us into "writes and write-nots." He opposes MBA/professional-management orthodoxy (Ben Horowitz, Reed Hastings, scale-management à la Jensen Huang), the bootstrapper/anti-VC camp (Naval Ravikant on staying small), zero-sum views of wealth, and the "validate-before-you-build" lean reflex. Use him for early-stage product, founder selection, idea evaluation, fundraising tactics, and writing-as-thinking; distrust him on slow-growth, bootstrapped, capital-intensive, or non-tech businesses, where critics flag heavy survivorship bias and founder-worship.

text: Paul Graham (b. 1964) is an English-American programmer, essayist, and investor. With Robert Morris he built Viaweb in 1995 — one of the first software-as-a-service applications, "written by just three people" (*The Other Road Ahead*) — which Yahoo acquired in 1998 (~$49.6M) and rebranded Yahoo Store. In 2005 he co-founded Y Combinator with Jessica Livingston, Robert Morris, and Trevor Blackwell, pioneering the batch-funded, founder-first accelerator model; by 2026 YC had funded roughly 6,500 companies, including Airbnb, Stripe, Dropbox, Coinbase, and DoorDash. Since 2001 his essays at paulgraham.com — written in deliberately plain prose, read aloud and cut to the bone — have become a foundational text for founders, and he still publishes prolifically (e.g. *Good Writing* and *What to Do*, 2025; *The Brand Age* and *How to Earn a Billion Dollars*, 2026). He is simultaneously one of the most cited and most criticized voices in startup culture: the same instincts that make his advice unusually concrete also make it prone to survivorship bias and founder-worship.

Founder wealth then reduces to two numbers: "There are two numbers that determine how big a startup gets, and thus how rich its founders become: the growth rate and how long it continues." (*earn*.)

text: **Black swan farming** — startup returns follow a power law so extreme that "effectively all the returns are concentrated in a few big winners, and ... the best ideas look initially like bad ideas." (*swan*.) *Worked example:* "But just two companies, Dropbox and Airbnb, account for about three quarters of it." (*swan*.) The selection rule: "ignore the elephant in front of you, the likelihood they'll succeed, and focus instead on ... whether they'll succeed really big." (*swan*.) text: **Moral fashions & the conformist test** — "It would be a remarkable coincidence if ours were the first era to get everything just right." Now we admire the genius." (*wisdom*.)

(*genius*.) *Worked example:* "An obsessive interest in a topic is both a proxy for ability and a substitute for determination" (*genius*); "a bus ticket collector's love is disinterested ... not doing it to impress us or to make themselves rich, but for its own sake." text: **Good procrastination** — "The question is not how to avoid procrastination, but how to procrastinate well." (*procrastination*.) *Worked example:* three variants — "(a) nothing, (b) something less important, or (c) something more important. That last type ... is good procrastination." (*procrastination*.) "The most dangerous form of procrastination is unacknowledged type-B procrastination, because it doesn't feel like procrastination." (*procrastination*.) (*herd*.) *Worked example:* fundraising as "some kind of primitive, multi-celled sea creature, where you irritate one extremity and the whole thing contracts violently." (*fundraising*.) text: **The equity equation: 1/(1−n)** — "when you make any decision involving equity, run it through 1/(1 - n) to see if it makes sense. You should always feel richer after trading equity." text: **Two kinds of judgement** — "Sometimes judging you correctly is the end goal. But there's a second much more common type of judgement where it isn't." (*judgement*.) *Worked example:* "If you regard someone judging you as a customer instead of a judge, the expectation of fairness goes away" (*judgement*) — applied to admissions, hiring, dating: "This is a rare case where being less self-centered will make people more confident." (*judgement*.)

text: **The runway / the mosquito** — funding measured in time: "when the money runs out you're going to be airborne or dead." (*startupmistakes*.) *Worked example:* "A startup is like a mosquito. A bear can absorb a hit and a crab is armored against one, but a mosquito is designed for one thing: to score." (*wealth*.)

text: **Holding a program in one's head** — "A good programmer working intensively on his own code can hold it in his mind the way a mathematician holds a problem he's working on." (*head*.) *Worked example:* "Your code is your understanding of the problem you're exploring. So it's only when you have your code in your head that you really understand the problem." text: **The conservation of pain** — "if you want to make a million dollars, you have to endure a million dollars' worth of pain." (*wealth*.) *Worked example:* a startup doesn't eliminate the effort/stress of wealth creation, it *concentrates* it — "a way to compress your whole working life into a few years"; "instead of working at an ordinary rate for 40 years, you work like hell for four." text: **The low end eats the high end** — "In technology, the low end always eats the high end. It's easier to make an inexpensive product more powerful than to make a powerful product cheaper." text: **The brand age** — industries shift from competing on substance to competing on identity once technology commoditizes quality. *Worked example:* Swiss watches' golden age competed on accuracy; after quartz, Patek Philippe pivoted to status, the Golden Ellipse's crown made *harder* to wind to look distinctive. "Branding is centrifugal; design is centripetal." (*brandage*.)
quotes: Branding is centrifugal; design is centripetal.

text: **Your mind is a compiled program whose source you've lost** — reading and experience permanently train your model of the world even after you forget the content. "Your mind is like a compiled program you've lost the source of. It works, but you don't know why." (*know*.) *Worked example:* PG's unease at forgetting most of what he reads dissolves once he sees the harvest isn't recalled facts but an updated model: "Reading and experience train your model of the world. And even if you forget the experience or what you read, its effect on your model of the world persists." (*know*.) Hence reading still matters even if knowledge could somehow be loaded directly.

text: **Behavior follows structural role, not character (the unified theory of VCs)** — to predict how a class of people will act, look at how they're paid, not who they are. "It's not so much that the business attracts jerks, or even that the power they wield corrupts them. The real problem is the way they're paid." (*venturecapital*.) *Worked example:* "The problem with VC funds is that they're funds. Like the managers of mutual funds or hedge funds, VCs get paid a percentage of the money they manage" — so fund size forces multi-million-dollar deals, which forces control and meddling. The generalization: "VCs are like car salesmen or bureaucrats: the nature of their work turns them into jerks." (*venturecapital*.)

"The problem is not that most towns kill startups. It's that death is the default for startups, and most towns don't save them." (*hubs*.) *Worked example:* the two-part antidote is local norms plus chance meetings, so "In the Valley, lightning has a sign bit" — random encounters skew toward the compensating miracle rather than the disaster. They're the limiting reagents in the reaction that produces startups" (*siliconvalley*.) *Worked example:* the policy corollary is that you can't engineer the result top-down — "A government that asks \"How can we build a silicon valley?\" has probably ensured failure by the way they framed the question. You don't build a silicon valley; you let one grow." (*siliconvalley*.)

text: **Writing to persuade vs. writing to discover** — the two are opposed, and optimizing for the reader quietly corrupts the ideas. "So writing to persuade and writing to discover are diametrically opposed." (*discover*.) *Worked example:* the failure mode isn't just lost truth but self-deception — "It's that you start to lie to yourself. The ideas start to get mixed together with the spin you've added to get them past the readers' misconceptions." (*discover*.) PG's stance: "But I don't write to persuade; I write to figure out. I write to persuade a hypothetical perfectly unbiased reader." (*discover*.)

text: **Make distraction visible; treat it as an adversary.** "The biggest ingredient in most bad habits is denial. So you have to make it so that you can't merely slip into ... it. It has to set off alarms." (*distraction*.) "Addictive things have to be treated as if they were sentient adversaries." (*distraction*.)
quotes: The biggest ingredient in most bad habits is denial. So you have to make it so that you can't merely slip into ... it. It has to set off alarms.
Addictive things have to be treated as if they were sentient adversaries.
title: Make distraction visible; treat it as an adversary

text: **Find your working limit by crossing it.** "The only way to find the limit is by crossing it. Cultivate a sensitivity to the quality of the work." (*hwh*) — and "there's [nothing] admirable about working too hard." (*hwh*.) Aim toward the center: "Many problems have a hard core at the center ... Working hard means aiming toward the center." (*hwh*.)
quotes: The only way to find the limit is by crossing it. Cultivate a sensitivity to the quality of the work.
there's [nothing] admirable about working too hard.
Many problems have a hard core at the center ... Working hard means aiming toward the center.
title: Find your working limit by crossing it

text: **If working hard isn't producing good-enough results, switch fields.** "If you're working hard but not getting good enough results, you should switch." (*hwh*.)
quotes: If you're working hard but not getting good enough results, you should switch.
title: If working hard isn't producing good-enough results, switch fields

text: **Write the bad draft fast, then rewrite ruthlessly.** "Write a bad version 1 as fast as you can; rewrite it over and over; cut out everything unnecessary; write in a conversational tone." (*writing44*.) "Expect 80% of the ideas in an essay to happen after you start writing it." (*writing44*.) Read it aloud; "before I publish a new essay, I read it out loud and fix everything that doesn't sound like conversation." (*talk*.)
quotes: Write a bad version 1 as fast as you can; rewrite it over and over; cut out everything unnecessary; write in a conversational tone.
Expect 80% of the ideas in an essay to happen after you start writing it.
before I publish a new essay, I read it out loud and fix everything that doesn't sound like conversation.
title: Write the bad draft fast, then rewrite ruthlessly

text: **Publish only what you're sure is worth hearing (the Morris technique).** "His trick is not to say anything unless he's sure it's worth hearing." (*useful*.) "In fact you constantly admit you're wrong. You just do it before publishing instead of after." (*useful*.)
quotes: His trick is not to say anything unless he's sure it's worth hearing.
In fact you constantly admit you're wrong. You just do it before publishing instead of after.
title: Publish only what you're sure is worth hearing (the Morris technique)

text: **Invert the regrets of the dying onto your todo list.** "Don't ignore your dreams; don't work too much; say what you think; cultivate friendships; be happy." (*todo*) — because "errors of omission are a particularly dangerous type of mistake ... you make them by default." (*todo*.) Compressed: "don't be a cog." (*todo*.)
quotes: Don't ignore your dreams; don't work too much; say what you think; cultivate friendships; be happy.
errors of omission are a particularly dangerous type of mistake ... you make them by default.
don't be a cog.
title: Invert the regrets of the dying onto your todo list

text: **Take risk early, while you can afford it.** "Take as much risk as you can afford ... If you're not failing occasionally, you're probably being too conservative." (*greatwork*.) "Take multiple shots. Which is another reason to start taking risks early." (*superlinear*.) "Always be learning." (*superlinear*.)
quotes: Take as much risk as you can afford ... If you're not failing occasionally, you're probably being too conservative.
Take multiple shots. Which is another reason to start taking risks early.
Always be learning.
title: Take risk early, while you can afford it

text: **Buying filter for stuff.** "Is this going to make my life noticeably better?" / "will this be something I use constantly? Or is it just something nice? Or worse still, a mere bargain?" (*stuff*.) "Beware of anything you find yourself describing as 'perfectly good.'" (*stuff*.)
quotes: Is this going to make my life noticeably better?
will this be something I use constantly? Or is it just something nice? Or worse still, a mere bargain?
Beware of anything you find yourself describing as 'perfectly good.'
title: Buying filter for stuff

text: **Don't force-fit your idea to the hot category.** On the AI rush, founders matter more than the idea, so "if you want to start a startup to work on a non-AI idea, go ahead." (CNBC, 2025.)
quotes: if you want to start a startup to work on a non-AI idea, go ahead.
title: Don't force-fit your idea to the hot category

text: **Express ideas in the most general form** — "If you express your ideas in the most general form, they'll be truer than you intended." (*greatwork*.) Aim high deliberately: "if you don't try to be the best, you won't even be good" (*greatwork*); a durability test — "try to make something that people will care about in a hundred years." (*greatwork*.)
quotes: If you express your ideas in the most general form, they'll be truer than you intended.
if you don't try to be the best, you won't even be good
try to make something that people will care about in a hundred years.
title: Express ideas in the most general form

text: **To beat status-quo bias, ask the reverse question.** "If I'd already made the change, would I want to revert to what I have now?" (*greatwork*.) And periodically: "Am I working on what I most want to work on?" (*greatwork*.)
quotes: If I'd already made the change, would I want to revert to what I have now?
Am I working on what I most want to work on?
title: To beat status-quo bias, ask the reverse question

text: **Begin with the simplest thing that could possibly work,** then make successive versions. (*greatwork*.) "Get a version 1.0 out there as soon as you can. Until you have some users to measure, you're optimizing based on guesses." (*wealth*.)
quotes: Get a version 1.0 out there as soon as you can. Until you have some users to measure, you're optimizing based on guesses.
title: Begin with the simplest thing that could possibly work,

text: **Copy only what you genuinely like — and copy the substance, not the flaws.** "How do you avoid copying the wrong things? Copy only what you genuinely like." (*copy*.) "Be careful to copy what makes them good, rather than their flaws." (*copy*.) Find your real taste: "would you pay for this at a garage sale, dirty and unattributed?" (*copy*.)
quotes: How do you avoid copying the wrong things? Copy only what you genuinely like.
Be careful to copy what makes them good, rather than their flaws.
would you pay for this at a garage sale, dirty and unattributed?
title: Copy only what you genuinely like — and copy the substance, not the flaws

text: **Work with people you want to become like.** "Colleagues don't just affect your work, though; they also affect you. So work with people you want to become like, because you will." (*greatwork*.) "You'll become like whoever you work with. Do you want to become like these people?" (*when*.)
quotes: Colleagues don't just affect your work, though; they also affect you. So work with people you want to become like, because you will.
You'll become like whoever you work with. Do you want to become like these people?
title: Work with people you want to become like

text: **Be prolific.** "Being prolific is underrated. The more different things you try, the greater the chance of discovering something new." (*greatwork*.) "Essays are for taking risks." (*best*.)
quotes: Being prolific is underrated. The more different things you try, the greater the chance of discovering something new.
Essays are for taking risks.
title: Be prolific

text: **Don't optimize for valuation; take the reasonable deal.** "If you get an offer from a reputable firm at a reasonable valuation with no unusually onerous terms, just take it and get on with building the company." (*startupmistakes*.) "What you want to optimize is your chance of a good outcome, not the percentage of the company you keep." (*guidetoinvestors*.) "Look down at your hands. Are you holding a termsheet?" (*guidetoinvestors*.)
quotes: If you get an offer from a reputable firm at a reasonable valuation with no unusually onerous terms, just take it and get on with building the company.
What you want to optimize is your chance of a good outcome, not the percentage of the company you keep.
Look down at your hands. Are you holding a termsheet?
title: Don't optimize for valuation; take the reasonable deal

text: **Treat rejection as a question.** "Rejection is a question, not an answer" (*guidetoinvestors*) — handle it "with precision," using the data in it, since "the average VC is a rejection machine." (*fundraising*.)
quotes: Rejection is a question, not an answer
the average VC is a rejection machine.
title: Treat rejection as a question

text: **Stay independent of investors** — "you shouldn't start a startup that's expensive to start, because then you'll be at the mercy of investors" (*guidetoinvestors*); cross into ramen profitability if "a little more effort expended on sales would carry you over the threshold." (*fundraising*.) "Always have some alternative plan ... Having one is the best insurance against needing one." (*guidetoinvestors*.)
quotes: you shouldn't start a startup that's expensive to start, because then you'll be at the mercy of investors
a little more effort expended on sales would carry you over the threshold.
Always have some alternative plan ... Having one is the best insurance against needing one.
title: Stay independent of investors

text: **Solve a problem that's easy *for you*; optimize in problem-space, not solution-space.** "With a startup ... find a problem that's easy for you to solve ... you can make enormous gains playing around in problem-space." (*really*.) "The best way to solve a problem is often to redefine it." (*ideas*.)
quotes: With a startup ... find a problem that's easy for you to solve ... you can make enormous gains playing around in problem-space.
The best way to solve a problem is often to redefine it.
title: Solve a problem that's easy *for you*; optimize in problem-space, not solution-space

text: **For angels, bet on people and ratchet down to a sum you wouldn't mind losing.** "Don't get hung up on mechanics or deal terms. What you should spend your time thinking about is whether the company is good." (*angelinvesting*.) "Ratchet down the size of your investment till it's an amount you wouldn't care too much about losing." (*angelinvesting*.) "If you like a startup enough to invest in it, then invest in it." (*angelinvesting*.)
quotes: Don't get hung up on mechanics or deal terms. What you should spend your time thinking about is whether the company is good.
Ratchet down the size of your investment till it's an amount you wouldn't care too much about losing.
If you like a startup enough to invest in it, then invest in it.
title: For angels, bet on people and ratchet down to a sum you wouldn't mind losing

text: **Equity is optimally split when everyone feels slightly cheated.** "When everyone feels they're getting a slightly bad deal ... the stock is optimally apportioned." (*start*.) Don't suppress cofounder misgivings: "It's much easier to fix problems before the company is started than after." (*startupmistakes*.)
quotes: When everyone feels they're getting a slightly bad deal ... the stock is optimally apportioned.
It's much easier to fix problems before the company is started than after.
title: Equity is optimally split when everyone feels slightly cheated

text: **Set goals slightly too small at first.** "Start by erring on the small side ... if you err on the side of making the goal too broad, you won't get anywhere." (*persistence*.) Solve a too-big problem by biting off a subset "then gradually expand from there." (*ideas*.)
quotes: Start by erring on the small side ... if you err on the side of making the goal too broad, you won't get anywhere.
then gradually expand from there.
title: Set goals slightly too small at first

text: **Treat your parents' career wishes as feature requests** — "figure out why and find a better way," don't just give them the literal ask. (*notnot*.)
quotes: figure out why and find a better way,
title: Treat your parents' career wishes as feature requests

text: **Approach big problems obliquely.** "You can't look a big problem too directly in the eye. You have to approach it somewhat obliquely." (*procrastination*.) Generalize Hamming: "What's the best thing you could be working on, and why aren't you?" (*procrastination*.)
quotes: You can't look a big problem too directly in the eye. You have to approach it somewhat obliquely.
What's the best thing you could be working on, and why aren't you?
title: Approach big problems obliquely

text: **Read your own draft as a stranger who knows only the words on the page.** "You have to pretend to be a neutral reader who knows nothing of what's in your head, only what you wrote." (*words*.) Begin from a question, not a thesis: "You notice a door that's ajar, and you open it and walk in to see what's inside." (*essay*.)
quotes: You have to pretend to be a neutral reader who knows nothing of what's in your head, only what you wrote.
You notice a door that's ajar, and you open it and walk in to see what's inside.
title: Read your own draft as a stranger who knows only the words on the page

text: **Silently fact-check everyone — take on the burden of evaluating, not proving.** "When you hear someone say something, stop and ask yourself 'Is that true?'" (*think*.) Curiosity is unusual: "indulging it tends to increase rather than to sate it" (*think*), and the independent-minded are "the gluttons of curiosity, who keep eating even after they're full." (*think*.)
quotes: When you hear someone say something, stop and ask yourself 'Is that true?'
indulging it tends to increase rather than to sate it
the gluttons of curiosity, who keep eating even after they're full.
title: Silently fact-check everyone — take on the burden of evaluating, not proving

text: **Get to profitability before raising, because fundraising is a productivity sink.** "Raising money is terribly distracting. You're lucky if your productivity is a third of what it was before. And it can last for months." (*ramenprofitable*.)
quotes: Raising money is terribly distracting. You're lucky if your productivity is a third of what it was before. And it can last for months.
title: Get to profitability before raising, because fundraising is a productivity sink

text: **Look for threats in the mirror, not the news — and run cheap enough to be unkillable.** "if you're worried about threats to the survival of your company, don't look for them in the news. Look in the mirror." (*badeconomy*.) "the surest route to success is to be the cockroaches of the corporate world. The immediate cause of death in a startup is always running out of money." (*badeconomy*.)
quotes: if you're worried about threats to the survival of your company, don't look for them in the news. Look in the mirror.
the surest route to success is to be the cockroaches of the corporate world. The immediate cause of death in a startup is always running out of money.
title: Look for threats in the mirror, not the news — and run cheap enough to be unkillable

text: **Take insane career risks while young.** "Your early twenties are exactly the time to take insane career risks." (*hiring*.) A failed attempt isn't a liability to employers — surveyed managers at Yahoo/Google/Amazon/Cisco/Microsoft said "they'd prefer the guy who'd tried to start his own company." (*hiring*.)
quotes: Your early twenties are exactly the time to take insane career risks.
they'd prefer the guy who'd tried to start his own company.
title: Take insane career risks while young

text: **Default to "yes" with your users; err on the side of generosity.** "if you find yourself asking \"should we allow users to do x?\" just answer \"yes\" whenever you're unsure. Err on the side of generosity." (*web20*.)
quotes: if you find yourself asking \
just answer \
whenever you're unsure. Err on the side of generosity.
title: Default to "yes" with your users; err on the side of generosity

text: **The "need" trap — judge a question by advantage, not necessity.** Whenever you catch yourself reasoning about whether you *need* some edge, you're framing it wrong: "if you hear someone saying \"we don't need to be in Silicon Valley,\" that use of the word \"need\" is a sign they're not even thinking about the question right." (*webstartups*) — anything that gives a competitor an advantage gives them one over you.
quotes: if you hear someone saying \
that use of the word \
is a sign they're not even thinking about the question right.
title: The "need" trap — judge a question by advantage, not necessity

text: **Pivot vs. persevere.** Stay attached to the *goal*, change the *method*. "You have to be determined, but flexible, like a running back." (*startuplessons*.) "Startups are more like science, where you need to follow the trail wherever it leads." (*startupmistakes*.) Obstinacy is "being wrong slowly."
quotes: You have to be determined, but flexible, like a running back.
Startups are more like science, where you need to follow the trail wherever it leads.
being wrong slowly.
title: Pivot vs. persevere

text: **How to evaluate a startup idea.** Favor ideas that look bad to smart people and involve schleps others avoid; "the most common mistake startups make is to solve problems no one has" (*startupideas*); "when something is described as a toy, that means it has everything an idea needs except being important." (*startupideas*.) Don't fear crowded markets "so long as you have a thesis about what everyone else in it is overlooking." (*startupideas*.) "It's exceptionally rare for startups to be killed by competitors." (*startupideas*.)
quotes: the most common mistake startups make is to solve problems no one has
when something is described as a toy, that means it has everything an idea needs except being important.
so long as you have a thesis about what everyone else in it is overlooking.
It's exceptionally rare for startups to be killed by competitors.
title: How to evaluate a startup idea

text: **How to price / how to grow.** Don't chase tactics; "build something users love, and spend less than you make." (*start*.) Word-of-mouth compounds: "it will happen automatically if you just keep making customers happy." (*earn*.) "There is no such thing as a killer feature." (*really*.) Big launches and big-partner deals usually fail (*ds*); "startups are powered aircraft, not projectiles."
quotes: build something users love, and spend less than you make.
it will happen automatically if you just keep making customers happy.
There is no such thing as a killer feature.
startups are powered aircraft, not projectiles.
title: How to price / how to grow

text: **When to hire.** Late, deliberately, and only for two jobs. "The only reason to hire someone is to do something you'd like to do but can't." (*start*.) Hire only people who "are either going to write code or go out and get users." (*startupmistakes*.) "Mediocre hires hurt you twice: they get less done, but they also make you big." (*boss*.) Look for "an animal." (*start*.)
quotes: The only reason to hire someone is to do something you'd like to do but can't.
are either going to write code or go out and get users.
Mediocre hires hurt you twice: they get less done, but they also make you big.
title: When to hire

text: **Raise vs. bootstrap.** Calibrated to venture-scale software: raise to fund growth, but only after product. "Don't raise money unless you want it and it wants you." (*fr*.) "The hardest part is making something people want." (*fundraising*.) Bootstrapping rarely works: "this apparently verdant territory is one from which few startups emerge alive" (*fundraising*) — though "for most people [selling] is merely the optimal case of [living off revenues]." (*prcmc*.) Don't fix an amount in advance; "different terms for different investors is clearly the way of the future." (*hiresfund*.)
quotes: Don't raise money unless you want it and it wants you.
The hardest part is making something people want.
this apparently verdant territory is one from which few startups emerge alive
for most people [selling] is merely the optimal case of [living off revenues].
different terms for different investors is clearly the way of the future.
title: Raise vs. bootstrap

text: **How to run fundraising.** "Avoid investors till you decide to raise money, and then when you do, talk to them all in parallel, prioritized by expected value, and accept offers greedily." (*fr*.) "Be in fundraising mode or not." (*fr*.) "Treat investors as saying no till they unequivocally say yes." (*fr*.) Underestimate the amount you hope to raise; "valuation is at best third." (*fr*.) "It's not a deal till the money's in the bank." (*fr*.) Convince investors by letting the startup do the work: "Make the truth good, then just tell it." (*convince*.) "Deals fall through." (*fundraising*.) Avoid novice investors — "so nervous." (*fundraising*.)
quotes: Avoid investors till you decide to raise money, and then when you do, talk to them all in parallel, prioritized by expected value, and accept offers greedily.
Be in fundraising mode or not.
Treat investors as saying no till they unequivocally say yes.
valuation is at best third.
It's not a deal till the money's in the bank.
Make the truth good, then just tell it.
Deals fall through.
title: How to run fundraising

text: **Focus vs. diversify.** Concentrate where the payoff is disproportionate; "the number one thing not to do is other things." (*die*.) Start in a deliberately narrow market — "keeping a fire contained at first to get it really hot." (*ds*.)
quotes: the number one thing not to do is other things.
keeping a fire contained at first to get it really hot.
title: Focus vs. diversify

text: **How to run the company once it's working.** Don't default to delegating-and-disappearing; founders can stay deep in the details ("founder mode"), against the professional-management default. "Hire good people and give them room" too often means "hire professional fakers and let them drive the company into the ground." (*foundermode*.) Founder board control after a Series A "will become the norm." (*control*.)
quotes: Hire good people and give them room
hire professional fakers and let them drive the company into the ground.
will become the norm.
title: How to run the company once it's working

text: **When to sell / talk to acquirers.** "It's usually a mistake to talk to corp dev unless (a) you want to sell your company right now and (b) you're sufficiently likely to get an offer at an acceptable price." (*corpdev*.) Their incentive is adversarial: "The only way their performance is measured is by how cheaply they can buy you." (*corpdev*.) Be profitable so "you'll get at least the average of the acquisition market." (*prcmc*.)
quotes: It's usually a mistake to talk to corp dev unless (a) you want to sell your company right now and (b) you're sufficiently likely to get an offer at an acceptable price.
The only way their performance is measured is by how cheaply they can buy you.
you'll get at least the average of the acquisition market.
title: When to sell / talk to acquirers

text: **How to react to a peer's wild idea.** Ask questions, don't dismiss; "people dismiss new ideas [because] it's an easy way to seem sophisticated." (*newideas*.) The adult response: "Really? Why do you think so?" (*notnot*.)
quotes: people dismiss new ideas [because] it's an easy way to seem sophisticated.
Really? Why do you think so?
title: How to react to a peer's wild idea

text: **How to react to criticism of your idea.** Sort it on the disagreement hierarchy: ignore DH0–DH2, lean into DH4–DH6. (*disagree*.) Online, "it's better most of the time not to defend yourself. Otherwise these people are literally taking your life." (*vb*.)
quotes: it's better most of the time not to defend yourself. Otherwise these people are literally taking your life.
title: How to react to criticism of your idea

text: **Where to live / build.** Place is strategy — move to the city whose ambient message matches your aim. (*cities*.)
title: Where to live / build

text: **What to work on (career).** Follow curiosity and what doesn't feel like work; "the way to get startup ideas is not to try to think of startup ideas." (*before*.) "Just learn." (*before*.) "Do not start a startup in college." (*before*.) For students: don't study "entrepreneurship"; "becoming the sort of person who can have organic startup ideas" is the hard part. (*startupideas*.)
quotes: the way to get startup ideas is not to try to think of startup ideas.
Do not start a startup in college.
becoming the sort of person who can have organic startup ideas
title: What to work on (career)

text: **What to build a life on (the meta-question).** "One should help people, and take care of the world," but "make good new things" is the third principle, "how to live to one's full potential" — and "if you make something amazing, you'll often be helping people or the world even if you didn't mean to." (*do*.)
quotes: One should help people, and take care of the world,
make good new things
how to live to one's full potential
if you make something amazing, you'll often be helping people or the world even if you didn't mean to.
title: What to build a life on (the meta-question)

text: **Which industry to enter.** Avoid mature "brand age" industries where competition is status games over a commoditized product. (*brandage*.) "If you're not a genius, just start a startup in some unsexy field where you'll have less competition." (*mit*.)
quotes: If you're not a genius, just start a startup in some unsexy field where you'll have less competition.
title: Which industry to enter

text: **On wealth and inequality (the political fork).** "Reducing economic inequality ... is identical with taking money from the rich" (*inequality*), and "economic inequality ... is the engine that drives [startups]." (*inequality*.) Attack the symptom's cause: "let's attack poverty, and if necessary damage wealth in the process." (*ineq*.) For the wealth→power link, "Log everything." (*inequality*.) "It's absolute poverty you want to avoid, not relative poverty." (*gap*.)
quotes: Reducing economic inequality ... is identical with taking money from the rich
economic inequality ... is the engine that drives [startups].
let's attack poverty, and if necessary damage wealth in the process.

text: **How not to waste a fortune (or a life).** "The way most fortunes are lost is not through excessive expenditure, but through bad investments." (*selfindulgence*.) For time, install new alarms against fake work; "if you love life, don't waste time, because time is what life is made of." (*startuplessons*.)
quotes: The way most fortunes are lost is not through excessive expenditure, but through bad investments.
if you love life, don't waste time, because time is what life is made of.
title: How not to waste a fortune (or a life)

text: **Don't worry about competitors.** "Competitors are rarely what kills startups. Poor execution does." (*ace*/*really*.) "What you should fear, as a startup, is not the established players, but other startups you don't know exist yet ... like you, they're cornered animals." (*startuplessons*.) "You can only avoid competition by avoiding good ideas." (*startupmistakes*.)
quotes: Competitors are rarely what kills startups. Poor execution does.
What you should fear, as a startup, is not the established players, but other startups you don't know exist yet ... like you, they're cornered animals.

text: **MBA vs. learning to hack.** "If you want to invest two years in something that will help you succeed in business, the evidence suggests you'd do better to learn how to hack than get an MBA." You just try to get people to pay you for stuff." (*start*.)
quotes: If you want to invest two years in something that will help you succeed in business, the evidence suggests you'd do better to learn how to hack than get an MBA.

is no great mystery ... You just try to get people to pay you for stuff.

text: **Don't go (back) to school.** "Going to (or back to) school is a huge predictor of death because in addition to the distraction it gives you something to say you're doing." (*die*.) A normal job can make you *less* able to found: it turns you into "a tame animal who thinks he needs an office to work in and a product manager to tell him what software to write." (*notnot*.)
quotes: Going to (or back to) school is a huge predictor of death because in addition to the distraction it gives you something to say you're doing.
a tame animal who thinks he needs an office to work in and a product manager to tell him what software to write.
