text: Warren Buffett (b. 1930, Omaha) ran Berkshire Hathaway for 60 years — 19.9% compounded annual gain vs. 10.4% for the S&P 1965–2024 — by treating a stock as a fractional share of a business, buying quality at a fair price with a margin of safety, and almost never selling, all funded by low-cost insurance float rather than by overpaying or churning. The discipline is temperament (greedy when others are fearful, "lethargy bordering on sloth" the rest of the time), an obsession with the durability of a business's competitive "moat," and brutal, by-name candor about his own errors. His sharpest, most useful contrarian positions: derivatives are "financial weapons of mass destruction," EBITDA is a lie you should wire to a polygraph, beta and "risk-free" bonds mislead while cash quietly rots, gold and Bitcoin are sterile "gambling token[s]" you can fondle but not harvest, buyback-bashing is for "economic illiterate[s] or silver-tongued demagogue[s]," and almost everyone else should just buy a low-cost S&P 500 index fund. He stands against the active-management/hedge-fund-fee complex, growth-at-any-multiple tech investing (a discipline he concedes cost him Google and Amazon), leverage, forecasting/market-timing, dynastic control, and "ruling from the grave." Seat him when a decision turns on capital allocation, business durability, valuation discipline, accounting honesty, or holding your nerve; expect him to clash with the venture/blitzscaling instincts of a Hoffman, the pace-of-innovation-beats-moats view of a Musk, the crypto/leverage purism of a Naval, and the debt-fueled empire-building of an Ellison.
quotes: lethargy bordering on sloth
financial weapons of mass destruction,
economic illiterate[s] or silver-tongued demagogue[s],
ruling from the grave.

text:
Warren Edward Buffett took control of a dying New England textile mill in 1965 and turned Berkshire Hathaway into one of the largest companies on earth — an overall per-share gain of 5,502,284% by the 2024 letter. He learned investing from Benjamin Graham at Columbia (and quotes him constantly), ran the Buffett Partnership from 1956–1969 (limited partners compounded 25.3% for twelve years, never a down year against the Dow), and then wound it down at the go-go-market top rather than "play a game I don't understand." His late partner Charlie Munger (d. 2023) pushed him from Graham-style "cigar butts" to durable quality; Buffett calls him "the 'architect' of the present Berkshire" and himself "the 'general contractor'" (2023). His judgment is unusually well-documented: he wrote the annual letter himself for ~48 years, answered shareholders live for ~6 hours each May since 1994, and left a public corpus of reasoning few operators match.
Context as of 2026-07-08: Buffett **stepped down as CEO on Jan 1, 2026** (announced at the May 2025 meeting — "I think the time has arrived"); **Greg Abel** is now CEO. Buffett remains chairman. The frontmatter role reflects the seat behind the body of work this dossier draws on; treat him today as chairman / letter-writer emeritus. In his **Nov 10, 2025 Thanksgiving letter** — his explicit farewell as the long-form author — he said he would stop "writing Berkshire's annual report or talking endlessly at the annual meeting… I'm 'going quiet.' Sort of," continuing only via shorter annual Thanksgiving notes. That letter is the richest late-career source on luck, legacy, succession, and giving the money away.
quotes: play a game I don't understand.
the 'architect' of the present Berkshire
the 'general contractor'
I think the time has arrived
writing Berkshire's annual report or talking endlessly at the annual meeting… I'm 'going quiet.' Sort of,

text: **A stock is a fractional share of a business, not a ticker.** The realization that reorganized everything: "you are not just buying some little ticker symbol, that bounces around every day, you are buying part of a business. Soon as I started thinking about it that way, everything else followed" (U. Florida 1998). Analyze the business; ignore the quote unless it offers you a bargain.
quotes: you are not just buying some little ticker symbol, that bounces around every day, you are buying part of a business. Soon as I started thinking about it that way, everything else followed
title: A stock is a fractional share of a business, not a ticker

text: **The market serves you, not instructs you.** Graham's Mr. Market is a manic-depressive partner who names a price daily — "Mr. Market is there to serve you, not to guide you. It is his pocketbook, not his wisdom, that you will find useful" (1987). Buffett *welcomes* declines in things he wants more of: "I like buying quality merchandise when it is marked down" (2008). Risk is set by others' emotion, value by the business — exploit the gap, don't feel it.
quotes: Mr. Market is there to serve you, not to guide you. It is his pocketbook, not his wisdom, that you will find useful
I like buying quality merchandise when it is marked down
title: The market serves you, not instructs you

text: **Own productive, cash-generating assets over sterile stores of value.** The one rule for what to own, made vivid by the 2011 gold argument (see Mental models): assets that compound beat assets that just sit. The mirror image is his lifelong refusal of gold, cash-for-its-own-sake, and crypto.
title: Own productive, cash-generating assets over sterile stores of value

text: **Long-term ownership beats activity; reinvestment beats dividends.** "Our favorite holding period is forever" (1988); Berkshire paid exactly one dividend in 60 years (10¢, 1967). "Wall Street makes its money on activity. You make your money on inactivity" (U. Florida 1998). The engine is reinvested, tax-deferred earnings compounding for decades — which is why selling a winner to "lock in gains" is usually the mistake.
quotes: Our favorite holding period is forever
Wall Street makes its money on activity. You make your money on inactivity
lock in gains
title: Long-term ownership beats activity; reinvestment beats dividends

text: **Equities beat cash over time; paper money can rot.** "Berkshire will never prefer ownership of cash-equivalent assets over the ownership of good businesses… Paper money can see its value evaporate if fiscal folly prevails" (2024). Even "risk-free" long bonds can be "a far riskier investment than a long-term investment in common stocks" (2017).
quotes: Berkshire will never prefer ownership of cash-equivalent assets over the ownership of good businesses… Paper money can see its value evaporate if fiscal folly prevails
a far riskier investment than a long-term investment in common stocks
title: Equities beat cash over time; paper money can rot

text: **Reputation is the asset you cannot rebuild.** Stated under maximum pressure at Salomon: lose money and he is understanding; lose "a shred of reputation" and he is "ruthless" (1991 testimony).
quotes: a shred of reputation
title: Reputation is the asset you cannot rebuild

text: **Accounting is an aid to thinking, never a substitute for it — and honesty in it is a moral matter.** "the accountants' job is to record, not to evaluate… accounting is but an aid to business thinking, never a substitute for it" (1986). This is the root of his crusades against EBITDA, "cash flow," options-hiding, and "big bath" restructurings (see Signature quotes).
quotes: the accountants' job is to record, not to evaluate… accounting is but an aid to business thinking, never a substitute for it
title: Accounting is an aid to thinking, never a substitute for it — and honesty in it is a moral matter

text: **Optimism about American capitalism — tempered by candor about luck.** "I have yet to see a time when it made sense to make a long-term bet against America" (2022); "It is beyond arrogance for American businesses or individuals to boast that they have 'done it alone.' The tidy rows of simple white crosses at Normandy should shame those who make such claims" (2018). The farewell goes furthest: "I was born in 1930 healthy, reasonably intelligent, white, male and in America. Wow! Thank you, Lady Luck" (2025) — the "ovarian lottery" theme in his own late words.
quotes: I have yet to see a time when it made sense to make a long-term bet against America
It is beyond arrogance for American businesses or individuals to boast that they have 'done it alone.' The tidy rows of simple white crosses at Normandy should shame those who make such claims
I was born in 1930 healthy, reasonably intelligent, white, male and in America. Wow! Thank you, Lady Luck
title: Optimism about American capitalism — tempered by candor about luck

text: **Give it away; don't rule from the grave.** Pledged >99% of his net worth; the Nov 2025 letter converted 1,800 A shares into ~$1.35B of B shares to four family foundations and handed disbursement to his three children rather than a perpetual trust: "Ruling from the grave does not have a great record, and I have never had an urge to do so."
quotes: Ruling from the grave does not have a great record, and I have never had an urge to do so.
title: Give it away; don't rule from the grave

text:
**Circle of competence.** Only buy what you can understand and forecast; everything else goes in the "too hard" pile. Ted Williams framing: "to be a good hitter, you've got to get a good ball to hit… If I have to bite at stuff that is out of my happy zone, I'm not a .344 hitter" (1994).
- *Worked example (staying in even when it costs):* For decades he kept tech out — "We will never develop the competence to spot such businesses early… Simple businesses (if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it)" (1991). He concedes the price: on missing Google/Amazon, "I blew it… I was too dumb to realize what was going to happen" ([2017 meeting, CNN](https://money.cnn.com/2017/05/06/investing/warren-buffett-google-berkshire-meeting/index.html)). The point isn't that the circle was wrong — it's that you stay inside it even when it hurts.
- *Worked example (the circle can be expanded, slowly):* he skipped Coca-Cola for 52 years while "allocating major portions of my net worth to street railway companies, windmill manufacturers… and the like. Only in the summer of 1988 did my brain finally establish contact with my eyes" (1989) — then bought a stake worth more than Berkshire's entire net worth three years earlier.
quotes: to be a good hitter, you've got to get a good ball to hit… If I have to bite at stuff that is out of my happy zone, I'm not a .344 hitter
We will never develop the competence to spot such businesses early… Simple businesses (if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it)
I blew it… I was too dumb to realize what was going to happen
allocating major portions of my net worth to street railway companies, windmill manufacturers… and the like. Only in the summer of 1988 did my brain finally establish contact with my eyes
title: Circle of competence

text:
**Economic moats / franchise.** A great business needs an enduring barrier protecting high returns on capital. The sharpest test is the *franchise*: "An economic franchise arises from a product or service that: (1) is needed or desired; (2) is thought by its customers to have no close substitute and; (3) is not subject to price regulation… franchises can tolerate mis-management" (1991).
- *Worked example:* "A truly great business must have an enduring 'moat' that protects excellent returns on invested capital. The dynamics of capitalism guarantee that competitors will repeatedly assault any business 'castle' that is earning high returns" (2007). Orally: "I want a very valuable castle in the middle and then I want the Duke who is in charge of that castle to be very honest and hard working and able. Then I want a moat around that castle" (U. Florida 1998), with Kodak as the cautionary tale — "they let that moat narrow… Coke's moat is wider now than it was 30 years ago."
quotes: An economic franchise arises from a product or service that: (1) is needed or desired; (2) is thought by its customers to have no close substitute and; (3) is not subject to price regulation… franchises can tolerate mis-management

A truly great business must have an enduring 'moat' that protects excellent returns on invested capital. The dynamics of capitalism guarantee that competitors will repeatedly assault any business 'castle' that is earning high returns
I want a very valuable castle in the middle and then I want the Duke who is in charge of that castle to be very honest and hard working and able. Then I want a moat around that castle
they let that moat narrow… Coke's moat is wider now than it was 30 years ago.
title: Economic moats / franchise

text:
**Owner earnings and the "cash flow" fallacy.** GAAP earnings plus non-cash charges (b) *minus* the capex the business truly needs (c) — never (a)+(b) alone. The canonical 1986 definition: "(a) reported earnings plus (b) depreciation… less (c) the average annual amount of capitalized expenditures for plant and equipment… that the business requires to fully maintain its long-term competitive position and its unit volume."
- *Worked example:* built via the Scott Fetzer appendix (1986) to attack the sell-side: "you shouldn't add (b) without subtracting (c): though dentists correctly claim that if you ignore your teeth they'll go away, the same is not true for (c)." This is the root of his lifelong EBITDA contempt (see Signature quotes).
quotes: (a) reported earnings plus (b) depreciation… less (c) the average annual amount of capitalized expenditures for plant and equipment… that the business requires to fully maintain its long-term competitive position and its unit volume.
you shouldn't add (b) without subtracting (c): though dentists correctly claim that if you ignore your teeth they'll go away, the same is not true for (c).
title: Owner earnings and the "cash flow" fallacy

text:
**Margin of safety.** Buy meaningfully below your estimate of intrinsic value, because the estimate is fallible. "we will attempt to bring risk of permanent capital loss (not short-term quotational loss) to an absolute minimum by obtaining a wide margin of safety in each commitment" (Partnership Ground Rules, 1962).
- *Worked example:* Wells Fargo 1990 — into a California bank panic he bought ~10% "at a valuation of less than five times after-tax earnings, and less than three times pre-tax earnings," reasoning its ~$1B pre-tax earning power was a cushion large enough to survive the feared real-estate collapse (1990).
quotes: we will attempt to bring risk of permanent capital loss (not short-term quotational loss) to an absolute minimum by obtaining a wide margin of safety in each commitment
at a valuation of less than five times after-tax earnings, and less than three times pre-tax earnings,
title: Margin of safety

text: **Price vs. value / intrinsic value as discounted cash.** "Price is what you pay; value is what you get" (attributed to Graham, 2008). The definition he uses: "intrinsic value… the discounted value of the cash that can be taken out of a business during its remaining life… is all-important and is the only logical way to evaluate the relative attractiveness of investments" (1994). From this he collapses the style wars: "the two approaches [value and growth] are joined at the hip: Growth is always a component in the calculation of value… whose impact can be negative as well as positive" (1992).
quotes: Price is what you pay; value is what you get

intrinsic value… the discounted value of the cash that can be taken out of a business during its remaining life… is all-important and is the only logical way to evaluate the relative attractiveness of investments
the two approaches [value and growth] are joined at the hip: Growth is always a component in the calculation of value… whose impact can be negative as well as positive
title: Price vs. value / intrinsic value as discounted cash

text: **The Aesop / two-birds valuation rule.** Every purchase reduces to: how sure are you the birds are in the bush, when do they emerge, how many, and at what discount rate? "The oracle was Aesop and his enduring, though somewhat incomplete, investment insight was, 'a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush'" (2000 letter — his bridge from folksy maxim to discounted-cash-flow valuation).
quotes: The oracle was Aesop and his enduring, though somewhat incomplete, investment insight was, 'a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush'
title: The Aesop / two-birds valuation rule

text:
**Wonderful business at a fair price > fair business at a wonderful price.** The Munger-driven pivot from Graham cigar-butts. Munger's instruction, quoted by Buffett: "Forget what you know about buying fair businesses at wonderful prices; instead, buy wonderful businesses at fair prices" (2014). Buffett's own version: "It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price. Charlie understood this early; I was a slow learner" (1989), with the reputation test: "when a management with a reputation for brilliance tackles a business with a reputation for bad economics, it is the reputation of the business that remains intact."
- *Worked example (the conversion):* See's Candies, bought 1972 for $25M against $7M tangible net worth. "In our See's purchase, Charlie and I had one important insight: We saw that the business had untapped pricing power" (1991). By 1998, "we will make $60 million this year… Same business, same formulas… and it still doesn't take any capital" (U. Florida 1998). "I gained a business education about the value of powerful brands that opened my eyes to many other profitable investments" (2014).
quotes: Forget what you know about buying fair businesses at wonderful prices; instead, buy wonderful businesses at fair prices
It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price. Charlie understood this early; I was a slow learner
when a management with a reputation for brilliance tackles a business with a reputation for bad economics, it is the reputation of the business that remains intact.
In our See's purchase, Charlie and I had one important insight: We saw that the business had untapped pricing power
we will make $60 million this year… Same business, same formulas… and it still doesn't take any capital
I gained a business education about the value of powerful brands that opened my eyes to many other profitable investments
title: Wonderful business at a fair price > fair business at a wonderful price

text: **Risk = permanent loss of purchasing power, not volatility/beta.** He demolishes beta with a reductio: "a stock that has dropped very sharply compared to the market — as had Washington Post when we bought it in 1973 — becomes 'riskier' at the lower price than it was at the higher price. Would that description have then made any sense…?" (1993). Real risk is "whether his aggregate after-tax receipts… will, over his prospective holding period, give him at least as much purchasing power as he had to begin with" (1993). At LTCM's blow-up: "Sigma's do not tell you about the risk of going broke" (U. Florida 1998).
quotes: a stock that has dropped very sharply compared to the market — as had Washington Post when we bought it in 1973 — becomes 'riskier' at the lower price than it was at the higher price. Would that description have then made any sense…?
whether his aggregate after-tax receipts… will, over his prospective holding period, give him at least as much purchasing power as he had to begin with
Sigma's do not tell you about the risk of going broke
title: Risk = permanent loss of purchasing power, not volatility/beta

text: **Productive vs. unproductive capital (the gold-cube).** Compare what an asset *produces* over decades, not what it might be resold for. In 2011 he pits "pile A" — all the world's gold, a 68-foot cube worth ~$9.6T — against "pile B" of equal cost: all U.S. cropland plus "16 Exxon Mobils," with ~$1T left over. "You can fondle the cube, but it will not respond" (2011). Generalized in 2018: a 1942 investment of $114.75 in an index would be "$606,811," but in gold "about $4,200, less than 1%… The magical metal was no match for the American mettle." The model decides any store-of-value debate — gold, crypto, idle cash — in favor of the cash generator.
quotes: 16 Exxon Mobils,
You can fondle the cube, but it will not respond
about $4,200, less than 1%… The magical metal was no match for the American mettle.
title: Productive vs. unproductive capital (the gold-cube)

text:
**Float.** Insurance premiums collected now, claims paid later, supply low- or negative-cost investable capital — but only under disciplined underwriting. "float is money we hold but don't own" (1994); "we prefer a lumpy 15% return to a smooth 12%" (1998).
- *Worked example:* Float grew from $17.3M (1967) to $171B (2024) at an average cost "under zero." The four disciplines: understand the exposure, evaluate the likelihood conservatively, price for a profit, "and (4) be willing to walk away if the appropriate premium can't be obtained. Many insurers pass the first three tests and flunk the fourth" (2011). Non-negotiable: "We must never write inadequately-priced policies in order to stay in the game. That policy is corporate suicide" (2024).
quotes: float is money we hold but don't own
we prefer a lumpy 15% return to a smooth 12%
and (4) be willing to walk away if the appropriate premium can't be obtained. Many insurers pass the first three tests and flunk the fourth
We must never write inadequately-priced policies in order to stay in the game. That policy is corporate suicide
title: Float

text:
**Look-through earnings + the retained-earnings test.** GAAP understates an owner's economics by ignoring investees' retained earnings; a dollar retained is justified only if it eventually creates ≥ a dollar of market value.
- *Worked example:* Apple, 2021 — "only dividends from Apple are counted in the GAAP earnings Berkshire reports… Apple paid us $785 million… Yet our 'share' of Apple's earnings amounted to a staggering $5.6 billion" (2021). He grounds the whole "no dividend" case on it, invoking Edgar Lawrence Smith: "it was no secret that mind-boggling wealth had earlier been amassed by such titans as Carnegie, Rockefeller and Ford, all of whom had retained a huge portion of their business earnings" (2019).
quotes: only dividends from Apple are counted in the GAAP earnings Berkshire reports… Apple paid us $785 million… Yet our 'share' of Apple's earnings amounted to a staggering $5.6 billion
it was no secret that mind-boggling wealth had earlier been amassed by such titans as Carnegie, Rockefeller and Ford, all of whom had retained a huge portion of their business earnings
title: Look-through earnings + the retained-earnings test

text: **The sell-off beats the dividend (the arithmetic).** For a company reinvesting above its cost of capital and trading above book, a shareholder who sells a sliver of stock each year ends up with both more cash and more capital than one taking a dividend — and is taxed only on the gain, not the whole distribution. Worked out over ten years on a hypothetical 12%-ROE business in the 2012 letter: "Voila! – you would have both more cash to spend annually and more capital value." Dividends also "impose a specific cash-out policy upon all shareholders," thwarting those who want more or less (2012).
quotes: Voila! – you would have both more cash to spend annually and more capital value.
impose a specific cash-out policy upon all shareholders,
title: The sell-off beats the dividend (the arithmetic)

text:
**Buybacks as reverse dilution — but only below intrinsic value.** "Charlie and I favor repurchases when… its stock is selling at a material discount to the company's intrinsic business value, conservatively calculated" (2011); "what is smart at one price is dumb at another."
- *Worked example:* Berkshire's Apple stake "rose to 5.4%… That increase was costless to us, coming about because Apple has continuously repurchased its shares" (2020). The counter-discipline: "American CEOs have an embarrassing record of devoting more company funds to repurchases when prices have risen than when they have tanked. Our approach is exactly the reverse" (2020).
quotes: Charlie and I favor repurchases when… its stock is selling at a material discount to the company's intrinsic business value, conservatively calculated
what is smart at one price is dumb at another.
rose to 5.4%… That increase was costless to us, coming about because Apple has continuously repurchased its shares
American CEOs have an embarrassing record of devoting more company funds to repurchases when prices have risen than when they have tanked. Our approach is exactly the reverse
title: Buybacks as reverse dilution — but only below intrinsic value

text: **The institutional imperative.** His 1989 name for the gravity that makes rational managers behave irrationally: institutions resist changing direction "as if governed by Newton's First Law of Motion"; "corporate projects or acquisitions will materialize to soak up available funds"; "any business craving of the leader, however foolish, will be quickly supported by detailed rate-of-return and strategic studies"; and peer behavior "will be mindlessly imitated." Recognizing it is half of resisting it. He applies it to CEO pay in 2025 (see Signature quotes).
quotes: as if governed by Newton's First Law of Motion
corporate projects or acquisitions will materialize to soak up available funds
any business craving of the leader, however foolish, will be quickly supported by detailed rate-of-return and strategic studies
will be mindlessly imitated.
title: The institutional imperative

text: **Interest rates as gravity.** Rates are the master variable beneath every asset price. At the 1999 dot-com peak: rates "act on financial valuations the way gravity acts on matter: The higher the rate, the greater the downward pull," and he pegged the most probable long-run stock return at "6%" — heresy at the time ([Fortune 1999](https://fortune.com/article/warren-buffett-on-stock-market/)). The corollary he built the same year: over 1964–1981 the Dow went nowhere (874→875) while GDP rose ~370% because long rates rose to ~15%; 1981–1998 the Dow rose tenfold as rates fell — so extrapolating the bull run forward was "the Tinker Bell approach — clap if you believe."
quotes: act on financial valuations the way gravity acts on matter: The higher the rate, the greater the downward pull,
the Tinker Bell approach — clap if you believe.
title: Interest rates as gravity

text: **"The Secret Sauce" — a few huge winners carry everything.** The record came not from a high batting average but a handful of decades-long compounders. "The weeds wither away in significance as the flowers bloom. Over time, it takes just a few winners to work wonders" (2022). Coca-Cola and Amex (bought ~1994–95): Coke dividends grew from $75M (1994) to $704M (2022), Amex $41M to $302M — on a fixed cost basis. "Our satisfactory results have been the product of about a dozen truly good decisions — that would be about one every five years" (2022).
quotes: The Secret Sauce
The weeds wither away in significance as the flowers bloom. Over time, it takes just a few winners to work wonders
Our satisfactory results have been the product of about a dozen truly good decisions — that would be about one every five years
title: "The Secret Sauce" — a few huge winners carry everything

text: **Four-filter buy test (1977):** a business "(1) one that we can understand, (2) with favorable long-term prospects, (3) operated by honest and competent people, and (4) available at a very attractive price." Later compressed into the **four building blocks of value** (2017): sizable stand-alone acquisitions; bolt-ons; internal sales growth and margin improvement; and investment earnings from the portfolio.
quotes: (1) one that we can understand, (2) with favorable long-term prospects, (3) operated by honest and competent people, and (4) available at a very attractive price.
title: Four-filter buy test (1977)

text: Folksy, plain-spoken, self-deprecating, teacherly — a brilliant analyst who deliberately talks like your smartest uncle so the lesson lands. He reaches for homely analogies (Mr. Market, the castle-and-moat, the gold cube, an elephant gun, robins and spring, "jumbo shrimp" and "lady mudwrestler" for institutional-investor oxymorons) and Midwestern understatement. He teaches by parable (Aesop; the Li'l Abner compounding tables; the golfer who "restructures" a 140 into four 80s; the commuter who cheers higher gas prices because his tank is full) and quotes a fixed cast — Graham, Keynes ("I would rather be vaguely right than precisely wrong"), Mae West ("Too much of a good thing can be wonderful"), Ben Franklin, Munger. He admits errors out loud, by name and with the dollar figure attached — Fannie Mae's "$1.4 billion," Dexter's "$5.7 billion," Precision Castparts' "$11 billion." He is blunt about fees, derivatives, EBITDA, executive pay, forecasters, and his own omissions; he hedges on macro and precise valuations (intrinsic value is "fuzzy," two honest people will differ). Note the register shift over time: the Partnership letters are precise and contractual (the numbered Ground Rules); the mature letters are literary and pedagogical; the Nov 2025 farewell is a memoirist's voice — openly mortal, still wry ("I'm 'going quiet.' Sort of"), closing on aphorism rather than arithmetic. Distinguish him from Munger: Munger is terser and more caustic ("If something is not worth doing at all, it's not worth doing well"; "invert, always invert"), and it was Munger who supplied the strategic pivot ("buy wonderful businesses at fair prices") that Buffett then spent decades narrating.
quotes: I would rather be vaguely right than precisely wrong
Too much of a good thing can be wonderful
I'm 'going quiet.' Sort of
If something is not worth doing at all, it's not worth doing well
invert, always invert
buy wonderful businesses at fair prices

text: **Tax hypocrisy, by the numbers.** ProPublica's "Secret IRS Files" found that 2014–2018 Buffett's wealth rose **$24.3 billion** while he paid **$23.7 million** in tax — "a true tax rate of 0.1%," the lowest of the 25 wealthiest Americans, "perhaps surprising, given his public stance as an advocate of higher taxes for the rich." The mechanism (no Berkshire dividend, rarely selling, the giving pledge) is exactly the buy-and-never-sell philosophy he preaches — which is what produces the 0.1% and the tension with "Stop Coddling the Super-Rich" (2011). His defense: the code "should be changed substantially" and the money will do more good "disbursed philanthropically." A separate ProPublica piece notes many Berkshire subsidiaries don't offer the low-cost index funds in their 401(k)s that he tells everyone else to buy.

text: **Decades-long tech avoidance was costly.** Google, Amazon, early Microsoft, and a money-losing IBM stake (bought ~2011, exited 2018). He concedes the misses; Munger flagged in 2014 that Berkshire's net worth "would now be at least $50 billion higher" absent errors of omission (e.g., not buying Walmart). The very discipline that built the record kept Berkshire underweight the basket that won the 2010s–20s. (Apple, bought 2016+, is the late correction.)
quotes: would now be at least $50 billion higher
title: Decades-long tech avoidance was costly

text: **The airlines round-trip.** After decades of shunning airlines as commodity/capital-intensive, he bought ~10% of the big four (~2016), then sold the entire stake at the 2020 trough — by his own account it was his mistake and his decision alone (2020 meeting; paraphrase — exact transcript wording could not be verified, see Provenance). The stocks recovered substantially within ~18 months.
title: The airlines round-trip

text: **Derivatives "rules for thee."** He booked >$10B in mark-to-market losses on equity-index puts during 2008 while lecturing the world on derivative danger (Yahoo Finance). On his own reading it's structure, not hypocrisy — his puts had no collateral triggers and 15–20-year maturities, ring-fencing the systemic risk he condemns — but the optics were real and his counterparties bore Berkshire-credit risk.
quotes: rules for thee.
title: Derivatives "rules for thee."

text: **Governance/transparency gaps he champions elsewhere.** Berkshire's board is widely described as handpicked friends/family; in 2023 shareholders rejected an independent-chair proposal ~10-to-1 (US News), and he recommended voting against TCFD-aligned climate-disclosure proposals despite substantial independent-shareholder support — a transparency stance at odds with his "candor" creed.
title: Governance/transparency gaps he champions elsewhere

text: **Philanthropy critique — from inside the family.** His son Peter Buffett called big billionaire philanthropy "conscience laundering" and "Philanthropic Colonialism" that "keeps the existing structure of inequality in place" (NYT 2013). Warren's own delegation logic ("finding someone better equipped than you… Who wouldn't select Tiger Woods…?", Fortune 2006) has a documented coda: he resigned as a Gates Foundation trustee in 2021 and redirected the estate to his children's foundations — a partial walk-back of the "give it through Gates" mechanism, though not of the >99% pledge.
quotes: keeps the existing structure of inequality in place
finding someone better equipped than you… Who wouldn't select Tiger Woods…?
give it through Gates
title: Philanthropy critique — from inside the family

text: **Scale now caps returns — by his own admission.** "A fat wallet… is the enemy of superior investment results" (1994); "there will be many companies that have done better than Berkshire; our size takes its toll" (2025). Berkshire trailed the S&P over much of the past decade.
quotes: A fat wallet… is the enemy of superior investment results
there will be many companies that have done better than Berkshire; our size takes its toll
title: Scale now caps returns — by his own admission

text: **Key-man / succession risk.** The "single winning decision"/one-genius model is the flip side of concentration risk. The handoff to Abel completed Jan 1, 2026; Buffett calls it "100% successful," but the fact that he keeps A-shares "until Berkshire shareholders develop the comfort with Greg" (2025) tells you the market's worry that capital-allocation skill and culture were personal to Buffett and Munger.
quotes: single winning decision
until Berkshire shareholders develop the comfort with Greg
title: Key-man / succession risk

text: **A recurring governance failure he names himself.** "a wonderful and loyal CEO… will succumb to dementia, Alzheimer's or another debilitating and long-term disease. Charlie and I encountered this problem several times and failed to act. This failure can be a huge mistake" (2025) — a rare admission of a *repeated* weakness, not a one-off.
quotes: a wonderful and loyal CEO… will succumb to dementia, Alzheimer's or another debilitating and long-term disease. Charlie and I encountered this problem several times and failed to act. This failure can be a huge mistake
title: A recurring governance failure he names himself

text: **Source base is thick and overwhelmingly first-person.** 63 sources: 34 Berkshire annual/owner documents (nearly the full 1977→2024 letter run plus the Owner's Manual, letters index, and the Nov 2025 farewell), the 1957–1970 Partnership letters, three annual-meeting transcripts (2009, 2020, 2025), the 1998 U. Florida talk, two long crisis interviews (Charlie Rose 2008, CNBC/Tokyo 2023), the CNBC Buffett Archive index, four op-eds/Fortune essays (Buy American 2008, Stop Coddling 2011, Fortune 1999, Fortune 2001), three philanthropy sources, the 1991 Salomon testimony, the 1984 Superinvestors talk, the Cunningham essays, and eight critique/secondary sources. Compiled from ~9 research batches (extraction dates 2026-07-07).
title: Source base is thick and overwhelmingly first-person

text: **Fetch caveat.** Throughout the research, `berkshirehathaway.com` was unreachable from the extraction environment; every letter was recovered byte-for-byte via the Wayback Machine raw endpoint or faithful full-text mirrors (GitHub buffett-letters, GuruFocus, Motley Fool, CNBC/Yahoo reproductions), with the canonical Berkshire URL attached to each. Quotes cross-confirmed across ≥2 mirrors are high-confidence; the highest-value verbatim lines (owner-earnings 1986, Mr. Market 1987, franchise 1991, value/growth 1992, moat 1993, intrinsic-value 1994, the 2011 gold-cube, 2016/2017 Bet figures, 2018 American Tailwind, 2019 retained-earnings, 2020 Apple/PCC) trace to primary-letter text via those mirrors.
title: Fetch caveat

text: **Munger vs. Buffett attribution kept explicit.** The "buy wonderful businesses at fair prices" blueprint, "if something is not worth doing at all, it's not worth doing well," the four-factor "why Berkshire worked" retrospective, and the "world-leading" successor verdict are **Munger's**, quoted by Buffett (chiefly 2014 and 2023). "Charlie was the 'architect'… I… the 'general contractor'" (2023) is Buffett on Munger.

if something is not worth doing at all, it's not worth doing well,
why Berkshire worked
Charlie was the 'architect'… I… the 'general contractor'
title: Munger vs. Buffett attribution kept explicit

text: **Year corrections carried in.** "The American Tailwind" is the **2018** letter; "The Power of Retained Earnings" the **2019**; the Aesop "bird in the hand" rule the **2000** letter (commonly misattributed) — all placed correctly here.

The Power of Retained Earnings
bird in the hand
title: Year corrections carried in

text: **Two distinct Fortune essays.** The Nov 22 1999 "Mr. Buffett on the Stock Market" and the Dec 10 2001 "Warren Buffett on the Stock Market" (both distilled by Carol Loomis) overlap in the interest-rate-gravity and two-17-year-periods arguments but are separate publications; both are cited.
quotes: Mr. Buffett on the Stock Market
Warren Buffett on the Stock Market
title: Two distinct Fortune essays

text: **Documented evolutions, not contradictions.** He was **pro** mark-to-market in 2008 (Charlie Rose — "I believe in Mark to market") and **against** the 2018 GAAP rule routing unrealized gains through net income ("worse-than-useless," 2023): the nuance is disclosure/valuation honesty (2008) vs. reported-earnings distortion (2018+). His "franchise" (1991) is the earlier vocabulary for the "moat" (1993→2007). Note also the drift from decades of deficit-doom preaching (which he retracts in 2018) to "fiscal policy… scares me more than monetary policy" (CNBC 2023).
quotes: I believe in Mark to market
fiscal policy… scares me more than monetary policy
title: Documented evolutions, not contradictions

text: **Marked non-verbatim items.** The 1997 "truck across the Grand-Canyon bridge" margin-of-safety image and the 2018 Musk "candy" moats exchange are well-attested via secondary transcripts but are **not** in this dossier's verified verbatim set — treated as paraphrase. The Giving Pledge letter's "claim checks"/"ovarian lottery" phrasings and the `webdonat.html` 2006 gift-letter mechanics were recoverable only in fragments/secondary paraphrase and are used accordingly. The Sokol affair is public-record context, not re-verified to a primary URL (see Blind spots). The **2020 annual-meeting airline-sale line** ("That was my mistake… I'm the one who made the decision") could not be confirmed against the raw source: `buffett.cnbc.com` serves only a JS shell with `transcript: null` (the transcript loads per-video via a separate API that returns 403), and every Wayback snapshot holds the same shell — retried via direct `curl` and `web.archive.org`. It is therefore carried as **paraphrase**, consistent with widely reported coverage but not raw-source-verified. The source URL itself is valid and retained.
quotes: truck across the Grand-Canyon bridge
That was my mistake… I'm the one who made the decision
title: Marked non-verbatim items

text: **Criticism is real and sourced.** *Buffett's Alpha* (NBER), the ProPublica IRS and 401(k) pieces, the Quartz Wells Fargo article, US News on the rejected independent-chair/climate proposals, the Yahoo Finance derivatives piece, Peter Buffett's NYT op-ed, and Buffett's own by-name confessions (Fannie Mae, Dexter, USAir, McDonald's, airlines, Precision Castparts, incapacitated-CEO inaction) are the backbone of Blind spots. "Sweetheart 2008 deal terms" and "value investing in crisis" are presented as critics' arguments, not settled fact.
